## Webcam Preview and Frame Capture to JPEG in C# WinForms
**URL:** https://www.visioforge.com/help/docs/dotnet/videocapture/video-tutorials/camera-video-preview/
**Description:** Show a live webcam preview in a C# WinForms app with VideoCaptureCore and save the current frame to a JPEG file with Frame_SaveAsync.
**Tags:** Video Capture SDK, .NET, VideoCaptureCore, Windows, WinForms, Capture, Webcam, Snapshot, JPEG, C#, NuGet
**API:** VideoCaptureCore, VideoCaptureSource, VideoView

# Webcam Preview and Frame Capture in C# WinForms

[Video Capture SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/video-capture-sdk-net)

## Overview

This tutorial shows a live webcam preview in a C# WinForms app with the VideoCaptureCore engine and saves the current frame to a JPEG file:

- the camera, its format and its frame rate are picked from lists;
- `VideoPreview` mode shows the camera without writing a file, so no encoder and no output format are needed;
- a Save Frame button writes the current frame with `Frame_SaveAsync`, at the camera's own resolution, to a new timestamped file in the Pictures folder;
- the app opens the saved file in the default image viewer.

Photo booths and ID photos, scanning a document or a label, inspection stations that keep a picture of each part, and any app that needs a still to process or to put into a report work this way.

This tutorial uses the Windows-only VideoCaptureCore engine, the SDK's DirectShow engine.

## Video Walkthrough

## Source Code Repository

The complete project, with the designer file, is on GitHub:

[Source code on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Video%20Capture%20SDK/_VideoTutorials/camera-video-preview-winforms)

## Required Packages

Install the [VisioForge.DotNet.Core](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core/) package and the video capture redist with its DirectShow filters. A preview writes no file, so it needs no encoder package.

Set `PlatformTarget` in the project file to match the redist (`x64` or `x86`).

```
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x64
```

For a 32-bit (x86) application, use the x86 package instead: `VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x86`.

`VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture`, the package in the Try it block at the top of this page, works as well: it installs the same `VisioForge.DotNet.Core`. The redist packages are needed either way.

## Implementation Example with C# Code

The form has a `VideoView`, combo boxes for the camera, format and frame rate, and Start, Stop and Save Frame buttons; Stop and Save Frame start disabled. The designer file is in the source code above. The project targets .NET 10 with implicit usings. On .NET Framework 4.7.2, the same code builds in an SDK-style project with `<LangVersion>10</LangVersion>` and `<ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>`; in `Program.cs`, replace `ApplicationConfiguration.Initialize()`, which .NET Framework does not generate, with `Application.EnableVisualStyles()` and `Application.SetCompatibleTextRenderingDefault(false)`, and set `<dpiAware>true</dpiAware>` in an `app.manifest` to keep the system DPI awareness that .NET 10 sets.

```
using System.ComponentModel;
using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Drawing.Imaging;
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoCapture;
using VisioForge.Core.UI;
using VisioForge.Core.VideoCapture;

namespace WebcamPreview;

public partial class Form1 : Form
{
    private VideoCaptureCore videoCapture1 = null!;

    public Form1()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private void Form1_Load(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        videoCapture1 = new VideoCaptureCore(VideoView1 as IVideoView);

        // Show SDK errors in the title bar
        videoCapture1.OnError += (_, args) => BeginInvoke(() => Text = args.Message);

        foreach (var device in videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices())
            cbCamera.Items.Add(device.Name);

        if (cbCamera.Items.Count > 0) cbCamera.SelectedIndex = 0;
    }

    private void cbCamera_SelectedIndexChanged(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        cbFormat.Items.Clear();
        cbFrameRate.Items.Clear();
        var device = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices().First(d => d.Name == cbCamera.Text);
        foreach (var format in device.VideoFormats)
            cbFormat.Items.Add(format.Name);

        var index = cbFormat.Items.IndexOf("1920x1080 MJPG, 24 bit");
        if (cbFormat.Items.Count > 0) cbFormat.SelectedIndex = index >= 0 ? index : 0;
    }

    private void cbFormat_SelectedIndexChanged(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        cbFrameRate.Items.Clear();
        var device = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices().First(d => d.Name == cbCamera.Text);
        var format = device.VideoFormats.First(f => f.Name == cbFormat.Text);
        foreach (var frameRate in format.FrameRates)
            cbFrameRate.Items.Add(frameRate);

        var rate = cbFrameRate.Items.IndexOf(VideoFrameRate.FPS_30);
        if (cbFrameRate.Items.Count > 0) cbFrameRate.SelectedIndex = rate >= 0 ? rate : 0;
    }

    private async void btStart_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        Text = cbFrameRate.SelectedItem is null ? "No camera, format or frame rate" : "Webcam preview";
        if (cbFrameRate.SelectedItem is null) return;

        videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevice = new VideoCaptureSource(cbCamera.Text);
        var camera = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevice;
        camera.Format_UseBest = false;
        camera.Format = cbFormat.Text;
        camera.FrameRate = (VideoFrameRate)cbFrameRate.SelectedItem;

        // Video only: audio playback is on by default
        videoCapture1.Audio_PlayAudio = false;
        videoCapture1.Mode = VideoCaptureMode.VideoPreview;

        btStart.Enabled = false;
        var started = await videoCapture1.StartAsync();
        btStop.Enabled = started;
        btSaveFrame.Enabled = started;
        btStart.Enabled = !started;
    }

    private async void btSaveFrame_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        // A new JPEG in Pictures on every click, at the camera's own resolution
        var file = Path.Combine(
            Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.MyPictures),
            $"frame-{DateTime.Now:yyyyMMdd-HHmmss-fff}.jpg");

        if (!await videoCapture1.Frame_SaveAsync(file, ImageFormat.Jpeg, 85)) return;

        // Open it in the default viewer; with no app for .jpg, the path in the title is all there is
        Text = file;
        try { Process.Start(new ProcessStartInfo(file) { UseShellExecute = true }); }
        catch (Win32Exception) { }
    }

    private async void btStop_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        btStop.Enabled = false;
        btSaveFrame.Enabled = false;
        await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
        btStart.Enabled = true;
    }

    private void Form1_FormClosing(object sender, FormClosingEventArgs e)
    {
        // Starting or stopping: wait for it before closing
        if (!btStart.Enabled && !btStop.Enabled)
        {
            e.Cancel = true;
            return;
        }

        // Dispose stops a running preview: there is no file to finish
        videoCapture1.Dispose();
    }
}
```

## Key Implementation Features

1. **Preview mode** - `Mode = VideoCaptureMode.VideoPreview` puts the camera on screen and writes no file, so there is no `Output_Filename` and no `Output_Format` to set. The frames still reach the app, which is what `Frame_SaveAsync` uses. Switch the mode to `VideoCapture`, add an output file and a format, and the same app records
2. **Camera format** - with `Format_UseBest` left on, the engine picks the highest resolution up to 1080p by itself; the sample turns it off and passes the format and the frame rate picked in the lists
3. **Audio** - `Audio_PlayAudio` is `true` by default and plays the audio source selected in `Audio_CaptureDevice` through the speakers, or, for a capture card whose video filter has an audio pin, the video source itself (`IsAudioSource`; a USB webcam microphone is a separate audio device). The sample shows video only, so it turns it off; left on with neither, the engine raises `OnError` ("The audio source is not configured"), sets `Audio_PlayAudio` to `false` and runs without sound
4. **Saving a frame** - `Frame_SaveAsync(filename, format, quality = 85, customWidth = 0, customHeight = 0)` writes the current frame in any `ImageFormat`, like JPEG, PNG, BMP or TIFF. The quality applies to JPEG only. Set both a width and a height to resize the frame; without them, the file has the camera's resolution (1920x1080 here), not the size of the preview on screen
5. **When saving fails** - `Frame_SaveAsync` returns `false` and raises `OnError` when the preview is not running or no frame has arrived yet. The sample enables Save Frame only after `StartAsync` returns `true`
6. **New file per click** - the file name carries the date and time down to the millisecond, so a frame never replaces the previous one
7. **Opening the file** - `Process.Start` with `UseShellExecute = true` opens the JPEG in the default image viewer. On a PC with no app for `.jpg` it throws a `Win32Exception`, and the path in the title bar is what is left
8. **Closing** - `Dispose()` stops a running preview, and a preview has no file to finish, so the close handler only waits while the preview is starting or stopping

## Frames in Memory

To work on a frame without a file:

- `Frame_GetCurrent()` returns the current frame as a `System.Drawing.Bitmap`;
- the `OnVideoFrameBitmap` event hands you every frame as it arrives.

## Video Transcript

### What we build

Let's show a live webcam preview in a C# WinForms app, and save frames from it, with the VisioForge Video Capture SDK. Here's what we build. A WinForms app with a live webcam preview. You pick the camera, its format and its frame rate from lists. A Save Frame button writes the current frame to a JPEG file, and the app opens that file in the default image viewer, so you can see what was saved. This is the finished app, previewing a Logitech C920 at 1920 by 1080. Nothing is recorded. The preview only shows the picture, and a frame is saved when you ask for one. Where does this help? Photo booths and ID photos. Scanning a document or a label with a webcam. Inspection stations that keep a picture of each part. And any app that needs a still to process, or to put into a report.

### Prerequisites

You need Windows 10 or 11, and Visual Studio 2022 or 2026 with the .NET desktop development workload. The project can target .NET 8 or later, or .NET Framework 4.7.2. And a webcam. VideoCaptureCore is the SDK's DirectShow engine, so this app runs on Windows only.

### Create a WinForms project

In Visual Studio, create a new project. Search for Windows Forms, and pick Windows Forms App for C#. Name the project WebcamPreview. Choose .NET 10 and click Create. Visual Studio opens the empty form in the designer.

### Add the NuGet packages

Now add two NuGet packages: the SDK itself, and the video capture redist with its DirectShow filters. A preview writes no file, so it needs no encoder package. In Visual Studio, that's Manage NuGet Packages. Browse for VisioForge.DotNet.Core and install it. Then install the video capture redist for x64. The redist is x64, so set PlatformTarget to x64 in the project file. An x86 app takes the x86 redist instead.

### Design the WinForms form

From the Toolbox, draw a VideoView for the live preview. Add a label and a combo box for the camera, and give every control a clear name in the Properties window. Do the same for the camera format and the frame rate. Add the Start, Stop and Save Frame buttons. Stop and Save Frame stay disabled until the preview runs. Double-click the form, the camera and format lists, and the three buttons. Visual Studio adds an empty handler for each one.

### Create the capture engine

At the top of Form1.cs, add these usings. System.Diagnostics opens the saved file, System.ComponentModel has the exception it can throw, and System.Drawing.Imaging names the image format. In the form's Load handler, create the VideoCaptureCore engine and pass it the VideoView, where the live preview is drawn. Engine errors arrive in the OnError event. Here they go to the title bar.

### List the camera formats

Video\_CaptureDevices returns every camera. We list their names and select the first. When the camera changes, its handler fills the format list with the formats of that camera, and picks 1920x1080 MJPG when it's there. When the format changes, its handler fills the frame rate list the same way, and picks thirty frames per second.

### Start the preview

The Start handler first checks that a frame rate is selected. Then it selects the camera by name, turns Format\_UseBest off, and passes the format and the frame rate from the lists. Left on, Format\_UseBest picks the highest resolution up to 1080p by itself. Audio\_PlayAudio is on by default: it plays the selected audio source through the speakers. This app shows video only, so it goes off. Left on with no audio source selected, the SDK reports an error and runs without sound. Mode VideoPreview shows the camera without writing a file. StartAsync returns once the preview is running, and then Stop and Save Frame are enabled. VideoPreview puts the camera on screen and writes no file, so there's no encoder and no output format to set. The frames still reach the app, which is what Save Frame uses. Switch the mode to VideoCapture, add an output file and a format, and the same app records.

### Save a frame

Save Frame builds a file name in the Pictures folder, with the date and time down to the millisecond, so every click makes a new file. Frame\_SaveAsync writes the current frame there as a JPEG, at quality 85, and returns false when it can't. Then the path goes to the title bar, and Process.Start with UseShellExecute opens the file in the default image viewer. On a PC with no app for JPEG files, Process.Start throws a Win32Exception, and the path in the title is what's left. Frame\_SaveAsync takes the file name and an image format, like JPEG, PNG, BMP or TIFF. The quality applies to JPEG only, and it's 85 by default. Set both a width and a height, and the frame is resized to them. Without them, the file has the camera's resolution, not the size of the preview on screen. It returns false, and raises OnError, when the preview isn't running or no frame has arrived yet.

### Stop and close

Stop disables Stop and Save Frame, and StopAsync stops the camera. In the Properties window, on the Events tab, double-click FormClosing to add this handler. While the preview is starting or stopping, both buttons are disabled, and the handler waits by cancelling the close. Otherwise it disposes the engine. Dispose stops a running preview, and there's no file to finish.

### Run it

Run the app from Visual Studio. The camera and format lists fill in from the devices. Start begins the preview. The C920 takes a few seconds to send its first frame, and then the picture appears. Click Save Frame. The JPEG opens in Photos. Its size is 1920 by 1080, the camera's format, although the preview on the form is much smaller. Close Photos, stop the preview, and close the window.

### Common mistakes

A few common mistakes. Audio\_PlayAudio left on with no audio source selected, so OnError reports a missing audio source. Saving before Start, or before the camera sends its first frame, so Frame\_SaveAsync returns false. One file name for every click, so each frame replaces the last. And a quality value with PNG or BMP, where it's ignored.

### Next steps

Next, the webcam to MP4 video records what you preview, and the text overlay video draws a caption, a clock and frame numbers over it. To work on a frame in memory instead of a file, Frame\_GetCurrent returns it as a Bitmap. And the OnVideoFrameBitmap event hands you every frame as it arrives. The full source is on GitHub, and the docs are at visioforge.com/help. Thanks for watching.

## Record IP Camera RTSP to MP4 in C# .NET — Code Sample
**URL:** https://www.visioforge.com/help/docs/dotnet/videocapture/video-tutorials/ip-camera-capture-mp4/
**Description:** Record an RTSP IP camera to MP4 in a C# WinForms app with VideoCaptureCoreX - URL, login and password, live preview, the camera's audio, H.264 on the GPU.
**Tags:** Video Capture SDK, .NET, VideoCaptureCoreX, Windows, WinForms, Capture, Streaming, IP Camera, RTSP, ONVIF, MP4, H.264, C#, NuGet
**API:** VideoCaptureCoreX, RTSPSourceSettings, MP4Output, VisioForgeX

# Record an IP Camera RTSP Stream to MP4 in C# WinForms

[Video Capture SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/video-capture-sdk-net)

## Overview

This tutorial records an IP camera to an MP4 file in a C# WinForms app with the cross-platform `VideoCaptureCoreX` engine:

- the camera's RTSP URL, its login and its password are typed into the form, and the password field shows dots;
- `RTSPSourceSettings.CreateAsync` connects to the camera and reads what the stream carries, so a camera without a microphone is recorded video-only;
- a `VideoView` shows a live preview while the file is written;
- `MP4Output` encodes H.264 on the GPU when the PC has a hardware encoder, OpenH264 on the CPU otherwise, with AAC audio;
- every recording gets its own file name, with the date and time, in the Videos folder.

The classic `VideoCaptureCore` engine records IP cameras as well: the [IP camera preview tutorial](../ip-camera-preview/) builds its app, and its `IPCapture` mode writes the file.

## Video Walkthrough

### The short version

The same recording as a console app in a few lines of C#, without the preview and the sound. The login and password are written in its code: replace `admin` and `password` with your camera's.

Its code: [ip-camera-mp4-short-console on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Video%20Capture%20SDK%20X/_VideoTutorials/ip-camera-mp4-short-console).

## Source Code Repository

The complete project, with the designer file, is on GitHub:

[Source code on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Video%20Capture%20SDK%20X/_VideoTutorials/ip-camera-capture-mp4-winforms)

## Required Packages

- [VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture/) — the SDK; the WinForms `VideoView` ships in it
- [VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Core.Windows.x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Core.Windows.x64/) — the GStreamer runtime the X engine runs on, with the RTSP source and the H.264 encoders
- [VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Libav.Windows.x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Libav.Windows.x64/) — the AAC audio encoder

These are the x64 packages, so the project sets `<PlatformTarget>x64</PlatformTarget>`; a 32-bit app takes the `.x86` packages instead. See [Windows deployment](../../../deployment-x/Windows/) for the full list.

```

dotnet add package VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Core.Windows.x64
dotnet add package VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Libav.Windows.x64
```

## Implementation Example with C# Code

The form has a `VideoView` named `VideoView1`, the text boxes `edURL`, `edLogin` and `edPassword` (with `UseSystemPasswordChar`), a **Record audio** check box `cbRecordAudio`, and the buttons `btStart` and `btStop`, both disabled in the designer. The form's `Load` and `FormClosing` events are wired to the handlers below.

```
using VisioForge.Core;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.X.Output;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.X.Sources;
using VisioForge.Core.VideoCaptureX;

namespace IpCameraCaptureMp4;

public partial class Form1 : Form
{
    private VideoCaptureCoreX videoCapture1 = null!;

    private string outputFile = string.Empty;

    public Form1()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private async void Form1_Load(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        await VisioForgeX.InitSDKAsync();

        videoCapture1 = new VideoCaptureCoreX(VideoView1);

        // Show SDK errors in the title bar
        videoCapture1.OnError += (_, args) => BeginInvoke(() => Text = args.Message);

        btStart.Enabled = true;
    }

    private async void btStart_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        if (!Uri.TryCreate(edURL.Text, UriKind.Absolute, out var url))
        {
            Text = "Enter the camera URL";
            return;
        }

        Text = "Connecting...";
        btStart.Enabled = false;
        cbRecordAudio.Enabled = false;

        var started = false;
        try
        {
            // Reads the stream info first: audio is recorded only when the info shows an audio track
            videoCapture1.Video_Source = await RTSPSourceSettings.CreateAsync(url, edLogin.Text, edPassword.Text, cbRecordAudio.Checked);

            videoCapture1.Audio_Record = cbRecordAudio.Checked;
            videoCapture1.Audio_Play = false; // record the camera's sound, don't play it

            // H.264 on the GPU encoder when there is one, OpenH264 otherwise; AAC audio
            outputFile = Path.Combine(Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.MyVideos), $"ipcam_{DateTime.Now:yyyyMMdd_HHmmss}.mp4");
            videoCapture1.Outputs_Clear();
            videoCapture1.Outputs_Add(new MP4Output(outputFile));

            started = await videoCapture1.StartAsync();
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            Text = ex.Message;
        }

        // An SDK error posted during the start stays in the title
        if (Text == "Connecting...") Text = started ? "Recording..." : "The recording did not start";
        btStop.Enabled = started;
        btStart.Enabled = !started;
        cbRecordAudio.Enabled = !started;
    }

    private async void btStop_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        btStop.Enabled = false;
        await videoCapture1.StopAsync(); // finishes the MP4 file
        Text = "Saved: " + outputFile;
        btStart.Enabled = true;
        cbRecordAudio.Enabled = true;
    }

    private async void Form1_FormClosing(object sender, FormClosingEventArgs e)
    {
        if (!btStart.Enabled && !btStop.Enabled)
        {
            e.Cancel = true; // loading, starting or stopping: wait for it
            return;
        }

        if (btStop.Enabled)
        {
            e.Cancel = true; // recording: finish the MP4 first
            btStop.Enabled = false;
            await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
            btStart.Enabled = true;
            BeginInvoke(Close);
            return;
        }

        videoCapture1.Dispose();
        VisioForgeX.DestroySDK();
    }
}
```

## Key Implementation Features

1. **SDK initialization** - `VisioForgeX.InitSDKAsync` runs once, when the form loads. The first run on a PC takes longer, so Start is enabled only after it returns. `VisioForgeX.DestroySDK` releases it when the form closes
2. **The camera's address** - `rtsp://`, the camera's IP address and port (usually 554), then a path that differs per brand. The login and the password are separate arguments of `CreateAsync`, so the URL does not carry them. An `http://` address is taken as the camera's ONVIF service, and the RTSP URL of its best profile is read from it. The [IP camera brands directory](../../../camera-brands/) lists the paths of many cameras
3. **Audio** - with **Record audio** checked, `CreateAsync` asks for the camera's audio and `Audio_Record` puts it in the file. The audio is recorded only when the stream info shows an audio track, so a camera without a microphone gives a video-only file. `Audio_Play` is `true` by default; the app sets it to `false`, so the sound is recorded but not played
4. **MP4 output** - `MP4Output` with no encoder settings picks NVIDIA NVENC, then AMD AMF, then Intel Quick Sync, and OpenH264 on the CPU when none of them is present. Audio is AAC. An output stays in the engine after a recording, so `Outputs_Clear` runs before each new one
5. **Starting** - a camera that does not answer takes a while to fail, so the title says "Connecting..." and Start is disabled until `StartAsync` returns. An `OnError` message posted during the start stays in the title
6. **Stopping and closing** - `StopAsync` finalizes the MP4 file. Closing the form during a recording cancels the close, awaits `StopAsync`, and closes again; while the SDK is loading, or a start or a stop is under way, the close waits

## Troubleshooting

- **The camera refuses the stream** - the path does not match the camera's brand, or the login or password is wrong. The error is shown in the window title
- **The file has no sound** - the camera sends no audio track, or audio is turned off in the camera's own settings
- **Choosing the encoder** - to stay on the CPU, pass `new OpenH264EncoderSettings()` (namespace `VisioForge.Core.Types.X.VideoEncoders`) to the `MP4Output` constructor; `H264EncoderBlock.CanEncodeAsync` (namespace `VisioForge.Core.MediaBlocks.VideoEncoders`) tests whether a GPU encoder can encode right now
- **Several cameras** - use one `VideoCaptureCoreX` and one `VideoView` for each

## Video Transcript

### What we build

Let's record an IP camera to an MP4 file in a C# WinForms app, with the VisioForge Video Capture SDK. Here's what we build. A WinForms app that records an IP camera to an MP4 file. You type the camera's RTSP address, its login and its password. The picture shows live while the app records. The video is H.264, and the camera's sound is recorded as AAC. This is the finished app, recording. The stream here comes from a test RTSP server on the local network, which plays the open movie Big Buck Bunny, so it needs no login. A real camera works the same way, with its login and password. Where does this help? A simple video recorder for your own cameras. Saving an event to a file as evidence. Recording a production line or a lab test. And clips you review or share later.

### Prerequisites

You need Windows 10 or 11, and Visual Studio 2022 or 2026 with the .NET desktop development workload. The project targets .NET 8 or later. And an IP camera that streams RTSP, with its address. The engine here is VideoCaptureCoreX, the SDK's cross-platform engine, built on GStreamer. The same code runs on macOS and Linux with their own UI.

### Create a WinForms project

In Visual Studio, create a new project. Search for Windows Forms, and pick Windows Forms App for C#. Name the project IpCameraCaptureMp4. Choose .NET 10 and click Create. Visual Studio opens the empty form in the designer.

### Add the NuGet packages

Now add three NuGet packages. The Video Capture SDK itself. The cross-platform core package, with the GStreamer runtime for Windows x64. And the Libav package, which brings the AAC audio encoder. In Visual Studio, that's Manage NuGet Packages. Browse for VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture and install it. Then install the cross-platform core package for Windows x64. And the Libav package for Windows x64. The runtime packages are x64, so set PlatformTarget to x64 in the project file.

### Design the WinForms form

From the Toolbox, draw a VideoView for the live picture. Add a label and a text box for the camera URL, and give every control a clear name in the Properties window. Do the same for the login and the password. On the password box, set UseSystemPasswordChar to True, so it shows dots. Add a Record audio check box, checked by default, and the Start and Stop buttons. Both buttons start disabled. Start is enabled once the SDK has loaded, and Stop once the recording runs. Double-click the form and the two buttons. Visual Studio adds an empty handler for each one.

### Create the capture engine

At the top of Form1.cs, add these usings. The X namespaces hold the cross-platform engine, its sources and its outputs. In the form's Load handler, InitSDKAsync loads the SDK and its GStreamer runtime, once per app. Then create the VideoCaptureCoreX engine and pass it the VideoView. Engine errors arrive in the OnError event, and here they go to the title bar. Finally, Start is enabled. A field keeps the output file name, to show it after the stop.

### Connect to the camera

The Start handler first checks that the URL is a valid address. Connecting can take a few seconds, so the title says Connecting, and Start and the check box are disabled. RTSPSourceSettings.CreateAsync takes the URL, the login, the password, and whether to use audio. The URL has no login or password in it, so they never show up in the address. CreateAsync reads the stream's info first. When the camera sends no sound, audio is left out, and the recording is video only. Audio\_Record follows the check box. Audio\_Play is on by default, and this app records the sound without playing it, so it goes off. The address starts with rtsp, then the camera's IP address and the port, usually 554. Then comes a path, and every brand has its own. Many cameras send a main stream at full resolution and a smaller sub stream. The camera's manual or its web page gives the exact path.

### Record to MP4

The file goes to the Videos folder, with the date and time in its name. Outputs\_Clear removes the output of the last run, and Outputs\_Add adds an MP4Output. With no encoders passed, MP4Output picks H.264 on the GPU encoder when there is one, NVIDIA, AMD or Intel, and OpenH264 otherwise. The sound is AAC. StartAsync connects, and returns once the recording runs. An exception, like a camera that refuses the connection, goes to the title. An error from the SDK during the start stays in the title too. Otherwise the title says Recording. Stop is enabled when the start worked, and Start when it didn't.

### Stop and close

Stop disables itself, and StopAsync stops the stream and finishes the MP4 file. The title then shows where the file was saved, and Start and the check box are enabled again. In the Properties window, on the Events tab, double-click FormClosing to add this handler. While the app is loading, starting or stopping, both buttons are disabled, and the handler cancels the close: close the window again once that is done. While it records, the close is cancelled too. StopAsync finishes the file, and then the form closes itself. Only then are the engine disposed and the SDK released. A file that is not finished cannot be played.

### Run it

Run the app from Visual Studio. Start is enabled once the SDK has loaded. Type the stream's RTSP address. This test stream needs no login. Click Start. The stream connects in a few seconds, the picture appears, and the title says Recording. Click Stop. The file is finished, and the title shows where it was saved, in the Videos folder. And close the window. This file has H.264 video at 1280 by 720, and AAC sound in stereo.

### Common mistakes

A few common mistakes. Leaving out the Libav package, so there is no AAC encoder for the sound. Creating the engine before InitSDKAsync has loaded the SDK. Putting the login and password into the URL, where they show up wherever the address does. And closing the app without StopAsync, which leaves an MP4 file that cannot be played.

### Next steps

Next, pass your own encoder settings to MP4Output, for a bitrate or a codec of your choice. Split a long recording into files by time. For several cameras, use one VideoCaptureCoreX and one VideoView for each. And ONVIF finds the cameras on the network for you. The full source is on GitHub, and the docs are at visioforge.com/help. Thanks for watching.

## RTSP IP Camera Live Preview in C# WinForms: .NET Tutorial
**URL:** https://www.visioforge.com/help/docs/dotnet/videocapture/video-tutorials/ip-camera-preview/
**Description:** Show a live RTSP IP camera in a C# WinForms app with VideoCaptureCore, keep the login and password out of the URL, and pixelate the picture.
**Tags:** Video Capture SDK, .NET, VideoCaptureCore, Windows, WinForms, Capture, IP Camera, RTSP, ONVIF, C#, NuGet
**API:** VideoCaptureCore, IPCameraSourceSettings, IPSourceEngine, VideoCaptureMode, VideoEffectMosaic, IVideoView

# IP Camera Preview over RTSP in C# WinForms

[Video Capture SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/video-capture-sdk-net)

## Overview

This tutorial shows a live IP camera over RTSP in a C# WinForms app with the VideoCaptureCore engine:

- the camera's RTSP URL, its login and its password are typed into the form, and the password field shows dots;
- the login and the password go into their own `IPCameraSourceSettings` properties, never into the URL;
- the LAV engine (`IPSourceEngine.Auto_LAV`) reads the stream;
- `IPPreview` mode shows the camera without writing a file;
- a Pixelate check box puts a `VideoEffectMosaic` over the whole picture.

A security monitor for your own cameras, checking a camera's view while it is installed, hiding faces or screens before the video is shown, and kiosks or lobby screens work this way. The camera in the video is a Dahua on the local network, pixelated on purpose by the app's own effect.

This tutorial uses the Windows-only VideoCaptureCore engine, the SDK's DirectShow engine.

## Video Walkthrough

## Source Code Repository

The complete project, with the designer file, is on GitHub:

[Source code on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Video%20Capture%20SDK/_VideoTutorials/ip-camera-preview-winforms)

## Required Packages

Install the [VisioForge.DotNet.Core](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core/) package, the video capture redist with its DirectShow filters, and the LAV redist, the decoder that reads the RTSP stream. A preview writes no file, so it needs no encoder package.

Set `PlatformTarget` in the project file to match the redists (`x64` or `x86`).

```
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x64
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.LAV.x64
```

For a 32-bit (x86) application, use the x86 packages instead: `VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x86` and `VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.LAV.x86`.

`VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture`, the package in the Try it block at the top of this page, works as well: it installs the same `VisioForge.DotNet.Core`. The redist packages are needed either way.

## Implementation Example with C# Code

The form has a `VideoView`, text boxes for the URL, the login and the password (`UseSystemPasswordChar` on), a Pixelate check box checked by default, and Start and Stop buttons; Stop starts disabled. The designer file is in the source code above. The project targets .NET 10 with implicit usings. On .NET Framework 4.7.2, the same code builds in an SDK-style project with `<LangVersion>10</LangVersion>` and `<ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>`; in `Program.cs`, replace `ApplicationConfiguration.Initialize()`, which .NET Framework does not generate, with `Application.EnableVisualStyles()` and `Application.SetCompatibleTextRenderingDefault(false)`, and set `<dpiAware>true</dpiAware>` in an `app.manifest` to keep the system DPI awareness that .NET 10 sets.

```
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoCapture;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoEffects;
using VisioForge.Core.UI;
using VisioForge.Core.VideoCapture;

namespace IpCameraPreview;

public partial class Form1 : Form
{
    private VideoCaptureCore videoCapture1 = null!;

    public Form1()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private void Form1_Load(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        videoCapture1 = new VideoCaptureCore(VideoView1 as IVideoView);

        // Show SDK errors in the title bar
        videoCapture1.OnError += (_, args) => BeginInvoke(() => Text = args.Message);
    }

    private async void btStart_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        if (!Uri.TryCreate(edURL.Text, UriKind.Absolute, out var url))
        {
            Text = "Enter the camera URL";
            return;
        }

        // The URL stays free of credentials: login and password go separately
        videoCapture1.IP_Camera_Source = new IPCameraSourceSettings
        {
            URL = url,
            Login = edLogin.Text,
            Password = edPassword.Text,
            Type = IPSourceEngine.Auto_LAV
        };

        // Video only: audio playback is on by default
        videoCapture1.Audio_PlayAudio = false;

        // Effects are set before the start
        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Clear();
        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Enabled = cbPixelate.Checked;
        if (cbPixelate.Checked)
            videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Add(new VideoEffectMosaic(true, 40));

        videoCapture1.Mode = VideoCaptureMode.IPPreview;

        // A camera that does not answer takes up to ~20 s to fail
        Text = "Connecting...";
        btStart.Enabled = false;
        cbPixelate.Enabled = false;
        var started = await videoCapture1.StartAsync();

        // An SDK error posted during the start stays in the title
        if (Text == "Connecting...") Text = started ? "IP camera preview" : "The preview did not start";
        btStop.Enabled = started;
        btStart.Enabled = !started;
        cbPixelate.Enabled = !started;
    }

    private async void btStop_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        btStop.Enabled = false;
        await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
        btStart.Enabled = true;
        cbPixelate.Enabled = true;
    }

    private void Form1_FormClosing(object sender, FormClosingEventArgs e)
    {
        // Starting or stopping: wait for it before closing
        if (!btStart.Enabled && !btStop.Enabled)
        {
            e.Cancel = true;
            return;
        }

        // Dispose stops a running preview: there is no file to finish
        videoCapture1.Dispose();
    }
}
```

## Key Implementation Features

1. **Credentials out of the URL** - `Login` and `Password` are properties of `IPCameraSourceSettings`, so the URL never carries them and they never show up wherever the address is shown or logged. The password text box sets `UseSystemPasswordChar`, so it shows dots
2. **The engine** - `IPSourceEngine.Auto_LAV` reads RTSP and HTTP streams with LAV Filters and can decode on the GPU. Without the LAV redist the start fails with "Unable to create LAV Splitter Source filter"
3. **The camera's address** - `rtsp://`, the camera's IP address and port (usually 554), then a path that differs per brand. Many cameras send a full-resolution main stream and a smaller sub stream; the camera's manual or web page gives the exact path, and the [IP camera brands directory](../../../camera-brands/) lists many of them
4. **Preview mode** - `Mode = VideoCaptureMode.IPPreview` shows the camera and writes no file. Add the MP4 redist ([x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.MP4.x64/), [x86](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.MP4.x86/)), switch to `IPCapture`, set an output file and a format, and the same app records; [Record RTSP stream to MP4](../ip-camera-capture-mp4/) shows the same recording on the cross-platform `VideoCaptureCoreX`
5. **Audio** - `Audio_PlayAudio` is `true` by default; the sample shows video only, so it turns it off
6. **Pixelate** - `VideoEffectMosaic(enabled, value)` takes the block size in pixels, from 1 to 255: 2 to 5 is a light effect, 16 and up leaves nothing readable. It covers the whole frame, in the preview and in a recording alike. Effects are set before `StartAsync`, so the check box is locked while the preview runs, and `Video_Effects_Clear` removes the previous run's effect
7. **Starting** - a camera that does not answer takes up to about 20 seconds to fail, so the title says "Connecting..." and Start is disabled until `StartAsync` returns. An `OnError` message posted during the start stays in the title
8. **Closing** - `Dispose()` stops a running preview, and a preview has no file to finish, so the close handler only waits while the preview is starting or stopping

## Troubleshooting

- **The camera connects but the picture stays black** - the LAV engine receives RTSP video over UDP, and a firewall, a NAT or a VPN that blocks UDP stops it; a virtual machine on NAT networking does this too. Allow UDP from the camera, or use `IPSourceEngine.RTSP_LowLatency`, which reads RTSP over TCP by default (`RTSP_LowLatency_UseUDP` is `false`)
- **The camera refuses the stream** - the path does not match the camera's brand, or the login or password is wrong
- **Several cameras** - use one `VideoCaptureCore` and one `VideoView` for each
- **Finding cameras** - `IP_Camera_ONVIF_ListSourcesAsync` discovers ONVIF cameras on the network

## Video Transcript

### What we build

Let's show a live IP camera over RTSP in a C# WinForms app, with the VisioForge Video Capture SDK. Here's what we build. A WinForms app that shows a live IP camera. You type the camera's RTSP address, its login and its password, and the password field shows dots. A Pixelate check box puts a mosaic effect over the picture. This is the finished app, previewing a Dahua camera on the local network. The picture is pixelated on purpose, by the app's own effect, so this real camera shows nothing private. Nothing is recorded. The preview only shows the picture. Where does this help? A security monitor for your own cameras. Checking what a camera sees while you install it. Hiding faces or screens before the video is shown to anyone. And kiosks or lobby screens.

### Prerequisites

You need Windows 10 or 11, and Visual Studio 2022 or 2026 with the .NET desktop development workload. The project can target .NET 8 or later, or .NET Framework 4.7.2. And an IP camera that streams RTSP, with its address, login and password. VideoCaptureCore is the SDK's DirectShow engine, so this app runs on Windows only.

### Create a WinForms project

In Visual Studio, create a new project. Search for Windows Forms, and pick Windows Forms App for C#. Name the project IpCameraPreview. Choose .NET 10 and click Create. Visual Studio opens the empty form in the designer.

### Add the NuGet packages

Now add three NuGet packages. The SDK itself. The video capture redist with its DirectShow filters. And the LAV redist, the decoder that reads the RTSP stream. A preview writes no file, so it needs no encoder package. In Visual Studio, that's Manage NuGet Packages. Browse for VisioForge.DotNet.Core and install it. Then install the video capture redist for x64. And the LAV redist for x64. Without it, the start fails, because there is nothing to read the stream. The redists are x64, so set PlatformTarget to x64 in the project file. An x86 app takes the x86 redists instead.

### Design the WinForms form

From the Toolbox, draw a VideoView for the live picture. Add a label and a text box for the camera URL, and give every control a clear name in the Properties window. Do the same for the login and the password. On the password box, set UseSystemPasswordChar to True, so it shows dots. Add a Pixelate check box, checked by default, and the Start and Stop buttons. Stop stays disabled until the preview runs. Double-click the form and the two buttons. Visual Studio adds an empty handler for each one.

### Create the capture engine

At the top of Form1.cs, add these usings. VideoEffects holds the mosaic effect. In the form's Load handler, create the VideoCaptureCore engine and pass it the VideoView, where the picture is drawn. Engine errors arrive in the OnError event. Here they go to the title bar.

### Connect to the camera

The Start handler first checks that the URL is a valid address. Then IP\_Camera\_Source gets an IPCameraSourceSettings object. The URL has no login or password in it. They go into their own properties, so they never show up in the address. Type Auto\_LAV picks the LAV engine, which reads RTSP and HTTP streams and can decode on the GPU. The address starts with rtsp, then the camera's IP address and the port, usually 554. Then comes a path, and every brand has its own. Many cameras send a main stream at full resolution and a smaller sub stream. The camera's manual or its web page gives the exact path.

### Pixelate the picture

Audio\_PlayAudio is on by default, and this app shows video only, so it goes off. Effects are set before the start. Video\_Effects\_Clear removes the effects of the last run, and Video\_Effects\_Enabled follows the check box. When it's checked, Video\_Effects\_Add adds a VideoEffectMosaic with blocks of 40 pixels. VideoEffectMosaic takes a block size in pixels, from 1 to 255. Two to five is a light effect, and from 16 up nothing is readable. It covers the whole frame, in the preview and in a recording alike. The effect is set before StartAsync, so the check box is locked while the preview runs.

### Start the preview

Mode IPPreview shows the camera without writing a file. A camera that doesn't answer can take about 20 seconds to fail, so the title says Connecting, and Start and the check box are disabled. StartAsync returns once the preview is running. An error from the SDK stays in the title, and Stop is enabled when the start worked.

### Stop and close

Stop disables itself, and StopAsync stops the stream. Then Start and the check box are enabled again. In the Properties window, on the Events tab, double-click FormClosing to add this handler. While the preview is starting or stopping, both buttons are disabled, and the handler waits by cancelling the close. Otherwise it disposes the engine. Dispose stops a running preview, and there's no file to finish.

### Run it

Run the app from Visual Studio, and type the camera's RTSP address. Then the login, and the password, which shows as dots. Click Start. The camera answers in about three seconds, and the live picture appears, pixelated. Stop the preview, and close the window.

### Common mistakes

A few common mistakes. Leaving out the LAV redist, so the start fails. Putting the login and password into the URL, where they show up wherever the address does. A wrong path for the camera's brand, so the camera refuses the stream. And a network that blocks UDP, like a firewall, a NAT or a VPN. The camera connects, but the picture stays black. The RTSP\_LowLatency engine reads RTSP over TCP by default.

### Next steps

Next, add the MP4 redist, switch the mode to IPCapture, set an output file, and the same app records the camera to MP4. Text can be drawn over the video, too. For several cameras, use one VideoCaptureCore and one VideoView for each. And ONVIF finds the cameras on the network for you. The full source is on GitHub, and the docs are at visioforge.com/help. Thanks for watching.

## IP Camera Two-Way Audio in C# WPF — Intercom Sample
**URL:** https://www.visioforge.com/help/docs/dotnet/videocapture/video-tutorials/ip-camera-two-way-audio/
**Description:** Talk through an IP camera speaker from C# WPF - RTSP preview with the camera's sound, PC microphone sent as G.711 over the ONVIF audio backchannel.
**Tags:** Video Capture SDK, .NET, VideoCaptureCoreX, Windows, WPF, Capture, IP Camera, RTSP, ONVIF, Audio, C#, NuGet
**API:** VideoCaptureCoreX, RTSPSourceSettings, AudioRendererSettings, DeviceEnumerator, VisioForgeX

# IP Camera Two-Way Audio in C# WPF

[Video Capture SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/video-capture-sdk-net)

## Overview

This tutorial builds a small intercom in a C# WPF app with the cross-platform `VideoCaptureCoreX` engine:

- the camera's RTSP URL, its login and its password are typed into the window;
- a `VideoView` shows the camera live, and the camera's own microphone plays on the PC speakers picked in the window;
- the PC microphone picked in the window plays on the camera speaker, sent over the ONVIF RTSP audio backchannel;
- Start and Stop open and close both directions at once.

It suits video doorbells, intercom stations and cameras with a speaker or an audio output. How the backchannel works, the Media Blocks version and the speaker volume over ONVIF are on the [two-way audio](../../video-sources/ip-cameras/two-way-audio/) page.

SDK version

`Audio_BackchannelSource` is in the SDK releases after 2026.11.16.

## Source Code Repository

The complete project is on GitHub:

[Source code on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Video%20Capture%20SDK%20X/_VideoTutorials/ip-camera-two-way-audio-wpf)

## Required Packages

- [VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture/) — the SDK; the WPF `VideoView` ships in it
- [VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Core.Windows.x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Core.Windows.x64/) — the GStreamer runtime the X engine runs on, with the RTSP source, the decoders and the G.711 encoder the backchannel uses
- [VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Libav.Windows.x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Libav.Windows.x64/) — the AAC decoder, for cameras that send AAC sound

These are the x64 packages, so the project sets `<PlatformTarget>x64</PlatformTarget>`; a 32-bit app takes the `.x86` packages instead. See [Windows deployment](../../../deployment-x/Windows/) for the full list.

```
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture
dotnet add package VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Core.Windows.x64
dotnet add package VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Libav.Windows.x64
```

## Implementation Example with C# Code

### The window (MainWindow.xaml)

The settings are on the left, the camera on the right. `PasswordBox` shows dots. Start is disabled until the SDK has loaded, and Stop until the camera has started.

```
<Window x:Class="IpCameraTwoWayAudioWpf.MainWindow"
        xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
        xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
        xmlns:vf="clr-namespace:VisioForge.Core.UI.WPF;assembly=VisioForge.Core"
        Title="IP Camera Two-Way Audio" Height="560" Width="1000"
        Loaded="Window_Loaded" Closing="Window_Closing">
    <Grid Margin="10">
        <Grid.ColumnDefinitions>
            <ColumnDefinition Width="260" />
            <ColumnDefinition Width="*" />
        </Grid.ColumnDefinitions>

        <StackPanel Grid.Column="0" Margin="0,0,10,0">
            <Label Content="Camera URL" />
            <TextBox x:Name="edURL" />
            <Label Content="Login" Margin="0,10,0,0" />
            <TextBox x:Name="edLogin" />
            <Label Content="Password" Margin="0,10,0,0" />
            <PasswordBox x:Name="edPassword" />
            <Label Content="Microphone (to the camera speaker)" Margin="0,10,0,0" />
            <ComboBox x:Name="cbMicrophone" />
            <Label Content="Speakers (the camera's sound)" Margin="0,10,0,0" />
            <ComboBox x:Name="cbSpeakers" />

            <StackPanel Orientation="Horizontal" Margin="0,20,0,0">
                <Button x:Name="btStart" Content="Start" Width="100" IsEnabled="False"
                        Click="btStart_Click" />
                <Button x:Name="btStop" Content="Stop" Width="100" Margin="10,0,0,0"
                        IsEnabled="False" Click="btStop_Click" />
            </StackPanel>
        </StackPanel>

        <vf:VideoView x:Name="VideoView1" Grid.Column="1" Background="Black" />
    </Grid>
</Window>
```

### The code (MainWindow.xaml.cs)

```
using System.ComponentModel;
using System.Windows;
using VisioForge.Core;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.X.AudioRenderers;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.X.Output;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.X.Sources;
using VisioForge.Core.VideoCaptureX;

namespace IpCameraTwoWayAudioWpf;

public partial class MainWindow : Window
{
    private VideoCaptureCoreX videoCapture1 = null!;

    private AudioCaptureDeviceInfo[] microphones = null!;

    private AudioOutputDeviceInfo[] speakers = null!;

    public MainWindow()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private async void Window_Loaded(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        await VisioForgeX.InitSDKAsync();

        videoCapture1 = new VideoCaptureCoreX(VideoView1);

        // Show SDK errors in the title bar
        videoCapture1.OnError += (_, args) => Dispatcher.InvokeAsync(() => Title = args.Message);

        microphones = await DeviceEnumerator.Shared.AudioSourcesAsync();
        foreach (var device in microphones)
            cbMicrophone.Items.Add(device.DisplayName);

        if (cbMicrophone.Items.Count > 0) cbMicrophone.SelectedIndex = 0;

        speakers = await DeviceEnumerator.Shared.AudioOutputsAsync(AudioOutputDeviceAPI.WASAPI2);
        foreach (var device in speakers)
            cbSpeakers.Items.Add(device.DisplayName);

        // Preselect the system's default output
        if (cbSpeakers.Items.Count > 0) cbSpeakers.SelectedIndex = Math.Max(0, Array.FindIndex(speakers, device => device.IsDefault));

        btStart.IsEnabled = true;
    }

    private async void btStart_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        if (!Uri.TryCreate(edURL.Text, UriKind.Absolute, out var url))
        {
            Title = "Enter the camera URL";
            return;
        }

        if (cbMicrophone.SelectedIndex < 0)
        {
            Title = "No microphone";
            return;
        }

        Title = "Connecting...";
        btStart.IsEnabled = false;

        var started = false;
        try
        {
            // The camera's video and its own microphone, played on the chosen speakers
            videoCapture1.Video_Source = await RTSPSourceSettings.CreateAsync(url, edLogin.Text, edPassword.Password, audioEnabled: true);
            videoCapture1.Audio_OutputDevice = cbSpeakers.SelectedIndex < 0 ? null : new AudioRendererSettings(speakers[cbSpeakers.SelectedIndex]);
            videoCapture1.Audio_Play = true;

            // The PC microphone, sent to the camera speaker over the ONVIF audio backchannel
            videoCapture1.Audio_BackchannelSource = microphones[cbMicrophone.SelectedIndex].CreateSourceSettingsVC();

            started = await videoCapture1.StartAsync();
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            Title = ex.Message;
        }

        // An SDK error posted during the start stays in the title
        if (Title == "Connecting...") Title = started ? "Talking to the camera" : "The camera did not start";
        btStop.IsEnabled = started;
        btStart.IsEnabled = !started;
    }

    private async void btStop_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        btStop.IsEnabled = false;
        await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
        Title = "IP Camera Two-Way Audio";
        btStart.IsEnabled = true;
    }

    private async void Window_Closing(object sender, CancelEventArgs e)
    {
        if (btStart.IsEnabled)
        {
            videoCapture1.Dispose();
            VisioForgeX.DestroySDK();
            return;
        }

        e.Cancel = true; // still loading or talking: stop first
        if (!btStop.IsEnabled) return; // already loading, starting or stopping
        btStop.IsEnabled = false;
        await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
        btStart.IsEnabled = true;
        await Dispatcher.InvokeAsync(Close); // not Close(): WPF throws inside Closing
    }
}
```

## Key Implementation Features

1. **SDK initialization** - `VisioForgeX.InitSDKAsync` runs once, when the window loads. The first run on a PC takes longer, so Start is enabled only after it returns. `VisioForgeX.DestroySDK` releases it when the window closes
2. **The camera** - `RTSPSourceSettings.CreateAsync` takes the URL, the login and the password as separate arguments, so the URL does not carry them. With `audioEnabled: true` the camera's own sound is used when its stream has one, and `Audio_Play` plays it on the speakers set in `Audio_OutputDevice`, since `Audio_Source` is left empty. Without `Audio_OutputDevice` it plays on the system default output. The [IP camera brands directory](../../../camera-brands/) lists the RTSP paths of many cameras
3. **The backchannel** - `Audio_BackchannelSource` takes the same audio sources as `Audio_Source`; `CreateSourceSettingsVC` turns the chosen microphone into one. At the start the SDK asks the camera for its ONVIF audio backchannel and sends the microphone to it as G.711 mu-law (PCMU), 8000 Hz, the codec ONVIF requires from every camera with an audio output; a camera whose backchannel offers only G.711 A-law (PCMA) gets A-law. The sound leaves the PC as it is captured, without the RTSP receive buffer added on top
4. **Starting** - a camera that does not answer takes a while to fail, so the title says "Connecting..." and Start is disabled until `StartAsync` returns. An `OnError` message posted during the start stays in the title
5. **Stopping and closing** - `StopAsync` closes both directions. Closing the window while it runs cancels the close, awaits `StopAsync`, and closes again; while the SDK is loading, or a start or a stop is under way, the close is cancelled: close the window again once it is done

## Troubleshooting

- **The camera refuses the connection** - the path does not match the camera's brand, or the login or password is wrong. Several wrong passwords in a row make many cameras lock the account for a while
- **No picture at all, with the right URL and password** - asking for the backchannel adds the ONVIF `Require: www.onvif.org/ver20/backchannel` header to the DESCRIBE request and to the backchannel's SETUP, and a camera without a backchannel may refuse either (it answers 551 Option Not Supported): an error then replaces the title, even when the start has already reported success. Leave `Audio_BackchannelSource` empty and start again: if the picture comes, the camera has no backchannel
- **The picture comes, but the camera speaker is silent** - the camera offers no backchannel, or neither G.711 mu-law nor A-law at 8000 Hz: the SDK names the codecs the camera offers in the window title. Check that two-way audio is on in the camera's web interface, that no vendor app or NVR holds its talk channel, and raise the speaker volume (see [Speaker Volume over ONVIF](../../video-sources/ip-cameras/two-way-audio/#speaker-volume-over-onvif))
- **You do not hear yourself through the camera's microphone** - this is expected. Cameras with a speaker cancel it in their microphone, so check the speaker by ear, next to the camera
- **The person at the camera hears an echo** - the PC plays the camera's sound on its speakers while its microphone sends to the camera, so the PC microphone picks the camera's sound up again and sends it back. Use a headset on the PC, or set `Audio_Play` to `false`

## Record the Screen to AVI in C# WinForms (MJPEG, PCM, MP3)
**URL:** https://www.visioforge.com/help/docs/dotnet/videocapture/video-tutorials/screen-capture-avi/
**Description:** Record the screen and the speaker sound to AVI in a C# WinForms app with VideoCaptureCore - pick the monitor, frame rate and codec, check the file with ffprobe.
**Tags:** Video Capture SDK, .NET, DirectShow, VideoCaptureCore, VideoCaptureCoreX, Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, WinForms, Capture, Encoding, Screen Capture, MP4, AVI, H.264, MJPEG, MP3, C#, NuGet
**API:** VideoCaptureCore, ScreenCaptureSourceSettings, AudioCaptureSource, AVIOutput, MP3Output, VideoCaptureCoreX, MJPEGEncoderSettings, VideoView

# C# Screen Capture to AVI Implementation Guide

[Video Capture SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/video-capture-sdk-net)

## Overview

This tutorial records a whole monitor and the sound from the speakers to an AVI file in a C# WinForms app with the VideoCaptureCore engine. The monitor, the frame rate and the mouse cursor are picked on the form, the sound comes from the VisioForge What You Hear source, the video codec is picked from the ones installed on the PC (MJPEG by default), and the audio is uncompressed PCM or MP3.

This part uses the Windows-only VideoCaptureCore engine, the SDK's DirectShow engine. On macOS, Linux, Android and iOS, VideoCaptureCoreX records AVI as well: see [VideoCaptureCoreX](#modern-api-video-capture-sdk-x) below.

## Video Walkthrough

## Source Code Repository

The complete project, with the designer file, is on GitHub:

[Source code on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Video%20Capture%20SDK/_VideoTutorials/screen-capture-avi-winforms)

## When to Use AVI for Screen Recording

- **Every frame is a whole picture** - with MJPEG, you can cut and edit on any frame, and read each frame on its own for analysis, without decoding the frames before it
- **No audio loss** - a plain `AVIOutput` writes uncompressed PCM
- **DirectShow tools** - AVI with MJPEG opens in DirectShow-based editors and players on Windows

**Trade-off:** size. In the video, a 4K screen at 10 frames per second with MJPEG takes about 30 MB a second: 679 MB for 22 seconds, about 110 GB an hour. For the web, phones and sharing, record [MP4 with H.264](../screen-capture-mp4/) instead.

## Required Packages

Install the [VisioForge.DotNet.Core](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core/) package and the video capture redist. Its DirectShow filters include the screen source and the What You Hear sound source; AVI needs nothing more.

Set `PlatformTarget` in the project file to match the redist (`x64` or `x86`).

```
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x64
```

For a 32-bit (x86) application, use the x86 package instead: `VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x86`.

`VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture`, the package in the Try it block at the top of this page, works as well: it installs the same `VisioForge.DotNet.Core`. The redist packages are needed either way.

## Implementation Example with C# Code

The form has a `VideoView`, combo boxes for the monitor, frame rate, sound device and video codec, "Mouse cursor" and "Record sound" check boxes (both checked), an "MP3 audio" check box, and Start and Stop buttons; the designer file is in the source code above. The project targets .NET 10 with implicit usings. On .NET Framework 4.7.2, `Form1.cs` builds unchanged in an SDK-style project with `<LangVersion>10</LangVersion>` and `<ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>`; in `Program.cs`, replace `ApplicationConfiguration.Initialize()` with `Application.EnableVisualStyles()` and `Application.SetCompatibleTextRenderingDefault(false)`.

```
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.Output;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoCapture;
using VisioForge.Core.UI;
using VisioForge.Core.VideoCapture;

namespace ScreenCaptureAvi;

public partial class Form1 : Form
{
    private VideoCaptureCore videoCapture1 = null!;

    public Form1()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    // The engine names a monitor by the N of its device name, \\.\DISPLAYN
    private static int MonitorNumber(Screen screen) =>
        int.Parse(screen.DeviceName.Replace(@"\\.\DISPLAY", string.Empty));

    private void Form1_Load(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        videoCapture1 = new VideoCaptureCore(VideoView1 as IVideoView);

        // Show SDK errors in the title bar
        videoCapture1.OnError += (_, args) => BeginInvoke(() => Text = args.Message);

        foreach (var screen in Screen.AllScreens)
            cbMonitor.Items.Add(MonitorNumber(screen));

        cbMonitor.SelectedItem = MonitorNumber(Screen.PrimaryScreen!);

        cbFrameRate.Items.AddRange(new object[] { 5, 10, 15, 25, 30 });
        cbFrameRate.SelectedItem = 10;

        // "VisioForge What You Hear Source" records what plays on the speakers
        foreach (var device in videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevices())
            cbSound.Items.Add(device.Name);

        cbSound.SelectedItem = "VisioForge What You Hear Source";
        if (cbSound.SelectedIndex < 0 && cbSound.Items.Count > 0) cbSound.SelectedIndex = 0;
        cbRecordSound.Enabled = cbMP3.Enabled = cbSound.Items.Count > 0;
        cbRecordSound.CheckedChanged += (_, _) => cbMP3.Enabled = cbRecordSound.Checked; // MP3 needs sound

        // The video codecs installed on this PC
        foreach (var codec in videoCapture1.Video_Codecs())
            cbVideoCodec.Items.Add(codec);

        cbVideoCodec.SelectedItem = "MJPEG Compressor";
        if (cbVideoCodec.SelectedIndex < 0 && cbVideoCodec.Items.Count > 0) cbVideoCodec.SelectedIndex = 0;
    }

    private async void btStart_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        if (cbVideoCodec.SelectedItem is null)
        {
            Text = "No video codec selected";
            return;
        }

        Text = "Screen to AVI";

        // The whole monitor at the frame rate from the list
        videoCapture1.Screen_Capture_Source = new ScreenCaptureSourceSettings
        {
            FullScreen = true,
            AllowDesktopDuplicationEngine = true, // DXGI Desktop Duplication: faster than GDI
            DisplayIndex = (int)cbMonitor.SelectedItem!,
            GrabMouseCursor = cbCursor.Checked,
            FrameRate = new VideoFrameRate((int)cbFrameRate.SelectedItem!)
        };

        var recordSound = cbRecordSound.Checked && cbSound.SelectedItem is not null;
        videoCapture1.Audio_RecordAudio = recordSound;
        // No device when the sound is off: a What You Hear device left here still opens the speakers
        videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevice = recordSound ? new AudioCaptureSource(cbSound.Text) : null;
        videoCapture1.Audio_PlayAudio = false; // never play the captured sound back into the speakers

        // Audio: MP3, or uncompressed PCM
        var avi = recordSound && cbMP3.Checked ? new AVIOutput(new MP3Output()) : new AVIOutput();
        avi.Video_Codec = cbVideoCodec.Text;

        videoCapture1.Output_Filename = Path.Combine(
            Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.MyVideos), "output.avi");
        videoCapture1.Output_Format = avi;
        videoCapture1.Mode = VideoCaptureMode.ScreenCapture;

        btStart.Enabled = false;
        var started = await videoCapture1.StartAsync();
        btStop.Enabled = started;
        btStart.Enabled = !started;
    }

    private async void btStop_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        btStop.Enabled = false;
        await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
        btStart.Enabled = true;
    }

    private async void Form1_FormClosing(object sender, FormClosingEventArgs e)
    {
        // Finish the AVI before the window goes away
        if (!btStart.Enabled)
        {
            e.Cancel = true;
            if (!btStop.Enabled) return; // already starting or stopping

            btStop.Enabled = false;
            await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
            btStart.Enabled = true;
            BeginInvoke(Close); // close again once this handler has returned
            return;
        }

        videoCapture1.Dispose();
    }
}
```

## Key Implementation Features

1. **Monitor** - `DisplayIndex` takes the number at the end of the monitor's Windows device name, `\\.\DISPLAY1` → `1`; `MonitorNumber` reads it from `Screen.DeviceName`, and the primary monitor is selected
2. **Screen Source** - `FullScreen` records the whole monitor at its full resolution, and `AllowDesktopDuplicationEngine` captures through Windows Desktop Duplication instead of GDI. `GrabMouseCursor` is off by default and `FrameRate` is 10 by default
3. **Speaker Sound** - `VisioForge What You Hear Source`, from the video capture redist, records what plays on the speakers. With Record sound off, the app sets `Audio_RecordAudio` to `false` and clears `Audio_CaptureDevice` too, and `Audio_PlayAudio` stays `false` so the recorded sound isn't played back into the speakers
4. **Video Codec** - `Video_Codecs()` returns the DirectShow video compressors installed on the PC; `AVIOutput.Video_Codec` takes one of those names and defaults to `MJPEG Compressor`, which stores every frame as a JPEG picture
5. **Audio** - A plain `AVIOutput` writes uncompressed PCM, 16-bit stereo at 44.1 kHz, about ten megabytes a minute; `new AVIOutput(new MP3Output())` writes MP3 at 192 kbps, about one and a half megabytes a minute
6. **Asynchronous Operation** - `StartAsync` and `StopAsync` keep the UI responsive, and closing the form finishes the AVI file first

## Check the File with ffprobe

```
cd ([Environment]::GetFolderPath('MyVideos'))
ffprobe -v error -of compact output.avi -show_entries format=format_name,duration,size:stream=codec_name,width,height,sample_rate,channels

# stream|codec_name=mjpeg|width=3840|height=2160
# stream|codec_name=pcm_s16le|sample_rate=44100|channels=2
# format|format_name=avi|duration=22.400000|size=679261184
```

Twenty-two seconds of a 4K screen at 10 frames per second is 679 megabytes, roughly 240 megabits per second, which is why AVI is for editing and analysis, not for sharing.

## Video Capture SDK X (VideoCaptureCoreX)

The cross-platform API uses `VideoCaptureCoreX`. For the complete console application pattern with screen capture setup, audio configuration, and recording lifecycle, see the [Screen Capture to MP4](../screen-capture-mp4/#modern-api-video-capture-sdk-x) guide. To output AVI instead of MP4, replace the output configuration:

```
// AVI with default codecs (H.264 video + MP3 audio)
var aviOutput = new AVIOutput(outputPath);
videoCapture.Outputs_Add(aviOutput, autostart: true);
```

### AVI Codec Options

Choose the video encoder based on your workflow:

```
// MJPEG — frame-independent, larger files, ideal for editing
var aviOutput = new AVIOutput(outputPath);
aviOutput.Video = new MJPEGEncoderSettings();

// H.264 in AVI container — smaller files, less editing-friendly
var h264AviOutput = new AVIOutput(outputPath);
h264AviOutput.Video = new OpenH264EncoderSettings();
```

Region capture, multi-monitor recording, audio, cursor highlighting, and GPU encoding options are covered in the [MP4 guide](../screen-capture-mp4/) — all source configuration features work identically with AVI output.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why is my AVI screen recording file so large?

MJPEG compresses each frame on its own, trading file size for editing convenience: a 4K screen at 10 frames per second takes about 30 MB a second. To reduce the size, lower the frame rate, capture a smaller region instead of the full screen (`FullScreen = false` with `Left`, `Top`, `Right` and `Bottom`), or switch to [MP4 output](../screen-capture-mp4/), whose H.264 compresses across frames.

### How do I record the sound of the computer, not the microphone?

Select `VisioForge What You Hear Source` as the `AudioCaptureSource`: it records what plays on the speakers, and it ships in the video capture redist. Keep `Audio_PlayAudio` at `false`, so the recorded sound isn't played back into the speakers.

### When should I use AVI instead of MP4 for screen recording?

Choose AVI when you need frame-independent access for video editing (MJPEG allows scrubbing to any frame without decoding previous frames), when you need lossless PCM audio, or when working with DirectShow-based tools. For all other cases, MP4 with H.264 offers better compression, smaller files, and broader cross-platform support.

## Video Transcript

### What we build

Let's record the screen and the sound from the speakers to an AVI file in a C# WinForms app with the VisioForge Video Capture SDK. Here's what we build. A WinForms app that records a whole monitor to an AVI file. The monitor, the frame rate and the mouse cursor are picked on the form. It also records the sound that plays on the speakers, as uncompressed PCM or as MP3. And the video codec is any one installed on the PC, MJPEG by default. This is the finished app, recording the screen it runs on.

### AVI or MP4

When is AVI the right choice over MP4? With MJPEG, every frame of the recording is a whole picture, so you can cut and edit on any frame, and read each frame on its own for analysis. PCM audio has no loss. The price is size: here about twenty-eight megabytes every second, for a 4K screen at ten frames per second. For the web, phones and sharing, MP4 with H.264 is the better choice. That's the screen capture to MP4 video.

### Prerequisites

You need Windows 10 or 11, and Visual Studio 2022 or 2026 with the .NET desktop development workload. The project can target .NET 8 or later, or .NET Framework 4.7.2. No camera and no microphone this time. VideoCaptureCore is the SDK's DirectShow engine, so this app runs on Windows only.

### Create a WinForms project

In Visual Studio, create a new project. Search for Windows Forms, and pick Windows Forms App for C#. Name the project ScreenCaptureAvi. Choose .NET 10 and click Create. Visual Studio opens the empty form in the designer.

### Add the NuGet packages

Now add two NuGet packages: the SDK itself, and the video capture redist. It carries the DirectShow filters, the screen source and the What You Hear sound source among them. AVI needs nothing more. In Visual Studio, that's Manage NuGet Packages. Browse for VisioForge.DotNet.Core and install it. Then install the video capture redist for x64. The redist is the x64 one, so set PlatformTarget to x64 in the project file. An x86 app takes the x86 redist instead.

### Design the WinForms form

From the Toolbox, draw a VideoView, where the app previews what it records. Add a label and a combo box for the monitor, and give every control a clear name in the Properties window. Do the same for the frame rate, the sound device and the video codec. Add three check boxes: the mouse cursor and Record sound, both checked, and MP3 audio. Then the Start and Stop buttons. Stop stays disabled until a recording starts. Double-click the form and both buttons. Visual Studio adds an empty handler for each one.

### Create the capture engine

At the top of Form1.cs, add these usings. In the form's Load handler, create the VideoCaptureCore engine and pass it the VideoView, where the preview is drawn. Engine errors arrive in the OnError event. Here they go to the title bar.

### Fill the lists

The engine names a monitor by the number at the end of its Windows device name: one for DISPLAY1, two for DISPLAY2. A small helper reads that number. The Load handler lists every monitor, and selects the primary one. The frame rate list holds a few fixed values. Ten frames per second is selected, the SDK's own default for the screen. Audio\_CaptureDevices lists the sound devices. VisioForge What You Hear Source records whatever plays on the speakers, so it's selected when it's there. With no sound device at all, both sound boxes are disabled. And MP3 only makes sense with sound, so it follows Record sound. Video\_Codecs lists the video codecs installed on this PC. We select MJPEG Compressor, or the first codec when MJPEG isn't there. Video\_Codecs returns the DirectShow video compressors on this PC. This one has two: MJPEG Compressor and DV Video Encoder. MJPEG stores every frame as a JPEG picture. DV writes standard-definition DV only. A codec you install yourself shows up in the same list.

### Capture the screen

The Start handler first checks that a video codec is selected. If not, it says so in the title bar. Then it describes the screen source. FullScreen records the whole monitor. AllowDesktopDuplicationEngine captures through Windows Desktop Duplication instead of GDI. DisplayIndex is the monitor number from the list, GrabMouseCursor draws the cursor into the video, and FrameRate is the rate from the list. A quick recap. FullScreen records the whole monitor at its full resolution. DisplayIndex is the number from the monitor's device name. The cursor is off by default, and the frame rate is ten. This video records a 4K screen at ten frames per second.

### Record the speaker sound

With Record sound checked, the app records the selected device. With it unchecked, the device is cleared too: a What You Hear device left in place still opens the speakers. Audio\_PlayAudio stays off, so the recorded sound isn't played back into the speakers it comes from.

### AVIOutput: PCM or MP3 audio

Now the output. A plain AVIOutput writes uncompressed PCM audio. Pass an MP3Output to its constructor, and the audio is MP3 instead. Set Video\_Codec to the name from the list, write output.avi into the Videos folder, and switch the engine to screen capture mode. A plain AVIOutput writes PCM: 16-bit stereo at 44.1 kilohertz, with no loss, about ten megabytes a minute. With an MP3Output it writes MP3 at 192 kilobits per second, about one and a half megabytes a minute. Next to MJPEG video, both are small.

### Start and stop

Start and Stop are async. StartAsync returns once the capture is running, and StopAsync finishes writing the AVI file.

### Close the window

Closing the window while it records would leave the AVI unfinished. In the Properties window, on the Events tab, double-click FormClosing to add this handler. While recording, it cancels the close. Then it stops the recording, and closes the window again once the handler has returned. With nothing recording, the handler disposes the engine.

### Run it

Run the app from Visual Studio. The lists fill in: the monitor, the frame rate, the sound device and the codec. The sound list has What You Hear and the microphones. What You Hear stays selected. A sound plays on the speakers, and Start begins the recording. The preview shows the screen with the cursor. Stop finishes output.avi, and then we close the window.

### Check the file with ffprobe

The file lands in Videos: about six hundred and fifty megabytes for twenty-three seconds. ffprobe shows what's inside. The container is AVI. The video is MJPEG at 3840x2160. The audio is PCM, 16-bit, 44.1 kilohertz stereo: the sound from the speakers. That's about 240 megabits per second, which is why AVI is for editing and analysis, not for sharing.

### Common mistakes

A few common mistakes. A missing redist package, so the engine won't start. A silent file, because Record sound was off, or a microphone was selected instead of What You Hear. x86 and x64 packages mixed in one project. Closing the window mid-recording: await StopAsync first. And AVI where MP4 belongs: an hour of 4K MJPEG runs to about a hundred gigabytes.

### Next steps

Next, the screen capture to MP4 video saves the screen to small H.264 files. The webcam to AVI video records a camera the same way as here. And the docs show how to record a region or a single window instead of the whole screen. The full source is on GitHub, and the docs are at visioforge.com/help. Thanks for watching.
