# Screen capture to MP4 file

[Video Capture SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/video-capture-sdk-net)

This tutorial records the screen and the system sound to an MP4 file from a WPF application. The `VideoCaptureCoreX` engine captures the primary monitor through Direct3D 11, draws a live preview in a `VideoView`, and encodes H.264 on the GPU when the PC has a hardware encoder, with AAC audio. The sound that plays on the speakers is recorded through WASAPI loopback.

The classic `VideoCaptureCore` engine records the screen as well; its version of the app is [further down this page](#second-option-videocapturecore).

## YouTube tutorial

[Source code on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Video%20Capture%20SDK%20X/_VideoTutorials/screen-capture-mp4-wpf)

### The short version

The same recording as a console app in a few lines of C#, without the preview and the system sound.

Its code: [screen-mp4-short-console on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Video%20Capture%20SDK%20X/_VideoTutorials/screen-mp4-short-console).

## Required NuGet packages

- [VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture/) — the SDK; the WPF `VideoView` ships in it
- [VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Core.Windows.x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Core.Windows.x64/) — the GStreamer runtime the X engine runs on
- [VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Libav.Windows.x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Libav.Windows.x64/) — the AAC audio encoder

These are the x64 packages, so the project sets `<PlatformTarget>x64</PlatformTarget>`; a 32-bit app takes the `.x86` packages instead. See [Windows deployment](../../../deployment-x/Windows/) for the full list.

## The window in XAML

The `vf` prefix maps the `VisioForge.Core.UI.WPF` namespace of the `VisioForge.Core` assembly. The left column holds the speakers list, the sound check box and the buttons, the right column the `VideoView` where the live preview is drawn. Start stays disabled until the SDK has loaded.

```
<Window x:Class="ScreenCaptureMp4Wpf.MainWindow"
        xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
        xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
        xmlns:vf="clr-namespace:VisioForge.Core.UI.WPF;assembly=VisioForge.Core"
        Title="Screen to MP4" Height="560" Width="1000"
        Loaded="Window_Loaded" Closing="Window_Closing">
    <Grid Margin="10">
        <Grid.ColumnDefinitions>
            <ColumnDefinition Width="260" />
            <ColumnDefinition Width="*" />
        </Grid.ColumnDefinitions>

        <StackPanel Grid.Column="0" Margin="0,0,10,0">
            <Label Content="Speakers" />
            <ComboBox x:Name="cbSpeakers" />
            <CheckBox x:Name="cbRecordSound" Content="Record system sound" IsChecked="True"
                      Margin="0,10,0,0" />

            <StackPanel Orientation="Horizontal" Margin="0,20,0,0">
                <Button x:Name="btStart" Content="Start" Width="100" IsEnabled="False"
                        Click="btStart_Click" />
                <Button x:Name="btStop" Content="Stop" Width="100" Margin="10,0,0,0"
                        IsEnabled="False" Click="btStop_Click" />
            </StackPanel>
        </StackPanel>

        <vf:VideoView x:Name="VideoView1" Grid.Column="1" Background="Black" />
    </Grid>
</Window>
```

## The code behind the window

```
using System.ComponentModel;
using System.IO;
using System.Windows;
using VisioForge.Core;
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.X.Output;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.X.Sources;
using VisioForge.Core.VideoCaptureX;

namespace ScreenCaptureMp4Wpf;

public partial class MainWindow : Window
{
    private VideoCaptureCoreX videoCapture1 = null!;

    private AudioOutputDeviceInfo[] speakers = null!;

    public MainWindow()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private async void Window_Loaded(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        await VisioForgeX.InitSDKAsync();

        videoCapture1 = new VideoCaptureCoreX(VideoView1);

        // Show SDK errors in the title bar
        videoCapture1.OnError += (_, args) => Dispatcher.InvokeAsync(() => Title = args.Message);

        // The sound of these outputs is recorded through WASAPI loopback
        speakers = await DeviceEnumerator.Shared.AudioOutputsAsync(AudioOutputDeviceAPI.WASAPI2);
        foreach (var device in speakers)
            cbSpeakers.Items.Add(device.Name);

        if (cbSpeakers.Items.Count > 0) cbSpeakers.SelectedIndex = 0;

        btStart.IsEnabled = true;
    }

    private async void btStart_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        // The whole primary monitor, with the mouse cursor
        videoCapture1.Video_Source = new ScreenCaptureD3D11SourceSettings
        {
            FrameRate = new VideoFrameRate(30)
        };

        var recordSound = cbRecordSound.IsChecked == true && cbSpeakers.SelectedIndex >= 0;
        videoCapture1.Audio_Source = recordSound
            ? new LoopbackAudioCaptureDeviceSourceSettings(speakers[cbSpeakers.SelectedIndex])
            : null;
        videoCapture1.Audio_Record = recordSound;
        videoCapture1.Audio_Play = false; // never play the captured sound back into the speakers

        // H.264 on the GPU encoder when there is one, OpenH264 otherwise; AAC audio
        videoCapture1.Outputs_Clear();
        videoCapture1.Outputs_Add(new MP4Output(Path.Combine(
            Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.MyVideos), $"screen_{DateTime.Now:yyyyMMdd_HHmmss}.mp4")));

        btStart.IsEnabled = false;
        var started = await videoCapture1.StartAsync();
        btStop.IsEnabled = started;
        btStart.IsEnabled = !started;
    }

    private async void btStop_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        btStop.IsEnabled = false;
        await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
        btStart.IsEnabled = true;
    }

    private async void Window_Closing(object sender, CancelEventArgs e)
    {
        if (btStart.IsEnabled)
        {
            videoCapture1.Dispose();
            VisioForgeX.DestroySDK();
            return;
        }

        e.Cancel = true; // still loading or recording: finish the MP4 first
        if (!btStop.IsEnabled) return; // already loading, starting or stopping
        btStop.IsEnabled = false;
        await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
        btStart.IsEnabled = true;
        await Dispatcher.InvokeAsync(Close); // not Close(): WPF throws inside Closing
    }
}
```

## How it works

1. **SDK initialization** — `VisioForgeX.InitSDKAsync` runs once, when the window loads. The first run on a PC takes longer, so Start is enabled only after it returns. `VisioForgeX.DestroySDK` releases it when the window closes.
2. **Screen source** — `ScreenCaptureD3D11SourceSettings` captures the whole primary monitor with the mouse cursor by default. It uses DXGI Desktop Duplication, which starts at once even on a still screen, and falls back to Windows Graphics Capture where Desktop Duplication is not supported. The default frame rate is 10 fps, so the code sets 30.
3. **System sound** — `AudioOutputsAsync(AudioOutputDeviceAPI.WASAPI2)` lists the speakers and headphones, and `LoopbackAudioCaptureDeviceSourceSettings` records what plays on the one picked. `Audio_Play` is `false`, so the recorded sound is not played back.
4. **MP4 output** — `MP4Output` with no encoder settings picks NVIDIA NVENC, then AMD AMF, then Intel Quick Sync, and OpenH264 on the CPU when none of them is present. Audio is AAC. An output stays in the engine after a recording, so `Outputs_Clear` runs before each new one.
5. **Start, stop and close** — `StartAsync` returns whether the capture started, and `StopAsync` finalizes the MP4 file. Closing the window during a recording cancels the close, awaits `StopAsync`, and closes again.

## Notes

- A WPF project leaves `System.IO` out of its implicit usings, so the file adds it for `Path`.
- The preview shows the screen it records, so the app window appears inside itself, in the preview and in the file. On a PC with two monitors, move the window to the one that is not recorded; with one monitor, minimize it after Start and restore it to stop.
- With **Record system sound** cleared, or with no speakers in the list, the MP4 holds video only.
- `MP4Output` picks a GPU encoder because its GStreamer element exists, which does not prove it can encode right now. `H264EncoderBlock.CanEncodeAsync` encodes a few test frames to find out; to stay on the CPU, pass `new OpenH264EncoderSettings()` to the `MP4Output` constructor.

## Second option: VideoCaptureCore

The classic Windows engine, `VideoCaptureCore`, records the screen to MP4 in a WinForms app, with or without the microphone.

[Source code on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Video%20Capture%20SDK/_CodeSnippets/screen-capture-mp4)

### Required redists

- Video capture redist [x86](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x86/) [x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x64/)
- MP4 redist [x86](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.MP4.x86/) [x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.MP4.x64/)

### Code Example

```
using System;
using System.IO;
using System.Windows.Forms;
using VisioForge.Core.VideoCapture;
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.Output;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoCapture;

namespace screen_capture_mp4
{
    public partial class Form1 : Form
    {
        // Main VideoCapture component that handles all recording operations
        private VideoCaptureCore videoCapture1 = null!;

        public Form1()
        {
            InitializeComponent();
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// Starts screen recording with audio from the default device
        /// </summary>
        private async void btStartWithAudio_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
        {
            // Configure screen capture to record the entire screen
            // ScreenCaptureSourceSettings allows fine control of capture region and parameters
            videoCapture1.Screen_Capture_Source = new ScreenCaptureSourceSettings() {
                FullScreen = true  // Capture the entire screen rather than a specific region
            };

            // Configure audio capture by selecting the first available audio input device
            // Audio_CaptureDevices() returns all connected microphones and audio inputs
            // We select the first device (index 0) in the collection
            videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevice = new AudioCaptureSource(
                videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevices()[0].Name);

            // Disable audio monitoring/playback during recording to prevent feedback
            // This means we won't hear the captured audio while recording
            videoCapture1.Audio_PlayAudio = false;

            // Enable audio recording to include sound in the output file
            videoCapture1.Audio_RecordAudio = true;

            // Set the output file location to the user's Videos folder
            // Environment.GetFolderPath ensures the path works across different Windows systems
            videoCapture1.Output_Filename = Path.Combine(
                Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.MyVideos),
                "output.mp4");

            // Use MP4 container format with H.264 video and AAC audio codecs (standard format)
            // MP4Output can be further configured with custom encoding parameters if needed
            videoCapture1.Output_Format = new MP4Output();

            // Set the capture mode to screen recording
            // Other modes include camera capture, video file processing, etc.
            videoCapture1.Mode = VideoCaptureMode.ScreenCapture;

            // Begin the capture process asynchronously
            // Using async/await pattern to prevent UI freezing during operation
            await videoCapture1.StartAsync();
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// Starts screen recording without audio (video only)
        /// </summary>
        private async void btStartWithoutAudio_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
        {
            // Configure screen capture for full screen recording
            // Same ScreenCaptureSourceSettings as in audio recording
            videoCapture1.Screen_Capture_Source = new ScreenCaptureSourceSettings() {
                FullScreen = true
            };

            // Disable both audio playback and recording in a single line
            // This creates a video-only MP4 file with no audio track
            videoCapture1.Audio_PlayAudio = videoCapture1.Audio_RecordAudio = false;

            // Set output file path to user's Videos directory with MP4 extension
            videoCapture1.Output_Filename = Path.Combine(
                Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.MyVideos),
                "output.mp4");

            // Configure output as MP4 (H.264 video codec)
            videoCapture1.Output_Format = new MP4Output();

            // Set mode to screen capture
            videoCapture1.Mode = VideoCaptureMode.ScreenCapture;

            // Start screen recording asynchronously
            await videoCapture1.StartAsync();
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// Stops the current recording process safely
        /// </summary>
        private async void btStop_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
        {
            // Stop the recording asynchronously
            // This properly finalizes the MP4 file and releases resources
            // Using async ensures UI remains responsive during file finalization
            await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// Initializes the VideoCapture component when the form loads
        /// </summary>
        private void Form1_Load(object sender, EventArgs e)
        {
            // Initialize the video capture component and connect it to a video preview control
            // VideoView1 should be a control on your form that implements IVideoView interface
            // This allows for live preview of the capture when desired
            videoCapture1 = new VideoCaptureCore(VideoView1 as IVideoView);
        }
    }
}
```

### How it works — VideoCaptureCore

This Windows Forms application demonstrates screen capture functionality with and without audio using VisioForge Video Capture SDK:

1. **Setup**: The `VideoCaptureCore` object is initialized in the form load event, connecting it to a video view component.
2. **Capturing with Audio**:
3. Sets screen capture to full screen mode
4. Selects the first available audio device for recording
5. Disables audio playback but enables audio recording
6. Sets the output file to MP4 format in the user's Videos folder
7. Uses asynchronous method to start capture
8. **Capturing without Audio**:
9. Similar to above but disables both audio playback and recording
10. Uses the same MP4 output format and capture mode
11. **Stopping Capture**:
12. Provides a simple stop method that asynchronously stops the recording

The application demonstrates how to configure different capture scenarios with minimal code using the SDK's fluent interface and async patterns.

#### Audio Configuration

The code example above captures microphone audio by selecting the first available device. You can select a specific audio device by name, including system audio (loopback) devices for capturing desktop sound:

```
// Select a loopback device (e.g., "Stereo Mix") for system audio capture
var devices = videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevices();
var loopbackDevice = devices.FirstOrDefault(d => d.Name.Contains("Stereo Mix"));

if (loopbackDevice != null)
{
    videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevice = new AudioCaptureSource(loopbackDevice.Name);
}
else
{
    // Fallback: use the first available audio device
    videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevice = new AudioCaptureSource(devices[0].Name);
}

// Enable recording, disable playback to prevent feedback
videoCapture1.Audio_RecordAudio = true;
videoCapture1.Audio_PlayAudio = false;
```

To create a silent recording with no audio track, disable both audio properties:

```
videoCapture1.Audio_PlayAudio = false;
videoCapture1.Audio_RecordAudio = false;
```

#### Region Capture

Instead of recording the full screen, capture a specific rectangular area by setting `FullScreen = false` and providing pixel coordinates:

```
videoCapture1.Screen_Capture_Source = new ScreenCaptureSourceSettings()
{
    FullScreen = false,
    Left = 100,
    Top = 100,
    Right = 1380,
    Bottom = 820
};
```

The coordinates define the capture rectangle in screen pixels. This is useful for recording a specific application window or a portion of the desktop.

#### Multi-Monitor Recording

Select which display to record using the `DisplayIndex` property. `0` is the primary monitor. A positive value is that monitor's Windows number, the digits in its device name: `\\.\DISPLAY2` is `2`. It is the same number the screen-capture samples show in the monitor list, not the monitor's position in that list, so `1` is not "the secondary monitor" (on most PCs the primary monitor is `\\.\DISPLAY1`).

```
videoCapture1.Screen_Capture_Source = new ScreenCaptureSourceSettings()
{
    FullScreen = true,
    DisplayIndex = 0  // The primary monitor
};
```

#### Recording Quality Settings

Customize the MP4 output by configuring the H.264 encoder. The default bitrate is 3500 kbps, which produces approximately 25 MB per minute at 1080p:

```
var mp4Output = new MP4Output();
mp4Output.Video.Bitrate = 5000;                          // Higher quality (kbps)
mp4Output.Video.Profile = H264Profile.ProfileMain;       // Better compression than Baseline
mp4Output.Video.RateControl = H264RateControl.VBR;       // Variable bitrate
videoCapture1.Output_Format = mp4Output;
```

#### Mouse Cursor Options

Include the mouse cursor in the recording and optionally add a highlight effect for tutorial-style screencasts:

```
videoCapture1.Screen_Capture_Source = new ScreenCaptureSourceSettings()
{
    FullScreen = true,
    GrabMouseCursor = true,
    MouseHighlight = true,
    MouseHighlightColor = System.Drawing.Color.Yellow,
    MouseHighlightRadius = 40,
    MouseHighlightOpacity = 0.4
};
```

The highlight draws a translucent circle around the cursor, making it easier for viewers to follow mouse movements.

## Console app — VideoCaptureCoreX

The cross-platform `VideoCaptureCoreX` engine also runs without a window, with Direct3D 11 screen capture (Desktop Duplication). This console application records the full screen to MP4 with optional system audio.

It takes the same packages as the WPF app: see [Required NuGet packages](#required-nuget-packages).

The same packages are used for the 30-day trial and licensed applications. See the [VisioForge licensing page](https://www.visioforge.com/licensing) for trial terms and `.vflicense` activation.

### Complete Example

```
using System;
using System.IO;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using VisioForge.Core;
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.X.Output;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.X.Sources;
using VisioForge.Core.VideoCaptureX;

class Program
{
    static async Task Main(string[] args)
    {
        // Initialize SDK
        await VisioForgeX.InitSDKAsync();

        var videoCapture = new VideoCaptureCoreX();

        try
        {
            // Configure Direct3D 11 screen capture (Desktop Duplication by default)
            var screenSource = new ScreenCaptureD3D11SourceSettings
            {
                FrameRate = new VideoFrameRate(25, 1),
                CaptureCursor = true,
                MonitorIndex = -1  // Primary monitor (0 is the first monitor)
            };

            videoCapture.Video_Source = screenSource;
            videoCapture.Video_Play = false;
            videoCapture.Audio_Play = false;
            videoCapture.Audio_Record = false;

            // Configure MP4 output (H.264 + AAC, auto-selected encoders)
            string outputPath = Path.Combine(
                Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.MyVideos),
                $"screen_{DateTime.Now:yyyyMMdd_HHmmss}.mp4");

            var mp4Output = new MP4Output(outputPath);
            videoCapture.Outputs_Add(mp4Output, autostart: true);

            // Start recording
            await videoCapture.StartAsync();
            Console.WriteLine($"Recording to: {outputPath}");
            Console.WriteLine("Press ENTER to stop...");
            Console.ReadLine();

            // Stop and save
            await videoCapture.StopAsync();
            Console.WriteLine("Recording saved.");
        }
        finally
        {
            await videoCapture.DisposeAsync();
            VisioForgeX.DestroySDK();
        }
    }
}
```

### Adding System Audio (Loopback)

To include desktop audio in the recording, add WASAPI2 loopback capture:

```
// Enumerate WASAPI2 output devices for loopback capture
var audioOutputs = await DeviceEnumerator.Shared.AudioOutputsAsync(
    AudioOutputDeviceAPI.WASAPI2);

if (audioOutputs.Length > 0)
{
    var loopbackSource = new LoopbackAudioCaptureDeviceSourceSettings(audioOutputs[0]);
    videoCapture.Audio_Source = loopbackSource;
    videoCapture.Audio_Record = true;
    videoCapture.Audio_Play = false;
}
```

For microphone audio instead, use `DeviceEnumerator.Shared.AudioSourcesAsync()` — see the [Audio Capture guide](../../audio-capture/) for complete examples.

## GPU-Accelerated Encoding

Hardware-accelerated encoding offloads H.264/HEVC compression to your GPU, significantly reducing CPU usage during high-resolution or high-FPS recording.

```
// NVIDIA NVENC H.264
var mp4Output = new MP4Output(
    outputPath,
    new NVENCH264EncoderSettings());

// Intel Quick Sync Video H.264
var mp4Output = new MP4Output(
    outputPath,
    new QSVH264EncoderSettings());

// AMD AMF H.264
var mp4Output = new MP4Output(
    outputPath,
    new AMFH264EncoderSettings());
```

HEVC (H.265) encoders are also available for better compression at the same quality: `NVENCHEVCEncoderSettings`, `QSVHEVCEncoderSettings`, `AMFHEVCEncoderSettings`.

Engine note: `MP4Output` and the X-engine

The `MP4Output` class shown in this section refers to the **X-engine** `VisioForge.Core.Types.X.Output.MP4Output`, which accepts cross-platform `*EncoderSettings` types (`NVENCH264EncoderSettings`, `OpenH264EncoderSettings`, etc.). When hardware encoding is unavailable on the X engine and you use the parameterless ctor `new MP4Output(filename)`, the SDK selects an available software encoder automatically. The classic Windows-only DirectShow engine has its own `VisioForge.Core.Types.Output.MP4Output` with a different settings shape — don't mix them.

## Screen Capture with Media Blocks SDK

The Media Blocks SDK uses a pipeline approach where you connect source, processing, and output blocks. This gives full control over the data flow and allows splitting the video stream to multiple outputs simultaneously.

```
using System;
using System.IO;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using VisioForge.Core;
using VisioForge.Core.MediaBlocks;
using VisioForge.Core.MediaBlocks.Sources;
using VisioForge.Core.MediaBlocks.Sinks;
using VisioForge.Core.MediaBlocks.Special;
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.X.Sources;

class Program
{
    static async Task Main(string[] args)
    {
        await VisioForgeX.InitSDKAsync();

        var pipeline = new MediaBlocksPipeline();

        try
        {
            // Screen capture source
            var screenSettings = new ScreenCaptureD3D11SourceSettings
            {
                FrameRate = new VideoFrameRate(25, 1),
                CaptureCursor = true
            };
            var screenSource = new ScreenSourceBlock(screenSettings);

            // MP4 output
            string outputPath = Path.Combine(
                Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.MyVideos),
                $"screen_mb_{DateTime.Now:yyyyMMdd_HHmmss}.mp4");
            var mp4Sink = new MP4OutputBlock(outputPath);

            // Connect source to output
            pipeline.Connect(screenSource.Output, mp4Sink.CreateNewInput(MediaBlockPadMediaType.Video));

            // Start pipeline
            await pipeline.StartAsync();
            Console.WriteLine($"Recording to: {outputPath}");
            Console.WriteLine("Press ENTER to stop...");
            Console.ReadLine();

            await pipeline.StopAsync();
            Console.WriteLine("Recording saved.");
        }
        finally
        {
            await pipeline.DisposeAsync();
            VisioForgeX.DestroySDK();
        }
    }
}
```

## Cross-Platform Screen Capture

The SDK supports screen capture on Windows, macOS, and Linux with platform-specific source settings:

| Platform | Capture Method | Settings Class | Requirements |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Windows | Direct3D 11 / WGC | `ScreenCaptureD3D11SourceSettings` | Windows 8+ (WGC: Windows 10 v1803+) |
| macOS | AVFoundation | `ScreenCaptureMacOSSourceSettings` | macOS 10.15+ (screen recording permission) |
| Linux | X11 / XDisplay | `ScreenCaptureXDisplaySourceSettings` | X11 server |

On Windows, the SDK uses DXGI Desktop Duplication by default: it starts at once, even on a still screen, and falls back to WGC where Desktop Duplication is not supported. Window capture always uses WGC. You can select WGC for a screen too; it also starts at once on a still screen:

```
var screenSource = new ScreenCaptureD3D11SourceSettings
{
    API = D3D11ScreenCaptureAPI.WGC  // Windows Graphics Capture instead of Desktop Duplication
};
```

For Android and iOS, and a .NET MAUI recorder that runs on Windows, Mac Catalyst, Android and iOS, see [Cross-platform screen recording in C# and .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/solutions/screen-recording-csharp).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What license do I need for a C# screen capture application?

Video Capture SDK .NET requires a license for development and distribution. A Developer license removes the evaluation watermark and unlocks all features during development. A Release license is required when distributing your application to end users. The SDK is available in Premium edition which includes all capture modes, MP4/AVI/WMV output, and both DirectShow and GStreamer engines. You can evaluate the SDK without a license — screen capture works fully but includes a watermark overlay. Visit the [product page](https://www.visioforge.com/video-capture-sdk-net) for pricing and license options.

### How do I control recording quality and file size for MP4 screen capture?

Configure the `MP4Output` video bitrate to balance quality and file size. The default is 3500 kbps, which works well for most screen recordings. Lower the bitrate to 1500–2000 kbps for smaller files, or increase to 5000–8000 kbps for high-quality captures. Use `H264Profile.ProfileMain` or `ProfileHigh` instead of `ProfileBaseline` for better compression at the same quality. Frame rate also affects file size — 15 FPS is sufficient for presentations, while 30 FPS is better for software demos. A 1080p recording at 3500 kbps produces roughly 25 MB per minute.

### Can I capture system audio (desktop sound) instead of microphone input?

Yes. With `VideoCaptureCoreX`, pass a speaker from `DeviceEnumerator.Shared.AudioOutputsAsync(AudioOutputDeviceAPI.WASAPI2)` to `LoopbackAudioCaptureDeviceSourceSettings`, as the WPF app above does: it records whatever plays on that device, with no special driver. With `VideoCaptureCore`, call `Audio_CaptureDevices()` to enumerate all available audio devices, then select a loopback or system audio device (such as "Stereo Mix" or "What U Hear") by name. Set `Audio_RecordAudio = true` and `Audio_PlayAudio = false`. The available loopback device names depend on your audio hardware and drivers. You can record both microphone and system audio simultaneously by configuring additional audio sources.

### How do I record a specific monitor in a multi-monitor setup?

With `VideoCaptureCoreX`, set `MonitorIndex` on `ScreenCaptureD3D11SourceSettings` (`0` is the first monitor, `-1` the primary) and leave `Rectangle` empty, as it is by default, to capture that monitor whole at its native resolution. With `VideoCaptureCore`, set `DisplayIndex` on `ScreenCaptureSourceSettings`. `0` is the primary monitor. A positive value is the number in that monitor's device name (`\\.\DISPLAY2` is `2`), which `Screen.AllScreens[i].DeviceName` gives; it is not `i`. Combine with `FullScreen = true` to capture the entire selected display. You can also set `FullScreen = false` with `Left/Top/Right/Bottom` coordinates to capture a specific region on the chosen monitor.

### What frame rate should I use for screen recording?

The default frame rate is 10 FPS. Use 15 FPS for presentations, slides, and mostly static content. Use 25–30 FPS for software tutorials and UI demonstrations where smooth mouse movement matters. Use 60 FPS for game recording or high-motion content. Higher frame rates increase file size and CPU usage proportionally. Set the frame rate via `ScreenCaptureD3D11SourceSettings.FrameRate` with `VideoCaptureCoreX`, or `ScreenCaptureSourceSettings.FrameRate` with `VideoCaptureCore`.

## Video Transcript

### What we build

Let's record the screen and the system sound to an MP4 file in a C# WPF app with the VisioForge Video Capture SDK. Here's what we build. The app records the whole primary monitor, with the mouse cursor, and the sound that plays on the speakers. It writes MP4, with H.264 encoded on the GPU when the PC has a hardware encoder, and AAC audio. A VideoView shows a live preview, and the window is laid out in XAML. The code behind it is about ninety lines of C#. This is the finished app, recording. The preview shows the screen, and the screen contains the preview, so it repeats itself like two facing mirrors.

### Prerequisites

You need Windows 10 or 11, and Visual Studio 2022 or 2026 with the .NET desktop development workload. The project targets .NET 8 or later. The written guide also shows screen recording on the classic VideoCaptureCore engine.

### Create a WPF project

In Visual Studio, create a new project. Search for WPF, and pick WPF Application for C#. Name the project ScreenCaptureMp4Wpf. Choose .NET 10 and click Create. Visual Studio opens MainWindow.xaml, with the designer above and the XAML below.

### Add the NuGet packages

Now add three NuGet packages. The Video Capture SDK itself. CrossPlatform Core, the GStreamer runtime the X engine runs on. And CrossPlatform Libav, which holds the AAC encoder. Or use the NuGet Package Manager: right-click the project, Manage NuGet Packages, and install VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture from the Browse tab. Then install the Core and Libav packages for Windows x64. The Installed tab lists all three. These are the x64 packages, so set PlatformTarget to x64 in the project file. A 32-bit app takes the x86 packages instead.

### Build the window in XAML

The window is written in XAML. First the window itself, with a two-column grid and a VideoView, and the designer draws it right away. Map the VisioForge.Core.UI.WPF namespace to a prefix, here vf. The VideoView goes into the right-hand column: that is where the live preview is drawn. The window also names its Loaded and Closing handlers. Next, the speakers list and a checkbox for the sound. The left-hand column is a StackPanel with a label, a combo box for the speakers, and a checkbox that turns the sound on or off. It starts checked. Last, the Start and Stop buttons. Each button names a Click handler. Both start disabled: Start until the SDK has loaded, and Stop until a recording runs. Every handler the XAML names goes into MainWindow.xaml.cs, and the next chapters write them.

### Initialize the SDK

MainWindow.xaml.cs starts with these usings. A WPF project leaves System.IO out of its implicit usings, so add it for Path. When the window loads, await VisioForgeX.InitSDKAsync once. Then create the VideoCaptureCoreX engine and pass it the VideoView, where the preview is drawn. Engine errors arrive in the OnError event; here they go to the title bar.

### List the speakers

AudioOutputsAsync with WASAPI2 lists the speakers and headphones. Their names fill the list, and the first one is selected. Start is enabled only now, once the SDK has loaded. WASAPI loopback records whatever plays on an output device. It needs no Stereo Mix and no virtual cable. Pick the device the sound actually plays on, because loopback records only that one.

### Capture the screen

In the Start handler, set the video source to ScreenCaptureD3D11SourceSettings. Out of the box it captures the whole primary monitor with the mouse cursor. The default frame rate is ten, so set thirty. The source uses DXGI Desktop Duplication, and Windows Graphics Capture where Desktop Duplication is not supported. MonitorIndex picks another monitor, and CaptureCursor set to false leaves the cursor out.

### Record the system sound

When the checkbox is checked and a device is selected, the audio source is LoopbackAudioCaptureDeviceSourceSettings for that device, and Audio\_Record is on. Otherwise there's no audio source, and the MP4 holds video only. Audio\_Play is false, so the recorded sound is not played back into the speakers.

### Write the MP4

Add an MP4Output that writes to the Videos folder, with the date and time in the file name, so a second recording never overwrites the first. An output stays in the engine after a recording, so Outputs\_Clear runs before each new one. With no encoder settings, MP4Output picks NVIDIA NVENC, then AMD AMF, then Intel Quick Sync, and OpenH264 on the CPU when the PC has none of them. The audio is AAC. H264EncoderBlock.CanEncodeAsync encodes a few test frames when you need to know that a GPU encoder really works.

### Start and stop

StartAsync returns whether the capture started, and the buttons follow it. StopAsync finalizes the MP4 file. If the window closes during a recording, cancel the close, await StopAsync, and close again. On that second pass the engine is disposed and the SDK released, so the file is always complete.

### Run it

Run the app from Visual Studio. Once the SDK has loaded, the speakers list fills and Start is enabled. Click Start. The preview shows the screen with the app inside it, again and again. The alarm sound that plays meanwhile goes into the file through loopback. Stop finalizes the MP4. Then close the window. The file lands in Videos: 4K at thirty frames per second, with the system sound.

### Common mistakes

A few common mistakes. Leaving out the Libav package, which holds the AAC encoder. Mixing x86 and x64 packages, or running an x86 app with the x64 ones. Forgetting that every window on the recorded monitor ends up in the video, the app's own window included: on a PC with two monitors, move it to the one that is not recorded. And loopback on a device the sound does not play on. Engine errors arrive in the OnError event.

### Next steps

There are also guides for recording a region or a single window, adding a microphone, webcam recording and network streaming. The full source is on GitHub, and the docs are at visioforge.com/help. Thanks for watching.

## Record the Screen to WMV in C# WinForms (WMV 9, WMA, CBR)
**URL:** https://www.visioforge.com/help/docs/dotnet/videocapture/video-tutorials/screen-capture-wmv/
**Description:** Record the screen and the speaker sound to WMV in C# WinForms with VideoCaptureCore - Windows Media codecs at a constant bitrate, checked with ffprobe.
**Tags:** Video Capture SDK, .NET, DirectShow, VideoCaptureCore, VideoCaptureCoreX, Windows, WinForms, Capture, Encoding, Screen Capture, MP4, AVI, WMV, C#, NuGet
**API:** VideoCaptureCore, ScreenCaptureSourceSettings, AudioCaptureSource, WMVOutput, VideoCaptureCoreX, VideoView

# C# Screen Capture to WMV Implementation Guide

[Video Capture SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/video-capture-sdk-net)

## Overview

This tutorial records a whole monitor and the sound from the speakers to a WMV file in a C# WinForms app with the VideoCaptureCore engine. The monitor, the frame rate and the mouse cursor are picked on the form, and the sound comes from the VisioForge What You Hear source. The output is a `WMVOutput` with custom settings: Windows Media Video 9 at a constant 10 Mbps and WMA audio, with the codecs and the audio format picked from the lists Windows reports.

This part uses the Windows-only VideoCaptureCore engine, the SDK's DirectShow engine. VideoCaptureCoreX writes WMV as well: see [VideoCaptureCoreX](#modern-api-video-capture-sdk-x) below.

## Video Walkthrough

## Source Code Repository

The complete project, with the designer file, is on GitHub:

[Source code on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Video%20Capture%20SDK/_VideoTutorials/screen-capture-wmv-winforms)

## When to Use WMV for Screen Recording

WMV (Windows Media Video) uses Microsoft's Windows Media codecs and the ASF container. It remains useful in specific Windows-centric scenarios:

- **Native Windows playback** - WMV files play on Windows out of the box, and the Windows Media encoders come with Windows: no GPU and no codec pack
- **A known file size** - at a constant bitrate, the size of the file has a ceiling you know before you record
- **Smaller files than AVI** - in the video, a 4K screen at 15 frames per second takes about 33 MB a minute; in the [AVI tutorial](../screen-capture-avi/), a 4K screen at only 10 frames per second with MJPEG takes about 30 MB a second
- **Legacy enterprise environments** - many corporate environments standardize on Windows Media formats for internal video distribution

**Trade-off:** WMV is a Windows-centric format with limited support on macOS, Linux and phones. For cross-platform compatibility, [MP4 is the recommended format](../screen-capture-mp4/).

## Required Packages

Install the [VisioForge.DotNet.Core](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core/) package and the video capture redist. Its DirectShow filters include the screen source and the What You Hear sound source; the WMV encoders come with Windows.

Set `PlatformTarget` in the project file to match the redist (`x64` or `x86`). On the N editions of Windows, install the Media Feature Pack for the Windows Media encoders.

```
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x64
```

For a 32-bit (x86) application, use the x86 package instead: `VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x86`.

`VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture`, the package in the Try it block at the top of this page, works as well: it installs the same `VisioForge.DotNet.Core`. The redist packages are needed either way.

## Implementation Example with C# Code

The form has a `VideoView`, combo boxes for the monitor, frame rate, sound device, video codec, audio codec and audio format, "Mouse cursor" and "Record sound" check boxes (both checked), and Start and Stop buttons; the designer file is in the source code above. The project targets .NET 10 with implicit usings. On .NET Framework 4.7.2, `Form1.cs` builds unchanged in an SDK-style project with `<LangVersion>10</LangVersion>` and `<ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>`; in `Program.cs`, replace `ApplicationConfiguration.Initialize()` with `Application.EnableVisualStyles()` and `Application.SetCompatibleTextRenderingDefault(false)`.

```
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.Output;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoCapture;
using VisioForge.Core.UI;
using VisioForge.Core.VideoCapture;

namespace ScreenCaptureWmv;

public partial class Form1 : Form
{
    private VideoCaptureCore videoCapture1 = null!;

    public Form1()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    // The engine names a monitor by the N of its device name, \\.\DISPLAYN
    private static int MonitorNumber(Screen screen) =>
        int.Parse(screen.DeviceName.Replace(@"\\.\DISPLAY", string.Empty));

    private void Form1_Load(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        videoCapture1 = new VideoCaptureCore(VideoView1 as IVideoView);

        // Show SDK errors in the title bar
        videoCapture1.OnError += (_, args) => BeginInvoke(() => Text = args.Message);

        foreach (var screen in Screen.AllScreens)
            cbMonitor.Items.Add(MonitorNumber(screen));

        cbMonitor.SelectedItem = MonitorNumber(Screen.PrimaryScreen!);

        cbFrameRate.Items.AddRange(new object[] { 5, 10, 15, 25, 30 });
        cbFrameRate.SelectedItem = 15;

        // "VisioForge What You Hear Source" records what plays on the speakers
        foreach (var device in videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevices())
            cbSound.Items.Add(device.Name);

        cbSound.SelectedItem = "VisioForge What You Hear Source";
        if (cbSound.SelectedIndex < 0 && cbSound.Items.Count > 0) cbSound.SelectedIndex = 0;
        cbRecordSound.Enabled = cbAudioCodec.Enabled = cbAudioFormat.Enabled = cbSound.Items.Count > 0;
        cbRecordSound.CheckedChanged += (_, _) => cbAudioCodec.Enabled = cbAudioFormat.Enabled = cbRecordSound.Checked; // audio settings need sound

        // The Windows Media codecs that can encode at a constant bitrate
        foreach (var codec in videoCapture1.WMV_CustomProfile_VideoCodecs(WMVStreamMode.CBR))
            cbVideoCodec.Items.Add(codec);

        foreach (var codec in videoCapture1.WMV_CustomProfile_AudioCodecs(WMVStreamMode.CBR))
            cbAudioCodec.Items.Add(codec);

        cbVideoCodec.SelectedItem = "Windows Media Video 9";
        if (cbVideoCodec.SelectedIndex < 0 && cbVideoCodec.Items.Count > 0) cbVideoCodec.SelectedIndex = 0;
        cbAudioCodec.SelectedItem = "Windows Media Audio 9.2";
        if (cbAudioCodec.SelectedIndex < 0 && cbAudioCodec.Items.Count > 0) cbAudioCodec.SelectedIndex = 0;
    }

    private void cbAudioCodec_SelectedIndexChanged(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        // The sample rates, channels and bitrates this audio codec offers
        cbAudioFormat.Items.Clear();
        foreach (var format in videoCapture1.WMV_CustomProfile_AudioFormats(cbAudioCodec.Text, WMVStreamMode.CBR))
            cbAudioFormat.Items.Add(format);

        var index = cbAudioFormat.Items.IndexOf("CBR 128 kbps, 44100 Hz, Stereo, 16 bit");
        if (cbAudioFormat.Items.Count > 0) cbAudioFormat.SelectedIndex = index >= 0 ? index : 0;
    }

    private async void btStart_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        if (cbVideoCodec.SelectedItem is null)
        {
            Text = "No video codec selected";
            return;
        }

        var recordSound = cbRecordSound.Checked && cbSound.SelectedItem is not null;
        if (recordSound && cbAudioFormat.SelectedItem is null)
        {
            Text = "No audio format selected";
            return;
        }

        Text = "Screen to WMV";

        // The whole monitor at the frame rate from the list
        var frameRate = (int)cbFrameRate.SelectedItem!;
        videoCapture1.Screen_Capture_Source = new ScreenCaptureSourceSettings
        {
            FullScreen = true,
            AllowDesktopDuplicationEngine = true, // DXGI Desktop Duplication: faster than GDI
            DisplayIndex = (int)cbMonitor.SelectedItem!,
            GrabMouseCursor = cbCursor.Checked,
            FrameRate = new VideoFrameRate(frameRate)
        };

        videoCapture1.Audio_RecordAudio = recordSound;
        // No device when the sound is off: a What You Hear device left here still opens the speakers
        videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevice = recordSound ? new AudioCaptureSource(cbSound.Text) : null;
        videoCapture1.Audio_PlayAudio = false; // never play the captured sound back into the speakers

        var wmv = new WMVOutput
        {
            Mode = WMVMode.CustomSettings,

            Custom_Video_StreamPresent = true,
            Custom_Video_Codec = cbVideoCodec.Text,
            Custom_Video_Mode = WMVStreamMode.CBR,
            Custom_Video_Bitrate = 10000, // kbps
            Custom_Video_SizeSameAsInput = true, // the monitor's resolution
            Custom_Video_FrameRate = frameRate,
            Custom_Video_KeyFrameInterval = 2, // seconds

            Custom_Audio_StreamPresent = recordSound,
            Custom_Audio_Codec = cbAudioCodec.Text,
            Custom_Audio_Format = cbAudioFormat.Text,
            Custom_Audio_Mode = WMVStreamMode.CBR,
        };

        videoCapture1.Output_Filename = Path.Combine(
            Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.MyVideos), "output.wmv");
        videoCapture1.Output_Format = wmv;
        videoCapture1.Mode = VideoCaptureMode.ScreenCapture;

        btStart.Enabled = false;
        var started = await videoCapture1.StartAsync();
        btStop.Enabled = started;
        btStart.Enabled = !started;
    }

    private async void btStop_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        btStop.Enabled = false;
        await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
        btStart.Enabled = true;
    }

    private async void Form1_FormClosing(object sender, FormClosingEventArgs e)
    {
        // Finish the WMV before the window goes away
        if (!btStart.Enabled)
        {
            e.Cancel = true;
            if (!btStop.Enabled) return; // already starting or stopping

            btStop.Enabled = false;
            await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
            btStart.Enabled = true;
            BeginInvoke(Close); // close again once this handler has returned
            return;
        }

        videoCapture1.Dispose();
    }
}
```

## Key Implementation Features

1. **Monitor** - `DisplayIndex` takes the number at the end of the monitor's Windows device name, `\\.\DISPLAY1` → `1`; `MonitorNumber` reads it from `Screen.DeviceName`, and the primary monitor is selected
2. **Screen Source** - `FullScreen` records the whole monitor at its full resolution, and `AllowDesktopDuplicationEngine` captures through Windows Desktop Duplication instead of GDI. `GrabMouseCursor` is off by default and `FrameRate` is 10 by default; the app records at 15
3. **Speaker Sound** - `VisioForge What You Hear Source`, from the video capture redist, records what plays on the speakers. With Record sound off, the app sets `Audio_RecordAudio` to `false` and clears `Audio_CaptureDevice` too, and `Audio_PlayAudio` stays `false` so the recorded sound isn't played back into the speakers
4. **Windows Media Codecs** - `WMV_CustomProfile_VideoCodecs(WMVStreamMode.CBR)` and `WMV_CustomProfile_AudioCodecs(WMVStreamMode.CBR)` list the Windows Media encoders that work at a constant bitrate, and `WMV_CustomProfile_AudioFormats(codec, WMVStreamMode.CBR)` lists the formats of one audio codec. Pick the names from these lists rather than typing them. Windows Media Video 9 records a 4K screen
5. **Custom Settings** - `new WMVOutput()` alone uses a built-in profile; `Mode = WMVMode.CustomSettings` takes the `Custom_Video_*` and `Custom_Audio_*` values instead. `Custom_Video_Bitrate` is in kbps, so `10000` is 10 Mbps; `Custom_Video_SizeSameAsInput` keeps the monitor's resolution, and `Custom_Video_KeyFrameInterval` is in seconds. The audio stream is written only when `Custom_Audio_StreamPresent` is `true`
6. **Asynchronous Operation** - `StartAsync` and `StopAsync` keep the UI responsive, and closing the form finishes the WMV file first

## Check the File with ffprobe

```
cd ([Environment]::GetFolderPath('MyVideos'))
ffprobe -v error -of compact output.wmv -show_entries format=format_name,duration,size:stream=codec_name,width,height,sample_rate,channels

# stream|codec_name=wmv3|width=3840|height=2160
# stream|codec_name=wmav2|sample_rate=44100|channels=2
# format|format_name=asf|duration=16.731000|size=9157531
```

The container is ASF, the format behind WMV. `wmv3` is ffprobe's name for Windows Media Video 9, and `wmav2` is the WMA stream. Seventeen seconds of a 4K screen is 9.2 megabytes (8.7 MB as Windows Explorer counts them), or 4.4 Mbps: 10000 kbps is the ceiling, and a desktop that barely moves takes less.

## Video Capture SDK X (VideoCaptureCoreX)

The cross-platform API uses `VideoCaptureCoreX`. For the complete console application pattern with screen capture setup, audio configuration, and recording lifecycle, see the [Screen Capture to MP4](../screen-capture-mp4/#modern-api-video-capture-sdk-x) guide. To output WMV instead of MP4, replace the output configuration:

```
using VisioForge.Core.Types.X.Output;

// WMV output (Windows Media Video + WMA audio codecs)
var wmvOutput = new WMVOutput(outputPath);
videoCapture.Outputs_Add(wmvOutput, autostart: true);
```

Region capture, multi-monitor recording, audio, cursor highlighting, and GPU encoding options are covered in the [MP4 guide](../screen-capture-mp4/) — all source configuration features work identically with WMV output.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### When should I use WMV instead of MP4 for screen recording?

Choose WMV when your target audience uses Windows and you need native playback without additional codec installation, when the file size has to stay under a known ceiling, or when working within enterprise environments that standardize on Windows Media formats. For cross-platform distribution or web publishing, MP4 with H.264 is the better choice: broader device support and better compression.

### Why does my WMV file have no sound?

Check that "Record sound" is on and that `VisioForge What You Hear Source` is selected, not a microphone: it records what plays on the speakers, and it ships in the video capture redist. With sound on, `Custom_Audio_StreamPresent` must be `true` and `Custom_Audio_Format` must be a name from `WMV_CustomProfile_AudioFormats` for the selected audio codec.

### How do I set the WMV bitrate?

Set `Mode = WMVMode.CustomSettings`, `Custom_Video_Mode = WMVStreamMode.CBR` and `Custom_Video_Bitrate` in kilobits per second: `10000` is 10 Mbps. The audio bitrate is part of the audio format name, such as `CBR 128 kbps, 44100 Hz, Stereo, 16 bit`.

## Video Transcript

### What we build

Let's record the screen and the sound from the speakers to a WMV file in a C# WinForms app with the VisioForge Video Capture SDK. Here's what we build. A WinForms app that records a whole monitor to a WMV file. The monitor, the frame rate and the mouse cursor are picked on the form. It also records the sound that plays on the speakers, as WMA audio. The video is Windows Media Video 9, at a constant bitrate we set ourselves: ten megabits per second. And the codecs and the audio format come from the lists Windows reports. This is the finished app, recording the screen it runs on.

### WMV, AVI or MP4

When is WMV the right choice? A WMV file plays on Windows out of the box. The Windows Media encoders come with Windows, so you need no GPU and no codec pack. With a constant bitrate, the size of the file has a known ceiling before you record. And it's small: here about thirty megabytes a minute, for a 4K screen at fifteen frames per second. The same screen in AVI with MJPEG took about twenty-eight megabytes every second. For the web, phones and Macs, MP4 with H.264 is the better choice. That's the screen capture to MP4 video.

### Prerequisites

You need Windows 10 or 11, and Visual Studio 2022 or 2026 with the .NET desktop development workload. The project can target .NET 8 or later, or .NET Framework 4.7.2. No camera and no microphone this time. VideoCaptureCore is the SDK's DirectShow engine, so this app runs on Windows only.

### Create a WinForms project

In Visual Studio, create a new project. Search for Windows Forms, and pick Windows Forms App for C#. Name the project ScreenCaptureWmv. Choose .NET 10 and click Create. Visual Studio opens the empty form in the designer.

### Add the NuGet packages

Now add two NuGet packages: the SDK itself, and the video capture redist. It carries the DirectShow filters, the screen source and the What You Hear sound source among them. The WMV encoders come with Windows, so that's all. In Visual Studio, that's Manage NuGet Packages. Browse for VisioForge.DotNet.Core and install it. Then install the video capture redist for x64. The redist is the x64 one, so set PlatformTarget to x64 in the project file. An x86 app takes the x86 redist instead.

### Design the WinForms form

From the Toolbox, draw a VideoView, where the app previews what it records. Add a label and a combo box for the monitor, and give every control a clear name in the Properties window. Do the same for the frame rate, the sound device, the video codec, the audio codec and the audio format. Add two check boxes, both checked: the mouse cursor, and Record sound. Then the Start and Stop buttons. Stop stays disabled until a recording starts. Double-click the form, the audio codec list and both buttons. Visual Studio adds an empty handler for each one.

### Create the capture engine

At the top of Form1.cs, add these usings. In the form's Load handler, create the VideoCaptureCore engine and pass it the VideoView, where the preview is drawn. Engine errors arrive in the OnError event. Here they go to the title bar.

### Fill the lists

The engine names a monitor by the number at the end of its Windows device name: one for DISPLAY1, two for DISPLAY2. A small helper reads that number. The Load handler lists every monitor, and selects the primary one. The frame rate list holds a few fixed values. Fifteen frames per second is selected. Audio\_CaptureDevices lists the sound devices. VisioForge What You Hear Source records whatever plays on the speakers, so it's selected when it's there. With no sound device at all, Record sound and both audio lists are disabled. And the audio codec and format only matter with sound, so they follow Record sound.

### Windows Media codecs

WMV\_CustomProfile\_VideoCodecs and WMV\_CustomProfile\_AudioCodecs list the Windows Media encoders that can work at a constant bitrate. We fill both lists, and select Windows Media Video 9 and Windows Media Audio 9.2, or the first codec when one isn't there. When the audio codec changes, WMV\_CustomProfile\_AudioFormats lists what that codec offers. We pick 128 kilobits per second, 44.1 kilohertz stereo: the rate What You Hear delivers here, so nothing is resampled. On this PC the video list has seven entries: Windows Media Video 9, its Advanced Profile, the Screen and Image codecs, and the older V7 and V8. Windows Media Video 9 records this 4K screen, so it's our default. For audio at a constant bitrate there's WMA 9.2 and WMA 10 Professional. Each audio format names its bitrate, sample rate, channels and bits. Always pick these names from the lists, never type them by hand.

### Capture the screen

The Start handler first checks that a video codec is selected. If not, it says so in the title bar. Sound is recorded only when Record sound is checked and a device is selected. Then an audio format is needed as well. Then it describes the screen source. FullScreen records the whole monitor. AllowDesktopDuplicationEngine captures through Windows Desktop Duplication instead of GDI. DisplayIndex is the monitor number from the list, GrabMouseCursor draws the cursor into the video, and FrameRate is the rate from the list. A quick recap. FullScreen records the whole monitor at its full resolution. DisplayIndex is the number from the monitor's device name. The cursor is off by default, and the frame rate is ten. This video records a 4K screen at fifteen frames per second.

### Record the speaker sound

With sound on, the app records the selected device. With it off, the device is cleared too: a What You Hear device left in place still opens the speakers. Audio\_PlayAudio stays off, so the recorded sound isn't played back into the speakers it comes from.

### WMVOutput: custom settings

Now the output. A WMVOutput in CustomSettings mode takes our own settings instead of a built-in profile. The video stream uses the codec from the list at a constant 10000 kilobits per second. SizeSameAsInput keeps the monitor's resolution, the frame rate is the one we picked, and there's a keyframe every two seconds. The audio stream takes the codec and the format from the lists, and it's there only when sound is on. Then write output.wmv into the Videos folder, and switch the engine to screen capture mode. A plain WMVOutput uses a built-in profile. CustomSettings gives us our own codec, bitrate and size. Custom\_Video\_Bitrate is in kilobits per second, so 10000 means ten megabits. That's the ceiling: a desktop that barely moves needs less, and this recording came to about four point four megabits per second. And a keyframe every two seconds gives the player a seek point every two seconds.

### Start and stop

Start and Stop are async. StartAsync returns once the capture is running, and StopAsync finishes writing the WMV file.

### Close the window

Closing the window while it records would leave the WMV unfinished. In the Properties window, on the Events tab, double-click FormClosing to add this handler. While recording, it cancels the close. Then it stops the recording, and closes the window again once the handler has returned. With nothing recording, the handler disposes the engine.

### Run it

Run the app from Visual Studio. The lists fill in: the monitor, the frame rate, the sound device, both codecs and the audio format. The audio format list has every bitrate and sample rate the codec offers. Ours stays selected. A sound plays on the speakers, and Start begins the recording. The preview shows the screen with the cursor. Stop finishes output.wmv, and then we close the window.

### Check the file with ffprobe

The file lands in Videos: under nine megabytes for seventeen seconds of a 4K screen. ffprobe shows what's inside. The container is ASF, the format behind WMV. The video is Windows Media Video 9, which ffprobe calls wmv3, at 3840x2160. The audio is WMA, 44.1 kilohertz stereo: the sound from the speakers.

### Common mistakes

A few common mistakes. A missing redist package, so the engine won't start. A silent file, because Record sound was off, or a microphone was selected instead of What You Hear. Codec and format names typed by hand: take them from the lists. Custom\_Video\_Bitrate written in bits per second: it's in kilobits. And closing the window mid-recording: await StopAsync first.

### Next steps

Next, the screen capture to MP4 video saves the screen to H.264 files that play everywhere. The screen capture to AVI video keeps every frame as a whole picture, for editing. And the webcam to WMV video records a camera with the same Windows Media settings as here. The full source is on GitHub, and the docs are at visioforge.com/help. Thanks for watching.

## Record Webcam to AVI in C# WinForms (MJPEG, PCM, MP3)
**URL:** https://www.visioforge.com/help/docs/dotnet/videocapture/video-tutorials/video-capture-camera-avi/
**Description:** Record a webcam to AVI in a C# WinForms app with VideoCaptureCore - pick the video codec, PCM or MP3 audio, and check the file with ffprobe.
**Tags:** Video Capture SDK, .NET, VideoCaptureCore, Windows, WinForms, Capture, Webcam, AVI, MJPEG, MP3, C#, NuGet
**API:** VideoCaptureCore, VideoCaptureSource, AudioCaptureSource, AVIOutput, MP3Output, VideoView

# Webcam to AVI File Recording in .NET C# Applications

[Video Capture SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/video-capture-sdk-net)

## Overview

This tutorial records a webcam to an AVI file in a C# WinForms app with the VideoCaptureCore engine. The video codec is picked from the ones installed on the PC (MJPEG by default), and the audio is uncompressed PCM or MP3.

**When AVI is the right choice over MP4:** with MJPEG, every frame is a whole picture, so you can cut and edit on any frame and read each frame on its own for analysis, and PCM audio has no loss. The price is size: about twenty megabytes every second at 1080p. For the web, phones and sharing, record [MP4 with H.264](../video-capture-webcam-mp4/) instead.

This tutorial uses the Windows-only VideoCaptureCore engine, the SDK's DirectShow engine. On macOS, Linux, Android and iOS, VideoCaptureCoreX records AVI as well: see [AVI output](../../../general/output-formats/avi/) and [Save Webcam Video in C#](../../guides/save-webcam-video/).

## Video Walkthrough

## Source Code Repository

The complete project, with the designer file, is on GitHub:

[Source code on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Video%20Capture%20SDK/_VideoTutorials/webcam-avi-winforms)

## Required Packages

Install the [VisioForge.DotNet.Core](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core/) package and the video capture redist with its DirectShow filters. AVI needs nothing more.

Set `PlatformTarget` in the project file to match the redist (`x64` or `x86`).

```
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x64
```

For a 32-bit (x86) application, use the x86 package instead: `VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x86`.

`VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture`, the package in the Try it block at the top of this page, works as well: it installs the same `VisioForge.DotNet.Core`. The redist packages are needed either way.

## Implementation Example with C# Code

The form has a `VideoView`, combo boxes for the camera, format, frame rate, microphone and video codec, an "MP3 audio" check box, and Start and Stop buttons; the designer file is in the source code above. The project targets .NET 10 with implicit usings. On .NET Framework 4.7.2, the same code builds in an SDK-style project with `<LangVersion>10</LangVersion>` and `<ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>`.

```
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.Output;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoCapture;
using VisioForge.Core.UI;
using VisioForge.Core.VideoCapture;

namespace WebcamAvi;

public partial class Form1 : Form
{
    private VideoCaptureCore videoCapture1 = null!;

    public Form1()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private void Form1_Load(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        videoCapture1 = new VideoCaptureCore(VideoView1 as IVideoView);

        // Show SDK errors in the title bar
        videoCapture1.OnError += (_, args) => BeginInvoke(() => Text = args.Message);

        foreach (var device in videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices())
            cbCamera.Items.Add(device.Name);

        foreach (var device in videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevices())
            cbMicrophone.Items.Add(device.Name);

        if (cbCamera.Items.Count > 0) cbCamera.SelectedIndex = 0;
        if (cbMicrophone.Items.Count > 0) cbMicrophone.SelectedIndex = 0;
        cbMP3.Enabled = cbMicrophone.Items.Count > 0;

        // The video codecs installed on this PC
        foreach (var codec in videoCapture1.Video_Codecs())
            cbVideoCodec.Items.Add(codec);

        cbVideoCodec.SelectedItem = "MJPEG Compressor";
    }

    private void cbCamera_SelectedIndexChanged(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        cbFormat.Items.Clear();
        cbFrameRate.Items.Clear();
        var device = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices().First(d => d.Name == cbCamera.Text);
        foreach (var format in device.VideoFormats)
            cbFormat.Items.Add(format.Name);

        var index = cbFormat.Items.IndexOf("1920x1080 MJPG, 24 bit");
        if (cbFormat.Items.Count > 0) cbFormat.SelectedIndex = index >= 0 ? index : 0;
    }

    private void cbFormat_SelectedIndexChanged(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        cbFrameRate.Items.Clear();
        var device = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices().First(d => d.Name == cbCamera.Text);
        var format = device.VideoFormats.First(f => f.Name == cbFormat.Text);
        foreach (var frameRate in format.FrameRates)
            cbFrameRate.Items.Add(frameRate);

        var rate = cbFrameRate.Items.IndexOf(VideoFrameRate.FPS_30);
        if (cbFrameRate.Items.Count > 0) cbFrameRate.SelectedIndex = rate >= 0 ? rate : 0;
    }

    private async void btStart_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        if (cbFrameRate.SelectedItem is null)
        {
            Text = "No camera, format or frame rate";
            return;
        }

        if (cbVideoCodec.SelectedItem is null)
        {
            Text = "No video codec selected";
            return;
        }

        Text = "Webcam to AVI";

        videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevice = new VideoCaptureSource(cbCamera.Text);
        var camera = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevice;
        camera.Format_UseBest = false;
        camera.Format = cbFormat.Text;
        camera.FrameRate = (VideoFrameRate)cbFrameRate.SelectedItem;

        var mic = cbMicrophone.SelectedItem as string;
        videoCapture1.Audio_RecordAudio = mic is not null; // no microphone: record video only
        if (mic is not null) videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevice = new AudioCaptureSource(mic);
        videoCapture1.Audio_PlayAudio = false; // record the microphone without playing it back

        // Audio: MP3, or uncompressed PCM
        var avi = cbMP3.Checked ? new AVIOutput(new MP3Output()) : new AVIOutput();
        avi.Video_Codec = cbVideoCodec.Text;

        videoCapture1.Output_Filename = Path.Combine(
            Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.MyVideos), "output.avi");
        videoCapture1.Output_Format = avi;
        videoCapture1.Mode = VideoCaptureMode.VideoCapture;

        btStart.Enabled = false;
        var started = await videoCapture1.StartAsync();
        btStop.Enabled = started;
        btStart.Enabled = !started;
    }

    private async void btStop_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        btStop.Enabled = false;
        await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
        btStart.Enabled = true;
    }

    private async void Form1_FormClosing(object sender, FormClosingEventArgs e)
    {
        // Finish the AVI before the window goes away
        if (!btStart.Enabled)
        {
            e.Cancel = true;
            if (!btStop.Enabled) return; // already starting or stopping

            btStop.Enabled = false;
            await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
            btStart.Enabled = true;
            BeginInvoke(Close); // close again once this handler has returned
            return;
        }

        videoCapture1.Dispose();
    }
}
```

## Key Implementation Features

1. **Device and Format Selection** - The camera, its format, its frame rate and the microphone are picked from lists filled from the devices themselves; with no microphone, `Audio_RecordAudio` is set to `false` and the AVI holds video only
2. **Camera Format** - `Format_UseBest` is on by default: it picks the highest resolution up to 1080p, then prefers MJPG and the fastest frame rate. To record 4K, or any format you choose, turn it off and set `Format` and `FrameRate`
3. **Video Codec** - `Video_Codecs()` returns the DirectShow video compressors installed on the PC; `AVIOutput.Video_Codec` takes one of those names and defaults to `MJPEG Compressor`, which stores every frame as a JPEG picture. A codec you install yourself shows up in the same list
4. **Audio** - A plain `AVIOutput` writes uncompressed PCM, 16-bit stereo at 44.1 kHz, about ten megabytes a minute; `new AVIOutput(new MP3Output())` writes MP3 at 192 kbps, about one and a half megabytes a minute
5. **Asynchronous Operation** - `StartAsync` and `StopAsync` keep the UI responsive, and closing the form finishes the AVI file first

## Check the File with ffprobe

```
cd ([Environment]::GetFolderPath('MyVideos'))
ffprobe -v error -of compact output.avi -show_entries format=format_name,duration,size:stream=codec_name,width,height,sample_rate,channels

# stream|codec_name=mjpeg|width=1920|height=1080
# stream|codec_name=pcm_s16le|sample_rate=44100|channels=2
# format|format_name=avi|duration=14.883073|size=316108288
```

Fifteen seconds of 1080p MJPEG is about three hundred megabytes, roughly 170 megabits per second, which is why AVI is for editing and analysis, not for sharing.

## Video Transcript

### What we build

Let's capture a webcam to an AVI file in a C# WinForms app with the VisioForge Video Capture SDK. Here's what we build. A WinForms window with a live camera preview. It records an AVI file with any video codec installed on the PC, MJPEG by default. The audio is uncompressed PCM, or MP3 when you tick a box. The camera, its format, the frame rate and the microphone are picked from lists. This is the finished app, recording from a Logitech C920.

### AVI or MP4

When is AVI the right choice over MP4? With MJPEG, every frame is a whole picture, so you can cut and edit on any frame, and read each frame on its own for analysis. PCM audio has no loss. Double-click the form, the camera and format lists, and both buttons. Visual Studio adds an empty handler for each one.

### Create the capture engine

At the top of Form1.cs, add these usings. In the form's Load handler, create the VideoCaptureCore engine and pass it the VideoView, where the live preview is drawn. Engine errors arrive in the OnError event. Here they go to the title bar.

### List the devices

Video\_CaptureDevices returns every camera, and Audio\_CaptureDevices every microphone. We list their names and select the first of each. Without a microphone, the MP3 box is disabled. When the camera changes, its handler fills the format list with the formats of that camera, and picks 1920x1080 MJPG when it's there. When the format changes, its handler fills the frame rate list the same way, and picks thirty frames per second.

### Choose the camera format

The Start handler first checks that a frame rate and a video codec are selected. If not, it says so in the title bar. Then it selects the camera by name, turns Format\_UseBest off, and passes the format and the frame rate picked from the lists. Format\_UseBest is on by default. It picks the highest resolution up to 1080p, then prefers MJPG and the fastest frame rate. To record 4K, or any format you choose, turn it off and set Format and FrameRate, as we do here.

### Select the microphone

With no microphone in the list, the app captures video only. Otherwise it records the selected one. Audio\_PlayAudio is off, so the microphone isn't played through the speakers while you record.

### Choose the video codec

Back in the Load handler, Video\_Codecs lists the video codecs installed on this PC. We fill the codec list and select MJPEG Compressor. Video\_Codecs returns the DirectShow video compressors on this PC. This one has two: MJPEG Compressor and DV Video Encoder. MJPEG stores every frame as a JPEG picture. DV writes standard-definition DV only. A codec you install yourself shows up in the same list.

### AVIOutput: PCM or MP3 audio

Now the output. A plain AVIOutput writes uncompressed PCM audio. Pass an MP3Output to its constructor, and the audio is MP3 instead. Set Video\_Codec to the name from the list, write output.avi into the Videos folder, and switch the engine to video capture mode, so it records and not just previews. A plain AVIOutput writes PCM: 16-bit stereo at 44.1 kilohertz, with no loss, about ten megabytes a minute. With an MP3Output it writes MP3 at 192 kilobits per second, about one and a half megabytes a minute. Next to MJPEG video, both are small.

### Start and stop

Start and Stop are async. StartAsync returns once the capture is running, and StopAsync finishes writing the AVI file.

### Close the window

Closing the window while it records would leave the AVI unfinished. In the Properties window, on the Events tab, double-click FormClosing to add this handler. While recording, it cancels the close. Then it stops the recording, and closes the window again once the handler has returned. With nothing recording, the handler disposes the engine.

### Run it

Run the app from Visual Studio. The camera, format and microphone lists fill in from the devices. The codec list shows the two codecs on this PC. MJPEG stays selected. Start begins the recording. The C920 takes a few seconds to send its first frame. Stop finishes output.avi, and then we close the window.

### Check the file with ffprobe

The file lands in Videos: about three hundred megabytes for fifteen seconds. ffprobe shows what's inside. The container is AVI. The video is MJPEG at 1920x1080. The audio is PCM, 16-bit, 44.1 kilohertz stereo. That's about 170 megabits per second, which is why AVI is for editing and analysis, not for sharing.

### Common mistakes

A few common mistakes. A missing redist package, so the engine won't start. A camera that's already open in another app. x86 and x64 packages mixed in one project. Closing the window mid-recording: await StopAsync first. And AVI where MP4 belongs: an hour of 1080p MJPEG runs to tens of gigabytes.

### Next steps

Next, the webcam to MP4 video saves the same camera to small H.264 files. There are also guides for IP cameras, screen recording and snapshots. The full source is on GitHub, and the docs are at visioforge.com/help. Thanks for watching.

# Webcam to MP4 Video Capture Implementation in .NET

## Introduction to Webcam Capture in .NET Applications

Creating applications that record video from webcams to MP4 files is a common requirement for many software projects. This tutorial provides a developer-focused approach to implementing this functionality using modern .NET techniques and the Video Capture SDK.

When implementing webcam recording capabilities, developers need to consider:

- Selecting the appropriate video and audio input devices
- Configuring video and audio compression settings
- Managing the capture lifecycle (initialization, start, stop)
- Handling output file creation and management

This tutorial uses the Windows-only VideoCaptureCore engine. [Video Capture SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/video-capture-sdk-net) also records webcams to MP4 on macOS, Linux, Android and iOS with VideoCaptureCoreX — see [Save Webcam Video in C#](../../guides/save-webcam-video/) and the [Android](../../../deployment-x/Android/) and [iOS](../../../deployment-x/iOS/) deployment guides.

Recording to MP4 needs the Premium edition of Video Capture SDK .NET — see [editions and pricing](https://www.visioforge.com/video-capture-sdk-net#pricing).
