## Implementation Example with C# Code

The following C# implementation demonstrates how to create a Windows Forms application that captures video from a webcam and saves it to an MP4 file. The form has a `VideoView`, combo boxes for the camera, format, frame rate and microphone, and Start and Stop buttons; the designer file is in the source code above. The project targets .NET 10 with implicit usings.

```
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.Output;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoCapture;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoEffects;
using VisioForge.Core.UI;
using VisioForge.Core.VideoCapture;

namespace WebcamMp4;

public partial class Form1 : Form
{
    private VideoCaptureCore videoCapture1 = null!;

    public Form1()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private void Form1_Load(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        videoCapture1 = new VideoCaptureCore(VideoView1 as IVideoView);

        // Show SDK errors in the title bar
        videoCapture1.OnError += (_, args) => BeginInvoke(() => Text = args.Message);

        foreach (var device in videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices())
            cbCamera.Items.Add(device.Name);

        foreach (var device in videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevices())
            cbMicrophone.Items.Add(device.Name);

        if (cbCamera.Items.Count > 0) cbCamera.SelectedIndex = 0;
        if (cbMicrophone.Items.Count > 0) cbMicrophone.SelectedIndex = 0;
    }

    private void cbCamera_SelectedIndexChanged(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        cbFormat.Items.Clear();
        cbFrameRate.Items.Clear();
        var device = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices().First(d => d.Name == cbCamera.Text);
        foreach (var format in device.VideoFormats)
            cbFormat.Items.Add(format.Name);

        var index = cbFormat.Items.IndexOf("1920x1080 MJPG, 24 bit");
        if (cbFormat.Items.Count > 0) cbFormat.SelectedIndex = index >= 0 ? index : 0;
    }

    private void cbFormat_SelectedIndexChanged(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        cbFrameRate.Items.Clear();
        var device = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices().First(d => d.Name == cbCamera.Text);
        var format = device.VideoFormats.First(f => f.Name == cbFormat.Text);
        foreach (var frameRate in format.FrameRates)
            cbFrameRate.Items.Add(frameRate);

        var rate = cbFrameRate.Items.IndexOf(VideoFrameRate.FPS_30);
        if (cbFrameRate.Items.Count > 0) cbFrameRate.SelectedIndex = rate >= 0 ? rate : 0;
    }

    private async void btStart_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        Text = cbFrameRate.SelectedItem is null ? "No camera, format or frame rate" : "Webcam to MP4";
        if (cbFrameRate.SelectedItem is null) return;

        videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevice = new VideoCaptureSource(cbCamera.Text);
        var camera = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevice;
        camera.Format_UseBest = false;
        camera.Format = cbFormat.Text;
        camera.FrameRate = (VideoFrameRate)cbFrameRate.SelectedItem;

        var mic = cbMicrophone.SelectedItem as string;
        videoCapture1.Audio_RecordAudio = mic is not null; // no microphone: record video only
        if (mic is not null) videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevice = new AudioCaptureSource(mic);
        videoCapture1.Audio_PlayAudio = false; // record the microphone without playing it back

        var mp4 = new MP4HWOutput();

        // NVIDIA, then Intel, then AMD, then the CPU encoder
        var gpu = VideoCaptureCore.HWEncodersAvailable();
        mp4.Video.Codec =
            gpu.NVENC_H264 ? MFVideoEncoder.NVENC_H264 :
            gpu.QSV_H264 ? MFVideoEncoder.QSV_H264 :
            gpu.AMD_H264 ? MFVideoEncoder.AMD_H264 :
            MFVideoEncoder.MS_H264;

        mp4.Video.AvgBitrate = 6000; // kbps
        mp4.Video.MaxBitrate = 9000;
        mp4.Video.RateControl = MFCommonRateControlMode.PeakConstrainedVBR;
        mp4.Video.Profile = MFH264Profile.Main;
        mp4.Audio.Bitrate = 192; // AAC, kbps

        videoCapture1.Output_Filename = Path.Combine(
            Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.MyVideos), "output.mp4");
        videoCapture1.Output_Format = mp4;
        videoCapture1.Mode = VideoCaptureMode.VideoCapture;

        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Enabled = true;
        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Clear();
        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Add(new VideoEffectTextLogo(true, "text")
        {
            Text = "Hello World!", Left = 50, Top = 50, FontColor = Color.Red
        });
        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Add(new VideoEffectTextLogo(true, "clock")
        {
            Mode = TextLogoMode.DateTime, DateTimeMask = "HH:mm:ss", Text = "",
            Left = 50, Top = 110
        });

        btStart.Enabled = false;
        var started = await videoCapture1.StartAsync();
        btStop.Enabled = started;
        btStart.Enabled = !started;
    }

    private async void btStop_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        btStop.Enabled = false;
        await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
        btStart.Enabled = true;
    }

    private async void Form1_FormClosing(object sender, FormClosingEventArgs e)
    {
        // Finish the MP4 before the window goes away
        if (!btStart.Enabled)
        {
            e.Cancel = true;
            if (!btStop.Enabled) return; // already starting or stopping

            btStop.Enabled = false;
            await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
            btStart.Enabled = true;
            BeginInvoke(Close); // close again once this handler has returned
            return;
        }

        videoCapture1.Dispose();
    }
}
```

## Key Implementation Features

This implementation provides several important capabilities for developers:

1. **Device and Format Selection** - The camera, its format, its frame rate and the microphone are picked from lists filled from the devices themselves; with no microphone, `Audio_RecordAudio` is set to `false` and the MP4 holds video only
2. **Hardware Encoding with a CPU Fallback** - `MP4HWOutput` encodes H.264 on an NVIDIA, Intel or AMD GPU; `HWEncodersAvailable` tells which encoders the PC has, and `MS_H264` runs on the CPU when none is present
3. **Encoder Settings** - An average of 6000 kbps, peaks up to 9000 kbps, the Main profile and AAC audio at 192 kbps
4. **Text Overlay** - A fixed text and a clock that shows the current time, added as video effects
5. **Asynchronous Operation** - `StartAsync` and `StopAsync` keep the UI responsive, and closing the form finishes the MP4 file first

## Advanced Configuration Options

Developers can extend the solution with additional features:

- HEVC instead of H.264: `NVENC_H265`, `QSV_H265` or `AMD_H265`
- Other on-the-fly video effects and transformations
- Multiple audio track support

## Video Transcript

### What we build

Let's record a webcam to an MP4 file in a C# WinForms app with the VisioForge Video Capture SDK. Here's what we build. A WinForms window with a live camera preview. It records MP4, with H.264 encoded on the GPU when the PC has one, and AAC audio. The camera, its format and the microphone are picked from lists, and the whole app is about a hundred lines of C#. This is the finished app, recording from a Logitech BRIO.

### Prerequisites

You need Windows 10 or 11, and Visual Studio 2022 or 2026 with the .NET desktop development workload. The project can target .NET 8 or later, or .NET Framework 4.7.2. This video is about WinForms. The WPF version comes next.

### Create a WinForms project

In Visual Studio, open File, New, Project. Search for Windows Forms, and pick Windows Forms App for C#. Name the project WebcamMp4. Choose .NET 10 and click Create. Visual Studio opens the empty form in the designer.

### Add the NuGet packages

Now add three NuGet packages: the SDK itself, the video capture redist and the MP4 redist. These are the x64 packages. An x86 app takes the x86 redists instead. You can also install the same three packages from the NuGet Package Manager.

### Design the WinForms form

From the Toolbox, draw a VideoView for the live preview. Add a label and a combo box for the camera, and give every control a clear name in the Properties window. Do the same for the camera format, the frame rate and the microphone. Add the Start and Stop buttons. Stop stays disabled until a recording starts. Double-click the form, the combo boxes and both buttons. Visual Studio adds an empty handler for each one.

### Create the capture engine

In the form's Load handler, create the VideoCaptureCore engine and pass it the VideoView, where the live preview is drawn.

### Enumerate cameras

Video\_CaptureDevices returns every camera on the machine. We list their names and select the first one. When the camera changes, its handler fills the format list with the formats of that camera. When the format changes, its handler fills the frame rate list the same way. A camera reports its name, formats like 1920x1080 MJPG or 1280x720 YUY2, and the frame rates of each format. MJPG is compressed in the camera, so high resolutions fit through USB. YUY2 is uncompressed, so USB 2 carries only lower resolutions.

### Choose the camera format

Select the camera by name. Then turn Format\_UseBest off, and pass the format and the frame rate picked from the lists. Format\_UseBest is on by default. It picks the highest resolution the camera offers, up to 1080p, and prefers MJPG. An empty format falls back to it as well.

### Select the microphone

The microphone works the same way. Audio\_CaptureDevices lists them, and we use the one picked in the list.

### MP4HWOutput: any GPU, CPU fallback

For the output, create an MP4HWOutput, write output.mp4 into the Videos folder, and switch the engine to video capture mode, so it records and not just previews. MP4HWOutput encodes on the GPU: NVENC on NVIDIA, Quick Sync on Intel, and AMF on AMD, in H.264 or HEVC. When there's no hardware encoder, the Windows encoder on the CPU takes over. The code and the file are the same on every PC. HWEncodersAvailable tells you which encoders this PC has. Take NVIDIA first, then Intel, then AMD, and fall back to the CPU encoder.

### Tune the H.264 encoder

Then tune the encoder: six thousand kilobits per second on average, peaks up to nine thousand, the Main profile, and AAC audio at a hundred and ninety-two. As a guide: 2500 to 4000 kilobits for 720p, 5000 to 8000 for 1080p, and 15000 to 25000 for 4K. Both bitrates are set in kilobits per second.

### Add a text overlay

Video effects add a text overlay: a fixed Hello World, and a clock that shows the current time on every frame.

### Start and stop

Start and Stop are async. StartAsync returns once the capture is running, and StopAsync finalizes the MP4 file. Run the app from Visual Studio. The format list comes straight from the camera. Start begins the recording, with the clock overlay ticking. Stop finalizes output.mp4. The file lands in Videos: 1920x1080, H.264 video and AAC audio.

### Common mistakes

A few common mistakes. A missing redist package, so the engine won't start. A camera that's already open in another app. x86 and x64 packages mixed in one project. And disposing the engine mid-capture: await StopAsync first. Engine errors arrive in the OnError event.

### Next steps

Next, we build the same app in WPF. There are also guides for IP cameras, screen recording, snapshots and network streaming. The full source is on GitHub, and the docs are at visioforge.com/help. Thanks for watching.

- The window, its lists and its buttons are written in XAML

<Window x:Class="WebcamMp4Wpf.MainWindow"

## Implementation Example with C# Code

The code behind the window. The project targets .NET 10 with implicit usings; a WPF project leaves `System.IO` out of them, so it is added for `Path`.

```
using System.ComponentModel;
using System.IO;
using System.Windows;
using System.Windows.Controls;
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.Output;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoCapture;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoEffects;
using VisioForge.Core.UI;
using VisioForge.Core.VideoCapture;

namespace WebcamMp4Wpf;

public partial class MainWindow : Window
{
    private VideoCaptureCore videoCapture1 = null!;

    public MainWindow()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private void Window_Loaded(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        videoCapture1 = new VideoCaptureCore(VideoView1 as IVideoView);

        // Show SDK errors in the title bar
        videoCapture1.OnError += (_, args) => Dispatcher.InvokeAsync(() => Title = args.Message);

        foreach (var device in videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices())
            cbCamera.Items.Add(device.Name);

        foreach (var device in videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevices())
            cbMicrophone.Items.Add(device.Name);

        if (cbCamera.Items.Count > 0) cbCamera.SelectedIndex = 0;
        if (cbMicrophone.Items.Count > 0) cbMicrophone.SelectedIndex = 0;
    }

    private void cbCamera_SelectionChanged(object sender, SelectionChangedEventArgs e)
    {
        cbFormat.Items.Clear();
        cbFrameRate.Items.Clear();
        var device = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices().First(d => d.Name == (string)cbCamera.SelectedItem);
        foreach (var format in device.VideoFormats)
            cbFormat.Items.Add(format.Name);

        var index = cbFormat.Items.IndexOf("1920x1080 MJPG, 24 bit");
        if (cbFormat.Items.Count > 0) cbFormat.SelectedIndex = index >= 0 ? index : 0;
    }

    private void cbFormat_SelectionChanged(object sender, SelectionChangedEventArgs e)
    {
        cbFrameRate.Items.Clear();
        if (cbFormat.SelectedItem is null) return; // the list was just cleared

        var device = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices().First(d => d.Name == (string)cbCamera.SelectedItem);
        var format = device.VideoFormats.First(f => f.Name == (string)cbFormat.SelectedItem);
        foreach (var frameRate in format.FrameRates)
            cbFrameRate.Items.Add(frameRate);

        var rate = cbFrameRate.Items.IndexOf(VideoFrameRate.FPS_30);
        if (cbFrameRate.Items.Count > 0) cbFrameRate.SelectedIndex = rate >= 0 ? rate : 0;
    }

    private async void btStart_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Title = cbFrameRate.SelectedItem is null ? "No camera, format or frame rate" : "Webcam to MP4";
        if (cbFrameRate.SelectedItem is null) return;

        videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevice = new VideoCaptureSource((string)cbCamera.SelectedItem);
        var camera = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevice;
        camera.Format_UseBest = false;
        camera.Format = (string)cbFormat.SelectedItem;
        camera.FrameRate = (VideoFrameRate)cbFrameRate.SelectedItem;

        var mic = (string)cbMicrophone.SelectedItem;
        videoCapture1.Audio_RecordAudio = mic is not null; // no microphone: record video only
        if (mic is not null) videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevice = new AudioCaptureSource(mic);
        videoCapture1.Audio_PlayAudio = false; // record the microphone without playing it back

        var mp4 = new MP4HWOutput();

        // NVIDIA, then Intel, then AMD, then the CPU encoder
        var gpu = VideoCaptureCore.HWEncodersAvailable();
        mp4.Video.Codec =
            gpu.NVENC_H264 ? MFVideoEncoder.NVENC_H264 :
            gpu.QSV_H264 ? MFVideoEncoder.QSV_H264 :
            gpu.AMD_H264 ? MFVideoEncoder.AMD_H264 :
            MFVideoEncoder.MS_H264;

        mp4.Video.AvgBitrate = 6000; // kbps
        mp4.Video.MaxBitrate = 9000;
        mp4.Video.RateControl = MFCommonRateControlMode.PeakConstrainedVBR;
        mp4.Video.Profile = MFH264Profile.Main;
        mp4.Audio.Bitrate = 192; // AAC, kbps

        videoCapture1.Output_Filename = Path.Combine(
            Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.MyVideos), "output.mp4");
        videoCapture1.Output_Format = mp4;
        videoCapture1.Mode = VideoCaptureMode.VideoCapture;

        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Enabled = true;
        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Clear();
        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Add(new VideoEffectTextLogo(true, "text")
        {
            Text = "Hello World!", Left = 50, Top = 50, FontColor = System.Drawing.Color.Red
        });
        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Add(new VideoEffectTextLogo(true, "clock")
        {
            Mode = TextLogoMode.DateTime, DateTimeMask = "HH:mm:ss", Text = "",
            Left = 50, Top = 110
        });

        btStart.IsEnabled = false;
        var started = await videoCapture1.StartAsync();
        btStop.IsEnabled = started;
        btStart.IsEnabled = !started;
    }

    private async void btStop_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        btStop.IsEnabled = false;
        await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
        btStart.IsEnabled = true;
    }

    private async void Window_Closing(object sender, CancelEventArgs e)
    {
        if (btStart.IsEnabled) { videoCapture1.Dispose(); return; }

        e.Cancel = true; // still recording: finish the MP4 first
        if (!btStop.IsEnabled) return; // already starting or stopping
        btStop.IsEnabled = false;
        await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
        btStart.IsEnabled = true;
        await Dispatcher.InvokeAsync(Close); // not Close(): WPF throws inside Closing
    }
}
```

## Key Implementation Features

1. **Window in XAML** - A two-column `Grid`: the lists and buttons on the left, the `VideoView` with the live preview on the right
2. **Device and Format Selection** - The camera, its format, its frame rate and the microphone are picked from lists filled from the devices themselves; the handlers read `SelectedItem`
3. **Hardware Encoding with a CPU Fallback** - `MP4HWOutput` encodes H.264 on an NVIDIA, Intel or AMD GPU; `HWEncodersAvailable` tells which encoders the PC has, and `MS_H264` runs on the CPU when none is present
4. **Encoder Settings** - An average of 6000 kbps, peaks up to 9000 kbps, the Main profile and AAC audio at 192 kbps
5. **Asynchronous Operation** - `StartAsync` and `StopAsync` keep the UI responsive, and closing the window during a recording awaits `StopAsync` before it closes

## WPF Notes

- `FontColor` of `VideoEffectTextLogo` is a `System.Drawing.Color`, not a WPF `Color`, so it is written in full
- The `OnError` handler sets the window title through `Dispatcher.InvokeAsync`, so it runs on the UI thread whichever thread raises the event
- `Format_UseBest` is on by default and picks the highest resolution up to 1080p, preferring MJPG at the same resolution; turn it off to record the format picked in the list
- With no microphone in the list, `Audio_RecordAudio` is set to `false` and the MP4 holds video only
- When the engine has already stopped (after an error), `StopAsync` completes at once and the code after the `await` still runs inside `Closing`, where WPF does not allow `Close()`; the window closes again through `Dispatcher.InvokeAsync` instead

## Video Transcript

### What we build

Let's record a webcam to an MP4 file in a C# WPF app with the VisioForge Video Capture SDK. Here's what we build. A WPF window with a live camera preview, laid out in XAML. It records MP4, with H.264 encoded on the GPU when the PC has one, and AAC audio. The camera, its format and the microphone are picked from lists, and the code behind the window is about a hundred lines of C#. This is the finished app, recording from a Logitech C920.

### Prerequisites

You need Windows 10 or 11, and Visual Studio 2022 or 2026 with the .NET desktop development workload. The project targets .NET 8 or later. The same app in WinForms has its own video.

### Create a WPF project

In Visual Studio, open File, New, Project. Search for WPF, and pick WPF Application for C#. Name the project WebcamMp4Wpf. Choose .NET 10 and click Create. Visual Studio opens MainWindow.xaml, with the designer above and the XAML below.

### Add the NuGet packages

Now add three NuGet packages: the SDK itself, the video capture redist and the MP4 redist. These are the x64 packages. An x86 app takes the x86 redists instead. You can also install the same three packages from the NuGet Package Manager. The WPF VideoView ships in the core package, so nothing else is needed.

### Build the window in XAML

In WPF, the window is written in XAML. First the window itself, with a two-column grid and a VideoView, and the designer above draws it right away. The VideoView is also in the Toolbox, under VisioForge. Map the VisioForge.Core.UI.WPF namespace to a prefix, here vf. Then a VideoView goes into the right-hand column of a grid: that is where the live preview is drawn. The window also names its Loaded and Closing handlers. Next, the labels and combo boxes go into the left column. The left-hand column is a StackPanel with a label and a combo box for the camera, the format, the frame rate and the microphone. The camera and format lists name a SelectionChanged handler. Last, the Start and Stop buttons. Each button names a Click handler. Stop stays disabled until a recording starts. Every handler named in the XAML goes into MainWindow.xaml.cs, and the next chapters write them.

### Create the capture engine

In the window's Loaded handler, create the VideoCaptureCore engine and pass it the VideoView, where the live preview is drawn.

### Enumerate cameras

Video\_CaptureDevices returns every camera on the machine. We list their names and select the first one. When the camera changes, its handler fills the format list with the formats of that camera. Read SelectedItem here, not Text: inside SelectionChanged, the Text of a WPF combo box still holds the previous item. When the format changes, its handler fills the frame rate list the same way. Clearing the format list raises SelectionChanged with nothing selected, so the handler returns early. A camera reports its name, formats like 1920x1080 MJPG or 1280x720 YUY2, and the frame rates of each format. MJPG is compressed in the camera, so high resolutions fit through USB. YUY2 is uncompressed, so USB 2 carries only lower resolutions.

### Choose the camera format

Select the camera by name. Then turn Format\_UseBest off, and pass the format and the frame rate picked from the lists. Format\_UseBest is on by default. It picks the highest resolution up to 1080p that the camera offers, and prefers MJPG at the same resolution. For a fixed format, set it to false and pass the format and the frame rate yourself.

### Select the microphone

The microphone works the same way. Audio\_CaptureDevices lists them, and we use the one picked in the list. Audio\_PlayAudio set to false records the microphone without playing it back.

### MP4HWOutput: any GPU, CPU fallback

For the output, create an MP4HWOutput, write output.mp4 into the Videos folder, and switch the engine to video capture mode, so it records and not just previews. A WPF project leaves System.IO out of its implicit usings, so add it for Path. MP4HWOutput encodes on the GPU: NVENC on NVIDIA, Quick Sync on Intel, and AMF on AMD, in H.264 or HEVC. When there's no hardware encoder, the Windows encoder on the CPU takes over. The code and the file are the same on every PC. HWEncodersAvailable tells you which encoders this PC has. Take NVIDIA first, then Intel, then AMD, and fall back to the CPU encoder.

### Tune the H.264 encoder

Then tune the encoder: six thousand kilobits per second on average, peaks up to nine thousand, the Main profile, and AAC audio at a hundred and ninety-two. As a guide: 2500 to 4000 kilobits for 720p, 5000 to 8000 for 1080p, and 15000 to 25000 for 4K. Both bitrates are set in kilobits per second.

### Add a text overlay

Video effects add a text overlay: a fixed Hello World, and a clock that shows the current time on every frame. The font color is a System.Drawing color, not a WPF one, so write it in full.

### Start and stop

Start and Stop are async. StartAsync returns once the capture is running, and StopAsync finalizes the MP4 file. If the window closes during a recording, cancel the close, await StopAsync, and close again. The file is complete, and the engine is disposed on the second pass. Run the app from Visual Studio. The format list comes straight from the camera. Start begins the recording, with the clock overlay ticking. Stop finalizes output.mp4. The file lands in Videos: 1920x1080, H.264 video and AAC audio.

### Common mistakes

A few common mistakes. A missing redist package, so the engine won't start. A camera that's already open in another app. x86 and x64 packages mixed in one project. And disposing the engine mid-capture: await StopAsync first. Engine errors arrive in the OnError event.

### Next steps

There are also guides for IP cameras, screen recording, snapshots and network streaming. The full source is on GitHub, and the docs are at visioforge.com/help. Thanks for watching.

## Record Webcam to WMV in C# WinForms (WMV 9, WMA, CBR)
**URL:** https://www.visioforge.com/help/docs/dotnet/videocapture/video-tutorials/video-capture-webcam-wmv/
**Description:** Record a webcam to WMV in a C# WinForms app with VideoCaptureCore - Windows Media Video 9 at a constant bitrate, WMA audio, and an ffprobe check.
**Tags:** Video Capture SDK, .NET, VideoCaptureCore, Windows, WinForms, Capture, Webcam, WMV, WMA, C#, NuGet
**API:** VideoCaptureCore, VideoCaptureSource, AudioCaptureSource, WMVOutput, WMVStreamMode, VideoView

# Webcam to WMV File Recording in .NET C# Applications

[Video Capture SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/video-capture-sdk-net)

## Overview

This tutorial records a webcam to a WMV file in a C# WinForms app with the VideoCaptureCore engine. The video is Windows Media Video 9 at the camera's own resolution and a constant 8 Mbps; the audio is WMA, in a format picked from the list the SDK returns.

**When WMV is the right choice over MP4:** a WMV file plays on Windows out of the box, and the Windows Media encoders come with Windows, so you need no GPU and no codec pack. With a constant bitrate, the file size is known before you record, and some systems already expect WMV or ASF files. For the web, phones and Macs, record [MP4 with H.264](../video-capture-webcam-mp4/) instead.

This tutorial uses the Windows-only VideoCaptureCore engine, the SDK's DirectShow engine. VideoCaptureCoreX, the cross-platform engine, has its own WMV encoder: see [Cross-platform WMV output](../../../general/output-formats/wmv/#cross-platform-wmv-output) and [Save Webcam Video in C#](../../guides/save-webcam-video/).

## Video Walkthrough

## Source Code Repository

The complete project, with the designer file, is on GitHub:

[Source code on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Video%20Capture%20SDK/_VideoTutorials/webcam-wmv-winforms)

## Required Packages

Install the [VisioForge.DotNet.Core](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core/) package and the video capture redist with its DirectShow filters. The Windows Media encoders come with Windows, so nothing more is needed.

Set `PlatformTarget` in the project file to match the redist (`x64` or `x86`). On the N editions of Windows, the Windows Media components come with the Media Feature Pack: install it first.

```
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x64
```

For a 32-bit (x86) application, use the x86 package instead: `VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x86`.

`VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture`, the package in the Try it block at the top of this page, works as well: it installs the same `VisioForge.DotNet.Core`. The redist packages are needed either way.

## Implementation Example with C# Code

The form has a `VideoView`, combo boxes for the camera, format, frame rate, microphone, video codec, audio codec and audio format, and Start and Stop buttons; the designer file is in the source code above. The project targets .NET 10 with implicit usings. On .NET Framework 4.7.2, the same code builds in an SDK-style project with `<LangVersion>10</LangVersion>` and `<ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>`.

```
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.Output;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoCapture;
using VisioForge.Core.UI;
using VisioForge.Core.VideoCapture;

namespace WebcamWmv;

public partial class Form1 : Form
{
    private VideoCaptureCore videoCapture1 = null!;

    public Form1()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private void Form1_Load(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        videoCapture1 = new VideoCaptureCore(VideoView1 as IVideoView);

        // Show SDK errors in the title bar
        videoCapture1.OnError += (_, args) => BeginInvoke(() => Text = args.Message);

        foreach (var device in videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices())
            cbCamera.Items.Add(device.Name);

        foreach (var device in videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevices())
            cbMicrophone.Items.Add(device.Name);

        if (cbCamera.Items.Count > 0) cbCamera.SelectedIndex = 0;
        if (cbMicrophone.Items.Count > 0) cbMicrophone.SelectedIndex = 0;

        // The Windows Media codecs that can encode at a constant bitrate
        foreach (var codec in videoCapture1.WMV_CustomProfile_VideoCodecs(WMVStreamMode.CBR))
            cbVideoCodec.Items.Add(codec);

        foreach (var codec in videoCapture1.WMV_CustomProfile_AudioCodecs(WMVStreamMode.CBR))
            cbAudioCodec.Items.Add(codec);

        cbVideoCodec.SelectedItem = "Windows Media Video 9";
        cbAudioCodec.SelectedItem = "Windows Media Audio 9.2";
    }

    private void cbCamera_SelectedIndexChanged(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        cbFormat.Items.Clear();
        cbFrameRate.Items.Clear();
        var device = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices().First(d => d.Name == cbCamera.Text);
        foreach (var format in device.VideoFormats)
            cbFormat.Items.Add(format.Name);

        var index = cbFormat.Items.IndexOf("1920x1080 MJPG, 24 bit");
        if (cbFormat.Items.Count > 0) cbFormat.SelectedIndex = index >= 0 ? index : 0;
    }

    private void cbFormat_SelectedIndexChanged(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        cbFrameRate.Items.Clear();
        var device = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices().First(d => d.Name == cbCamera.Text);
        var format = device.VideoFormats.First(f => f.Name == cbFormat.Text);
        foreach (var frameRate in format.FrameRates)
            cbFrameRate.Items.Add(frameRate);

        var rate = cbFrameRate.Items.IndexOf(VideoFrameRate.FPS_30);
        if (cbFrameRate.Items.Count > 0) cbFrameRate.SelectedIndex = rate >= 0 ? rate : 0;
    }

    private void cbAudioCodec_SelectedIndexChanged(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        // The sample rates, channels and bitrates this audio codec offers
        cbAudioFormat.Items.Clear();
        foreach (var format in videoCapture1.WMV_CustomProfile_AudioFormats(cbAudioCodec.Text, WMVStreamMode.CBR))
            cbAudioFormat.Items.Add(format);

        var index = cbAudioFormat.Items.IndexOf("CBR 128 kbps, 48000 Hz, Stereo, 16 bit");
        if (cbAudioFormat.Items.Count > 0) cbAudioFormat.SelectedIndex = index >= 0 ? index : 0;
    }

    private async void btStart_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        if (cbFrameRate.SelectedItem is null)
        {
            Text = "No camera, format or frame rate";
            return;
        }

        if (cbVideoCodec.SelectedItem is null)
        {
            Text = "No video codec selected";
            return;
        }

        var mic = cbMicrophone.SelectedItem as string;
        if (mic is not null && cbAudioFormat.SelectedItem is null)
        {
            Text = "No audio format selected";
            return;
        }

        Text = "Webcam to WMV";

        videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevice = new VideoCaptureSource(cbCamera.Text);
        var camera = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevice;
        var frameRate = (VideoFrameRate)cbFrameRate.SelectedItem;
        camera.Format_UseBest = false;
        camera.Format = cbFormat.Text;
        camera.FrameRate = frameRate;

        videoCapture1.Audio_RecordAudio = mic is not null; // no microphone: record video only
        if (mic is not null) videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevice = new AudioCaptureSource(mic);
        videoCapture1.Audio_PlayAudio = false; // record the microphone without playing it back

        var wmv = new WMVOutput
        {
            Mode = WMVMode.CustomSettings,

            Custom_Video_StreamPresent = true,
            Custom_Video_Codec = cbVideoCodec.Text,
            Custom_Video_Mode = WMVStreamMode.CBR,
            Custom_Video_Bitrate = 8000, // kbps
            Custom_Video_SizeSameAsInput = true, // the camera's resolution
            Custom_Video_FrameRate = frameRate.Value,
            Custom_Video_KeyFrameInterval = 2, // seconds

            Custom_Audio_StreamPresent = mic is not null,
            Custom_Audio_Codec = cbAudioCodec.Text,
            Custom_Audio_Format = cbAudioFormat.Text,
            Custom_Audio_Mode = WMVStreamMode.CBR,
        };

        videoCapture1.Output_Filename = Path.Combine(
            Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.MyVideos), "output.wmv");
        videoCapture1.Output_Format = wmv;
        videoCapture1.Mode = VideoCaptureMode.VideoCapture;

        btStart.Enabled = false;
        var started = await videoCapture1.StartAsync();
        btStop.Enabled = started;
        btStart.Enabled = !started;
    }

    private async void btStop_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        btStop.Enabled = false;
        await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
        btStart.Enabled = true;
    }

    private async void Form1_FormClosing(object sender, FormClosingEventArgs e)
    {
        // Finish the WMV before the window goes away
        if (!btStart.Enabled)
        {
            e.Cancel = true;
            if (!btStop.Enabled) return; // already starting or stopping

            btStop.Enabled = false;
            await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
            btStart.Enabled = true;
            BeginInvoke(Close); // close again once this handler has returned
            return;
        }

        videoCapture1.Dispose();
    }
}
```

## Key Implementation Features

1. **Device and Format Selection** - The camera, its format, its frame rate and the microphone are picked from lists filled from the devices themselves; with no microphone, `Audio_RecordAudio` and `Custom_Audio_StreamPresent` are `false` and the WMV holds video only
2. **Camera Format** - `Format_UseBest` is on by default: it picks the highest resolution up to 1080p, then prefers MJPG and the fastest frame rate. To record 4K, or any format you choose, turn it off and set `Format` and `FrameRate`
3. **Windows Media Codecs** - `WMV_CustomProfile_VideoCodecs(WMVStreamMode.CBR)` and `WMV_CustomProfile_AudioCodecs(WMVStreamMode.CBR)` return the Windows Media encoders that can work at a constant bitrate, and `WMV_CustomProfile_AudioFormats(codec, WMVStreamMode.CBR)` the formats of one audio codec, each named by its bitrate, sample rate, channels and bits. Windows Media Video 9 is the codec for camera video; the Screen and Image codecs are made for screen recordings and still pictures, Advanced Profile is the VC-1 profile made for interlaced and broadcast video, and V7 and V8 are older versions for old players. Take every codec and format name from these lists, never type it by hand
4. **Custom Settings** - A plain `new WMVOutput()` uses the built-in "Windows Media Video 9 High (2.5 Mbps)" profile from SDK 2026.11.16 on; up to 2026.11.13 it was "Windows Media Video 9 for Local Network (768 kbps)", the profile the video names. `WMVMode.CustomSettings` takes your own codec, bitrate and size: `Custom_Video_Bitrate` is in kilobits per second, so `8000` is 8 Mbps, `Custom_Video_SizeSameAsInput` keeps the camera's resolution, and `Custom_Video_KeyFrameInterval` is in seconds. With 128 kbps audio, that is about sixty megabytes a minute
5. **Asynchronous Operation** - `StartAsync` and `StopAsync` keep the UI responsive, and closing the form finishes the WMV file first

## Check the File with ffprobe

```
cd ([Environment]::GetFolderPath('MyVideos'))
ffprobe -v error -of compact output.wmv -show_entries format=format_name,duration,size:stream=codec_name,width,height,sample_rate,channels

# stream|codec_name=wmv3|width=1920|height=1080
# stream|codec_name=wmav2|sample_rate=48000|channels=2
# format|format_name=asf|duration=16.496000|size=16941531
```

Sixteen and a half seconds come to 16,941,531 bytes, about 16 MB as File Explorer shows it: 8 Mbps of video plus 128 kbps of audio. ffprobe calls WMV 9 `wmv3` and WMA 9.2 `wmav2`, and the container is ASF, the format behind WMV.

## Video Transcript

### What we build

Let's record a webcam to a WMV file in a C# WinForms app with the VisioForge Video Capture SDK. Here's what we build. A WinForms window with a live camera preview. It records Windows Media Video 9 at the camera's own resolution, with a constant bitrate we set ourselves: eight megabits per second. The audio is WMA, in a format picked from a list. The camera, its format, the frame rate and the microphone are picked from lists too. This is the finished app, recording from a Logitech C920.

### WMV or MP4

When is WMV the right choice? A WMV file plays on Windows out of the box. The Windows Media encoders come with Windows, so you need no GPU and no codec pack. With a constant bitrate, the file size is known before you record. And some systems already expect WMV or ASF files. For the web, phones and Macs, MP4 with H.264 is the better choice. That's the webcam to MP4 video.

### Prerequisites

You need Windows 10 or 11, and Visual Studio 2022 or 2026 with the .NET desktop development workload. The project can target .NET 8 or later, or .NET Framework 4.7.2. And a webcam with a microphone. VideoCaptureCore is the SDK's DirectShow engine, so this app runs on Windows only.

### Create a WinForms project

In Visual Studio, create a new project. Search for Windows Forms, and pick Windows Forms App for C#. Name the project WebcamWmv. Choose .NET 10 and click Create. Visual Studio opens the empty form in the designer.

### Add the NuGet packages

Now add two NuGet packages: the SDK itself, and the video capture redist with its DirectShow filters. The WMV encoders come with Windows, so that's all. In Visual Studio, that's Manage NuGet Packages. Browse for VisioForge.DotNet.Core and install it. Then install the video capture redist for x64. The redist is the x64 one, so set PlatformTarget to x64 in the project file. An x86 app takes the x86 redist instead.

### Design the WinForms form

From the Toolbox, draw a VideoView for the live preview. Add a label and a combo box for the camera, and give every control a clear name in the Properties window. Do the same for the camera format, the frame rate and the microphone, then for the video codec, the audio codec and the audio format. Add the Start and Stop buttons. Stop stays disabled until a recording starts. Double-click the form, the camera, format and audio codec lists, and both buttons. Visual Studio adds an empty handler for each one.

### Create the capture engine

At the top of Form1.cs, add these usings. In the form's Load handler, create the VideoCaptureCore engine and pass it the VideoView, where the live preview is drawn. Engine errors arrive in the OnError event. Here they go to the title bar.

### List the devices

Video\_CaptureDevices returns every camera, and Audio\_CaptureDevices every microphone. We list their names and select the first of each. When the camera changes, its handler fills the format list with the formats of that camera, and picks 1920x1080 MJPG when it's there. When the format changes, its handler fills the frame rate list the same way, and picks thirty frames per second.

### Windows Media codecs

Back in the Load handler, WMV\_CustomProfile\_VideoCodecs and WMV\_CustomProfile\_AudioCodecs list the Windows Media encoders that can work at a constant bitrate. We fill both lists, and select Windows Media Video 9 and Windows Media Audio 9.2. When the audio codec changes, WMV\_CustomProfile\_AudioFormats lists what that codec offers. We pick 128 kilobits per second, 48 kilohertz stereo. Windows Media Video 9 is the codec for camera video. The Screen and Image codecs are made for screen recordings and still pictures, and V7 and V8 are older versions, for old players. For audio at a constant bitrate there's WMA 9.2 and WMA 10 Professional. Each audio format names its bitrate, sample rate, channels and bits. Always pick these names from the lists, never type them by hand.

### Choose the camera format

The Start handler first checks that a frame rate and a video codec are selected. If not, it says so in the title bar. With a microphone in the list, it needs an audio format as well. Then it selects the camera by name, turns Format\_UseBest off, and passes the format and the frame rate picked from the lists. Format\_UseBest is on by default. It picks the highest resolution up to 1080p, then prefers MJPG and the fastest frame rate. To record 4K, or any format you choose, turn it off and set Format and FrameRate, as we do here.

### Select the microphone

With no microphone in the list, the app captures video only. Otherwise it records the selected one. Audio\_PlayAudio is off, so the microphone isn't played through the speakers while you record.

### WMVOutput: custom settings

Now the output. A WMVOutput in CustomSettings mode takes our own settings. The video stream uses the codec from the list at a constant 8000 kilobits per second. SizeSameAsInput keeps the camera's resolution, the frame rate is the one we picked, and there's a keyframe every two seconds. The audio stream takes the codec and the format from the lists, and it's there only when we have a microphone. Then write output.wmv into the Videos folder, and switch the engine to video capture mode, so it records and not just previews. A plain WMVOutput uses a built-in profile at 768 kilobits per second, made for a local network. (From SDK 2026.11.16 on, the default is "Windows Media Video 9 High (2.5 Mbps)".) CustomSettings gives us our own codec, bitrate and size. Custom\_Video\_Bitrate is in kilobits per second, so 8000 means eight megabits. With 128 kilobits of audio, that's about sixty megabytes a minute. And a keyframe every two seconds gives the player a seek point every two seconds.

### Start and stop

Start and Stop are async. StartAsync returns once the capture is running, and StopAsync finishes writing the WMV file.

### Close the window

Closing the window while it records would leave the WMV unfinished. In the Properties window, on the Events tab, double-click FormClosing to add this handler. While recording, it cancels the close. Then it stops the recording, and closes the window again once the handler has returned. With nothing recording, the handler disposes the engine.

### Run it

Run the app from Visual Studio. The camera, format and microphone lists fill in from the devices. The video codec list shows the Windows Media encoders. Windows Media Video 9 stays selected. Start begins the recording. The C920 takes a few seconds to send its first frame. Stop finishes output.wmv, and then we close the window.

### Check the file with ffprobe

The file lands in Videos: about sixteen megabytes for sixteen seconds. ffprobe shows what's inside. The container is ASF, the format behind WMV. The video is WMV 9, which ffprobe calls wmv3, at 1920x1080. The audio is WMA, 48 kilohertz stereo.

A few common mistakes. A missing redist package, so the engine won't start. Codec and format names typed by hand: take them from the lists. Custom\_Video\_Bitrate written in bits per second: it's in kilobits. On the N editions of Windows, the Windows Media components come with the Media Feature Pack, so install it first. And closing the window mid-recording: await StopAsync first.

## Webcam Text Overlay in C# WinForms (Date, Frame Number)
**URL:** https://www.visioforge.com/help/docs/dotnet/videocapture/video-tutorials/webcam-capture-text-overlay/
**Description:** Draw a caption you can change while recording, the date and time, the frame number and the recording time over a webcam MP4 in C# WinForms.
**Tags:** Video Capture SDK, .NET, VideoCaptureCore, Windows, WinForms, Capture, Webcam, MP4, Text Overlay, Video Effects, C#, NuGet
**API:** VideoCaptureCore, VideoEffectTextLogo, VideoCaptureSource, AudioCaptureSource, MP4Output, VideoView

# Webcam Capture with a Text Overlay in C# WinForms

[Video Capture SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/video-capture-sdk-net)

## Overview

This tutorial records a webcam to MP4 in a C# WinForms app with the VideoCaptureCore engine and draws four text overlays into the video frames with `VideoEffectTextLogo`:

- a caption at the bottom center, which you can change while recording;
- the date and time in the top-right corner;
- the frame number;
- the time since the recording started.

The text is part of every frame, so it is in the live preview and in the file. A date and time on each frame is what security and evidence recordings need, a frame number lets you find and compare an exact frame later, and the recording time lines the video up with logs and sensor data.

This tutorial uses the Windows-only VideoCaptureCore engine, the SDK's DirectShow engine. For fades, rotation and the cross-platform X engines, see [Text overlays](../../../general/video-effects/text-overlay/).

## Video Walkthrough

## Source Code Repository

The complete project, with the designer file, is on GitHub:

## Required Packages

Install the [VisioForge.DotNet.Core](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core/) package, the video capture redist with its DirectShow filters, and the MP4 redist, which writes the MP4 file.

Set `PlatformTarget` in the project file to match the redists (`x64` or `x86`).

```
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x64
dotnet add package VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.MP4.x64
```

For a 32-bit (x86) application, use the x86 packages instead: `VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoCapture.x86` and `VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.MP4.x86`.

`VisioForge.DotNet.VideoCapture`, the package in the Try it block at the top of this page, works as well: it installs the same `VisioForge.DotNet.Core`. The redist packages are needed either way.

## Implementation Example with C# Code

The form has a `VideoView`, combo boxes for the camera, format, frame rate and microphone, a caption text box with an Apply button that starts disabled, and Start and Stop buttons; the designer file is in the source code above. The project targets .NET 10 with implicit usings. On .NET Framework 4.7.2, the same code builds in an SDK-style project with `<LangVersion>10</LangVersion>` and `<ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>`.

```
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.Output;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoCapture;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoEffects;
using VisioForge.Core.UI;
using VisioForge.Core.VideoCapture;

namespace WebcamTextOverlay;

public partial class Form1 : Form
{
    private VideoCaptureCore videoCapture1 = null!;

    public Form1()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private void Form1_Load(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        videoCapture1 = new VideoCaptureCore(VideoView1 as IVideoView);

        // Show SDK errors in the title bar
        videoCapture1.OnError += (_, args) => BeginInvoke(() => Text = args.Message);

        foreach (var device in videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices())
            cbCamera.Items.Add(device.Name);

        foreach (var device in videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevices())
            cbMicrophone.Items.Add(device.Name);

        if (cbCamera.Items.Count > 0) cbCamera.SelectedIndex = 0;
        if (cbMicrophone.Items.Count > 0) cbMicrophone.SelectedIndex = 0;
    }

    private void cbCamera_SelectedIndexChanged(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        cbFormat.Items.Clear();
        cbFrameRate.Items.Clear();
        var device = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices().First(d => d.Name == cbCamera.Text);
        foreach (var format in device.VideoFormats)
            cbFormat.Items.Add(format.Name);

        var index = cbFormat.Items.IndexOf("1920x1080 MJPG, 24 bit");
        if (cbFormat.Items.Count > 0) cbFormat.SelectedIndex = index >= 0 ? index : 0;
    }

    private void cbFormat_SelectedIndexChanged(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        cbFrameRate.Items.Clear();
        var device = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevices().First(d => d.Name == cbCamera.Text);
        var format = device.VideoFormats.First(f => f.Name == cbFormat.Text);
        foreach (var frameRate in format.FrameRates)
            cbFrameRate.Items.Add(frameRate);

        var rate = cbFrameRate.Items.IndexOf(VideoFrameRate.FPS_30);
        if (cbFrameRate.Items.Count > 0) cbFrameRate.SelectedIndex = rate >= 0 ? rate : 0;
    }

    private void AddOverlays()
    {
        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Enabled = true;
        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Clear();

        // A caption at the bottom, changed with Apply while recording
        using var font = new Font("Segoe UI", 40, FontStyle.Bold); // the effect keeps its own copy
        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Add(new VideoEffectTextLogo(true, "caption")
        {
            Text = tbCaption.Text,
            Font = font,
            FontColor = Color.Yellow,
            HorizontalAlignment = TextLogoHorizontalAlignment.Center,
            VerticalAlignment = TextLogoVerticalAlignment.Bottom
        });

        // Date and time in the top-right corner
        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Add(new VideoEffectTextLogo(true, "clock")
        {
            Mode = TextLogoMode.DateTime,
            DateTimeMask = "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss",
            Text = "",
            HorizontalAlignment = TextLogoHorizontalAlignment.Right,
            VerticalAlignment = TextLogoVerticalAlignment.Top
        });

        // The frame number in the top-left corner
        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Add(new VideoEffectTextLogo(true, "frame")
        {
            Mode = TextLogoMode.FrameNumber,
            Text = "Frame ",
            Left = 20,
            Top = 20
        });

        // Time since the recording started, under the frame number
        videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Add(new VideoEffectTextLogo(true, "time")
        {
            Mode = TextLogoMode.Timestamp,
            TimeStampMask = @"hh\:mm\:ss\.fff",
            Text = "Rec ",
            Left = 20,
            Top = 140 // room between the rows
        });
    }

    private async void btStart_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        Text = cbFrameRate.SelectedItem is null ? "No camera, format or frame rate" : "Webcam with text overlay";
        if (cbFrameRate.SelectedItem is null) return;

        videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevice = new VideoCaptureSource(cbCamera.Text);
        var camera = videoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevice;
        camera.Format_UseBest = false;
        camera.Format = cbFormat.Text;
        camera.FrameRate = (VideoFrameRate)cbFrameRate.SelectedItem;

        var mic = cbMicrophone.SelectedItem as string;
        videoCapture1.Audio_RecordAudio = mic is not null; // no microphone: record video only
        if (mic is not null) videoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevice = new AudioCaptureSource(mic);
        videoCapture1.Audio_PlayAudio = false; // record the microphone without playing it back

        videoCapture1.Output_Filename = Path.Combine(
            Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.MyVideos), "output.mp4");
        videoCapture1.Output_Format = new MP4Output(); // H.264 and AAC
        videoCapture1.Mode = VideoCaptureMode.VideoCapture;

        AddOverlays();

        btStart.Enabled = false;
        var started = await videoCapture1.StartAsync();
        btStop.Enabled = started;
        btApply.Enabled = started;
        btStart.Enabled = !started;
    }

    private void btApply_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        // Change the caption while recording: new text, then Update to redraw it
        if (videoCapture1.Video_Effects_Get("caption") is VideoEffectTextLogo caption)
        {
            caption.Text = tbCaption.Text;
            caption.Update();
        }
    }

    private async void btStop_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        btStop.Enabled = false;
        btApply.Enabled = false;
        await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
        btStart.Enabled = true;
    }

    private async void Form1_FormClosing(object sender, FormClosingEventArgs e)
    {
        // Finish the MP4 before the window goes away
        if (!btStart.Enabled)
        {
            e.Cancel = true;
            if (!btStop.Enabled) return; // already starting or stopping

            btStop.Enabled = false;
            btApply.Enabled = false;
            await videoCapture1.StopAsync();
            btStart.Enabled = true;
            BeginInvoke(Close); // close again once this handler has returned
            return;
        }

        videoCapture1.Dispose();
    }
}
```

## Key Implementation Features

1. **Effects on** - `Video_Effects_Enabled` is `false` by default, and then no overlay is drawn. `Video_Effects_Clear` removes the overlays of the previous recording, so Start can run again
2. **Placement** - `HorizontalAlignment` and `VerticalAlignment` put an overlay at an edge or in the center whatever the frame size; without them, `Left` and `Top` place it in video pixels. With nothing set, an overlay is white Arial 36 in the top-left corner
3. **Modes** - `Mode` picks what an overlay shows: `Text` draws the `Text` property, `DateTime` the PC clock formatted by `DateTimeMask`, `Timestamp` the time since the recording started formatted by `TimeStampMask` (a `TimeSpan` format, so `:` and `.` need a backslash), and `FrameNumber` the number of the frame. In the last three, `Text` is drawn in front of the value, and its default is `Hello!!!`, so set it to an empty string or to your own prefix
4. **Changing an overlay while recording** - `Video_Effects_Get` returns the overlay with that name, or `null`. Change its properties and call `Update()`: the engine redraws it from the next frame, and the recording keeps the change from that frame on. Without `Update()`, the old text stays
5. **Fonts** - the `Font` setter keeps its own copy of the font, so the one you pass can be disposed right away
6. **Text size and the display scale** - since SDK 2026.11.13 a font size in points is drawn at 96 DPI, so a line of Arial 36 is about 55 pixels tall on every PC, whatever the Windows display scale, and it does not shrink with the frame. Earlier versions drew it at the screen's DPI, so it grew with the display scale: about 110 pixels at 200 percent. `Top = 140` in this sample leaves room for that up to 200 percent. A font in pixels has the same size on every version: `new Font("Arial", 36, GraphicsUnit.Pixel)`
7. **Cost** - an overlay whose text changes (the clock, the frame number, the recording time, or a caption after `Update()`) is redrawn on every frame; keep such overlays few

## Check the File with ffprobe

```
cd ([Environment]::GetFolderPath('MyVideos'))
ffprobe -v error -of compact output.mp4 -show_entries format=format_name,duration,size:stream=codec_name,width,height,sample_rate,channels

# stream|codec_name=h264|width=1920|height=1080
# stream|codec_name=aac|sample_rate=48000|channels=2
# format|format_name=mov,mp4,m4a,3gp,3g2,mj2|duration=30.698667|size=4843264
```

## Video Transcript

### What we build

Let's draw text over a webcam recording in a C# WinForms app with the VisioForge Video Capture SDK. Here's what we build. A WinForms app that records a webcam to MP4 with a live preview. Over the video it draws a caption that you can change while it records, the date and time, the frame number, and the time since the recording started. This is the finished app, recording from a Logitech C920. The text is drawn into the video frames, so it's in the preview and in the file. Where does this help? A date and time on every frame is what security and evidence recordings need. A frame number lets you find and compare an exact frame later. The recording time lines the video up with logs and sensor data. And a caption labels what's on camera, like the operator, the test or the station, and you can change it as things change.

### Prerequisites

You need Windows 10 or 11, and Visual Studio 2022 or 2026 with the .NET desktop development workload. The project can target .NET 8 or later, or .NET Framework 4.7.2. And a webcam, with a microphone if you want sound. VideoCaptureCore is the SDK's DirectShow engine, so this app runs on Windows only.

### Create a WinForms project

In Visual Studio, create a new project. Search for Windows Forms, and pick Windows Forms App for C#. Name the project WebcamTextOverlay. Choose .NET 10 and click Create. Visual Studio opens the empty form in the designer.

### Add the NuGet packages

Now add three NuGet packages: the SDK itself, the video capture redist with its DirectShow filters, and the MP4 redist, which writes the MP4 file. In Visual Studio, that's Manage NuGet Packages. Browse for VisioForge.DotNet.Core and install it. Then install the video capture redist for x64. And the MP4 redist for x64. Both redists are x64, so set PlatformTarget to x64 in the project file. An x86 app takes the x86 redists instead.

### Design the WinForms form

From the Toolbox, draw a VideoView for the live preview. Add a label and a combo box for the camera, and give every control a clear name in the Properties window. Do the same for the camera format, the frame rate and the microphone. Then a label and a text box for the caption, and an Apply button. Apply starts disabled, because it only works while recording. Add the Start and Stop buttons. Stop stays disabled until a recording starts. Double-click the form, the camera and format lists, and the three buttons. Visual Studio adds an empty handler for each one.

### Create the capture engine

At the top of Form1.cs, add these usings. The text overlay types live in VideoEffects. In the form's Load handler, create the VideoCaptureCore engine and pass it the VideoView, where the live preview is drawn. Engine errors arrive in the OnError event. Here they go to the title bar.

### List the devices

Video\_CaptureDevices returns every camera, and Audio\_CaptureDevices every microphone. We list their names and select the first of each. When the camera changes, its handler fills the format list with the formats of that camera, and picks 1920x1080 MJPG when it's there. When the format changes, its handler fills the frame rate list the same way, and picks thirty frames per second.

### Camera, microphone and MP4

The Start handler first checks that a frame rate is selected. Then it selects the camera by name, turns Format\_UseBest off, and passes the format and the frame rate from the lists. Left on, Format\_UseBest picks the highest resolution up to 1080p by itself. With no microphone, the app captures video only. Otherwise it records the selected one, without playing it through the speakers. The output is output.mp4 in the Videos folder. A plain MP4Output writes H.264 video and AAC audio, encoded on the CPU, or with Intel Quick Sync where the PC has it.

### Draw text over the video

The overlays get a method of their own. Video\_Effects\_Enabled turns video effects on: it's off by default, and then nothing is drawn. Video\_Effects\_Clear removes the overlays of the previous recording, so Start can run again. The first overlay is the caption: a VideoEffectTextLogo named caption, with the text from the text box. It's Segoe UI, 40 points, bold and yellow. The two alignments put it at the bottom center, whatever the frame size. The effect keeps its own copy of the font, so ours is disposed right away. Every text overlay is a VideoEffectTextLogo. Its name lets you find it again later. Text, Font and FontColor set what it draws. Left and Top place it in video pixels, or the alignment properties put it at an edge or in the center. Without them it's white Arial at 36 points, in the top-left corner.

### Text modes: clock, frame, time

Next, the date and time. Mode DateTime draws the PC clock, formatted by DateTimeMask with the usual .NET format strings. Text is drawn in front of the value, so we set it to an empty string. Its default is Hello. Right and Top alignment put the clock in the top-right corner. Mode picks what an overlay shows. Text draws the Text property. DateTime draws the PC clock. Timestamp draws the time since the recording started, formatted by TimeStampMask. FrameNumber draws the number of the frame. In the last three, Text goes in front of the value. The frame number goes in the top-left corner, with the prefix Frame. This time Left and Top place it, in pixels. And under it, the recording time, with the prefix Rec, in hours, minutes, seconds and milliseconds. In a TimeSpan format, the colons and the dot need a backslash. Leave room between the rows: the text size follows the Windows display scale, so at 200 percent it's twice as tall.

### Start and stop

Back in the Start handler, AddOverlays runs before StartAsync. StartAsync returns once the capture is running, and then Stop and Apply are enabled. Stop disables Stop and Apply, and StopAsync finishes writing the MP4 file.

### Change the caption while recording

Apply changes the caption while recording. Video\_Effects\_Get finds the overlay by its name. We set the new text and call Update, which tells the engine to draw the overlay again on the next frame. Without Update, the old text stays. Video\_Effects\_Get returns the overlay you added, or null when no overlay has that name. You can change any of its properties, like the text, the color or the position. Then call Update, and it's redrawn from the next frame. The recording keeps the change from that frame on.

### Close the window

Closing the window while it records would leave the MP4 unfinished. In the Properties window, on the Events tab, double-click FormClosing to add this handler. While recording, it cancels the close. Then it stops the recording, and closes the window again once the handler has returned. With nothing recording, the handler disposes the engine.

### Run it

Run the app from Visual Studio. The camera, format and microphone lists fill in from the devices. Start begins the recording. The C920 takes a few seconds to send its first frame. Then the caption, the clock, the frame number and the recording time appear over the video. Type a new caption and click Apply. The new text shows on the next frame. Stop finishes output.mp4, and then we close the window.

### Check the file

Here's a frame from output.mp4, a few seconds in. The caption, the clock, the frame number and the recording time are part of the picture. And a frame after Apply. From that frame on, the file has the new caption. ffprobe shows what's inside: H.264 video at 1920x1080, and AAC audio, in an MP4 file.

### Common mistakes

A few common mistakes. Video\_Effects\_Enabled left false, so nothing is drawn. A clock that starts with Hello, because Text wasn't cleared. A new Text without Update, so the old text stays. Video\_Effects\_Get with a different name, which returns null. And many overlays whose text changes: each one is redrawn on every frame, so keep them few.

### Next steps

Next, the webcam to MP4 video encodes on the GPU, and the webcam to AVI video makes files for editing. For pictures over the video there's VideoEffectImageLogo, and for a moving ticker, VideoEffectScrollingTextLogo. The full source is on GitHub, and the docs are at visioforge.com/help. Thanks for watching.

**API:** MediaPlayerCoreX, VideoView, UniversalSourceSettings, AudioRendererSettings, ErrorsEventArgs

# VisioForge Media Player SDK in C# .NET — Cheat Sheet

Use VisioForge Media Player SDK .NET when you need to play local files (MP4, MKV, MOV, WebM), network streams (RTSP, HLS, MPEG-DASH), and audio (MP3, AAC, FLAC) inside a C# app on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, or iOS. `MediaPlayerCoreX` is the primary cross-platform engine; `VideoView` is the UI control that binds the engine to the visual tree.

AI coding agents: use the VisioForge MCP server

Building this with **Claude Code**, **Cursor**, or another AI coding agent? Connect to the public [VisioForge MCP server](../../general/mcp-server-usage/) at `https://mcp.visioforge.com/mcp` for structured API lookups, runnable code samples, and deployment guides — more accurate than grepping `llms.txt`. No authentication required.

Claude Code: `claude mcp add --transport http visioforge-sdk https://mcp.visioforge.com/mcp`

- **Windows** (x64 and x86) — WinForms, WPF, WinUI, MAUI, Avalonia, Console
- **macOS** (native and MacCatalyst) — MAUI, Avalonia, Console
- **Linux** (x64, ARM64) — Avalonia, Console; requires system GStreamer 1.20+

- **iOS** — via MAUI

All cross-platform targets use a GStreamer-backed decoding pipeline with hardware acceleration where available. For the full codec × platform matrix, see [platform-matrix.md](../../platform-matrix/).

## Primary API classes

| Class | Role | See also |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MediaPlayerCoreX` | Main playback engine (cross-platform, GStreamer-backed) | [Quick Start](../) |
| `VideoView` | UI control that binds the player to the visual tree | [Avalonia guide](../guides/avalonia-player/) |
| `UniversalSourceSettings` | Builds a source descriptor from a URI (file, URL, stream) | [video-player-csharp.md](../guides/video-player-csharp/) |
| `AudioRendererSettings` | Configures audio output device | [video-player-csharp.md](../guides/video-player-csharp/) |

## Canonical minimum example

```
using System;
using VisioForge.Core;
using VisioForge.Core.MediaPlayerX;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.Events;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.X.AudioRenderers;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.X.Sources;

public partial class MainForm : Form
{
    private MediaPlayerCoreX _player;

    private async void MainForm_Load(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        // 1. Initialize the SDK (once per process)
        await VisioForgeX.InitSDKAsync();

        // 2. Create the player bound to a VideoView control
        _player = new MediaPlayerCoreX(VideoView1);
        _player.OnError += Player_OnError;

        // 3. (Optional) pick an audio output device
        var devices = await _player.Audio_OutputDevicesAsync(
            AudioOutputDeviceAPI.DirectSound);
        if (devices.Length > 0)
            _player.Audio_OutputDevice = new AudioRendererSettings(devices[0]);

        // 4. Build a source from a file path or stream URL
        var source = await UniversalSourceSettings.CreateAsync(
            "C:\\Videos\\sample.mp4");

        // 5. Open and play
        await _player.OpenAsync(source);
        await _player.PlayAsync();

        // Mid-playback control:
        //   await _player.PauseAsync();
        //   await _player.ResumeAsync();
        //   await _player.StopAsync();
    }

    private void Player_OnError(object sender, ErrorsEventArgs e)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Player error: {e.Message}");
    }

    protected override async void OnFormClosing(FormClosingEventArgs e)
    {
        // 6. Dispose the player and tear down the SDK
        if (_player != null) await _player.DisposeAsync();
        VisioForgeX.DestroySDK();
        base.OnFormClosing(e);
    }
}
```

## Typical workflow

1. Initialize the SDK with `VisioForgeX.InitSDKAsync()`.
2. Instantiate `MediaPlayerCoreX` bound to a `VideoView` (omit the view for audio-only).
3. Optionally configure audio output with `AudioRendererSettings`.
4. Create a source via `UniversalSourceSettings.CreateAsync(uri)`.
5. `OpenAsync(source)` → `PlayAsync()`; control with `PauseAsync`, `ResumeAsync`, `Position_SetAsync`, `Rate_SetAsync`, `StopAsync`.
6. Dispose the player and call `VisioForgeX.DestroySDK()` on app exit.

## Common pitfalls

- **SDK init/destroy must bracket all usage.** Forgetting `VisioForgeX.DestroySDK()` at shutdown leaks native handles and can leave GStreamer threads running. Always pair it with `InitSDKAsync()`.
- **AnyCPU on Windows needs both redistributables.** Deploy BOTH `VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Core.Windows.x86` AND `.x64` (plus the matching Libav packages) or the app will fail at runtime on whichever architecture is missing.
- **Enumerate audio devices asynchronously before assigning.** `Audio_OutputDevicesAsync(...)` must complete before you construct `AudioRendererSettings` and set `Audio_OutputDevice`; setting it against an uninitialized device list throws.
- **Linux requires system GStreamer 1.20+.** The Linux NuGet redistributable assumes system-installed GStreamer (`gstreamer1.0-*` packages) — it is NOT a substitute, and the Windows Libav packages do not apply to Linux.
- **`MediaPlayerCoreX` ≠ `MediaPlayerCore`.** `MediaPlayerCoreX` is the cross-platform GStreamer-backed engine used throughout this page. `MediaPlayerCore` (no `X`) is the first-class Windows-only DirectShow engine with different method signatures — both are fully supported; do not mix APIs between them.

## FAQ

### Can the SDK play RTSP streams?

Yes. Pass an `rtsp://` URI to `UniversalSourceSettings.CreateAsync(...)` and call `OpenAsync` / `PlayAsync` — the same code path as a local file. HTTP, HLS, and MPEG-DASH URIs work identically.

### Which platforms require GStreamer to be installed at the system level?

Linux. On Linux, GStreamer 1.20+ must be installed from the system packages; the `VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Core.Linux.x64` (or `.Linux.arm64` on ARM64) NuGet package adds the SDK's own native libraries and contains no GStreamer. Windows, macOS, Android, and iOS bundle everything through their NuGet redistributables — no system install needed.

### What is the difference between `MediaPlayerCoreX` and `MediaPlayerCore`?

`MediaPlayerCoreX` is the cross-platform engine used throughout this cheat sheet — it runs on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS via GStreamer and uses async method signatures. `MediaPlayerCore` (no `X`) is the Windows-only DirectShow engine with a synchronous, event-based API; it remains a first-class, fully supported engine (choose it when you target Windows-only and need DirectShow-specific behaviour). For new cross-platform projects, prefer `MediaPlayerCoreX`.

### How do I play audio without showing a video window?

Instantiate `MediaPlayerCoreX` without a `VideoView` (`new MediaPlayerCoreX()`) and proceed with the same `UniversalSourceSettings.CreateAsync` → `OpenAsync` → `PlayAsync` flow. Audio-only sources (MP3, AAC, FLAC, WAV) will play through the configured `Audio_OutputDevice`.

---END OF PAGE---

# Extracting Video Frames from Video Files in .NET

[Media Player SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/media-player-sdk-net)

Video frame extraction is a common requirement in many multimedia applications. Whether you're building a video editing tool, creating thumbnails, or performing video analysis, extracting specific frames from video files is an essential capability. This guide explains different approaches to capturing frames from video files in .NET applications.

No authentication required.

Claude Code: `claude mcp add --transport http visioforge-sdk https://mcp.visioforge.com/mcp`

## Why Extract Video Frames?

There are numerous use cases for video frame extraction:

- Creating thumbnail images for video galleries
- Extracting key frames for video analysis
- Generating preview images at specific timestamps
- Building video editing tools with frame-by-frame precision
- Creating timelapse sequences from video footage
- Capturing still images from video recordings

## Understanding Video Frame Extraction

Video files contain sequences of frames displayed at specific intervals to create the illusion of motion. When extracting a frame, you're essentially capturing a single image at a specific timestamp within the video. This process involves:

1. Opening the video file
2. Seeking to the specific timestamp
3. Decoding the frame data
4. Converting it to an image format

## Frame Extraction Methods in .NET

There are several approaches to extract frames from video files in .NET, depending on your requirements and environment.

### Using Windows-Specific SDK Components

For Windows-only applications, the classic SDK components offer straightforward methods for frame extraction:

```
// Using VideoEditCore for frame extraction
using VisioForge.Core.VideoEdit;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.MediaPlayer;

public void ExtractFrameWithVideoEditCore()
{
    var videoEdit = new VideoEditCore();
    var bitmap = videoEdit.Helpful_GetFrameFromFile(
        "C:\\Videos\\sample.mp4",
        TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5),
        oldWay: false,
        MediaPlayerSourceMode.LAV);
    bitmap.Save("C:\\Output\\frame.png");
}

// Using MediaPlayerCore for frame extraction
using VisioForge.Core.MediaPlayer;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.MediaPlayer;

public void ExtractFrameWithMediaPlayerCore()
{
    var mediaPlayer = new MediaPlayerCore();
    var bitmap = mediaPlayer.Helpful_GetFrameFromFile(
        "C:\\Videos\\sample.mp4",
        TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10),
        oldWay: false,
        MediaPlayerSourceMode.LAV);
    bitmap.Save("C:\\Output\\frame.png");
}
```

The `Helpful_GetFrameFromFile` method simplifies the process by handling the file opening, seeking, and frame decoding operations in a single call. All four arguments are required: the file path, the seek timestamp, an `oldWay` flag (pass `false` for the modern decoder path), and a `MediaPlayerSourceMode` engine selector (`LAV`, `FFMPEG`, or `File_DS`).

### Cross-Platform Solutions with X-Engine

Modern .NET applications often need to run on multiple platforms. The X-engine provides cross-platform capabilities for video frame extraction:

#### Extracting Frames as System.Drawing.Bitmap

The most common approach is to extract frames as `System.Drawing.Bitmap` objects:

```
using VisioForge.Core.MediaInfoReaderX;

public void ExtractFrameAsBitmap()
{
    // Extract the frame at the beginning of the video (TimeSpan.Zero)
    var bitmap = MediaInfoReaderX.GetFileSnapshotBitmap("C:\\Videos\\sample.mp4", TimeSpan.Zero);

    // Extract a frame at 30 seconds into the video
    var frame30sec = MediaInfoReaderX.GetFileSnapshotBitmap("C:\\Videos\\sample.mp4", TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));

    // Save the extracted frame
    bitmap.Save("C:\\Output\\first-frame.png");
    frame30sec.Save("C:\\Output\\frame-30sec.png");
}
```

#### Extracting Frames as SkiaSharp Bitmaps

For applications using SkiaSharp for graphics processing, you can extract frames directly as `SKBitmap` objects:

```
using VisioForge.Core.MediaInfoReaderX;
using SkiaSharp;

public void ExtractFrameAsSkiaBitmap()
{
    // Extract the frame at 15 seconds into the video
    var skBitmap = MediaInfoReaderX.GetFileSnapshotSKBitmap("C:\\Videos\\sample.mp4", TimeSpan.FromSeconds(15));

    // Work with the SKBitmap
    using (var image = SKImage.FromBitmap(skBitmap))
    using (var data = image.Encode(SKEncodedImageFormat.Png, 100))
    using (var stream = File.OpenWrite("C:\\Output\\frame-skia.png"))
    {
        data.SaveTo(stream);
    }
}
```

#### Working with Raw RGB Data

For more advanced scenarios or when you need direct pixel manipulation, you can extract frames as RGB byte arrays:

```
using VisioForge.Core.MediaInfoReaderX;

public void ExtractFrameAsRGBArray()
{
    // GetFileSnapshotRGB returns Tuple<byte[], int, int>: pixels + width + height.
    var snapshot = MediaInfoReaderX.GetFileSnapshotRGB("C:\\Videos\\sample.mp4", TimeSpan.FromSeconds(20));
    byte[] rgbData = snapshot.Item1;
    int width = snapshot.Item2;
    int height = snapshot.Item3;

    // Process the RGB data — the buffer holds R, G, B values for each pixel; width and
    // height come directly from the tuple, so no separate metadata call is needed.
}
```

## Best Practices for Video Frame Extraction

When implementing video frame extraction in your applications, consider these best practices:

### Performance Considerations

- Extracting frames can be CPU-intensive, especially for high-resolution videos
- Consider implementing caching mechanisms for frequently accessed frames
- For batch extraction, implement parallel processing where appropriate

```
// Example of parallel frame extraction
public void ExtractMultipleFramesInParallel(string videoPath, TimeSpan[] timestamps)
{
    Parallel.ForEach(timestamps, timestamp => {
        var bitmap = MediaInfoReaderX.GetFileSnapshotBitmap(videoPath, timestamp);
        bitmap.Save($"C:\\Output\\frame-{timestamp.TotalSeconds}.png");
    });
}
```

### Error Handling

Always implement proper error handling when working with video files:

```
public Bitmap SafeExtractFrame(string videoPath, TimeSpan position)
{
    try
    {
        return MediaInfoReaderX.GetFileSnapshotBitmap(videoPath, position);
    }
    catch (FileNotFoundException)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Video file not found");
    }
    catch (InvalidOperationException)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Invalid position in video");
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Error extracting frame: {ex.Message}");
    }

    return null;
}
```

### Memory Management

Proper memory management is crucial, especially when working with large video files:

```
public void ExtractFrameWithProperDisposal()
{
    Bitmap bitmap = null;
    try
    {
        bitmap = MediaInfoReaderX.GetFileSnapshotBitmap("C:\\Videos\\sample.mp4", TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
        // Process the bitmap...
    }
    finally
    {
        bitmap?.Dispose();
    }
}
```

Frame extraction is used in various multimedia applications:

- **Media Libraries**: Creating video thumbnails for gallery views
- **Video Analysis**: Extracting frames for computer vision processing
- **Content Management**: Creating preview images for video assets
- **Video Editing**: Providing visual reference for timeline editing

## Conclusion

Extracting frames from video files is a powerful capability for .NET developers working with multimedia content. Whether you're building Windows-specific applications or cross-platform solutions, the methods described in this guide provide efficient ways to capture and work with video frames.

By understanding the different approaches and following best practices, you can implement robust frame extraction functionality in your .NET applications.

# .NET Media Player SDK Implementation Examples
