This page collects ready-to-use C# recipes for the most common playback scenarios using the Media Player SDK .NET. Each snippet is verified against the SDK source and demos under [`Media Player SDK`](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Media%20Player%20SDK). The Windows-only `MediaPlayerCore` engine is used in the examples below; cross-platform code based on `MediaPlayerCoreX` follows the same overall shape with engine-specific source settings.

## Available Recipes

### Basic Playback

- Open a local file and start playback
- Pause, resume, and stop a running player
- Adjust the output volume

### Streaming

- Play a network stream (HTTP / RTSP) by URL
- Switch source engine to the FFmpeg backend for live streams

### Effects and Processing

- Capture the current frame as a `Bitmap`
- Seek to a specific position and read playback time

## Recipe — Simple Player

The following class wraps `MediaPlayerCore` with start/stop calls. The constructor receives an `IVideoView` instance (`VideoView` for WPF, `VideoViewWinForms` for WinForms, etc.) that is provided by your UI layer.

```
using System;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using VisioForge.Core.MediaPlayer;
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.Events;

public class SimplePlayer
{
    private readonly MediaPlayerCore _player;

    public SimplePlayer(IVideoView videoView)
    {
        _player = new MediaPlayerCore(videoView);

        // Subscribe to events.
        _player.OnStop += OnPlaybackStopped;
        _player.OnError += OnPlaybackError;
    }

    public async Task PlayFileAsync(string filePath)
    {
        _player.Playlist_Clear();
        _player.Playlist_Add(filePath);
        await _player.PlayAsync();
    }

    public Task StopAsync() => _player.StopAsync();

    private void OnPlaybackStopped(object sender, StopEventArgs e)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Playback finished.");
    }

    private void OnPlaybackError(object sender, ErrorsEventArgs e)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Error: {e.Message}");
    }
}
```

## Recipe — Player With Pause and Volume Controls

`MediaPlayerCore` exposes `PauseAsync`/`ResumeAsync` for in-flight playback control and a per-output-device volume API (`Audio_OutputDevice_Volume_Set`) that accepts an integer in the 0–100 range.

```
using System;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using VisioForge.Core.MediaPlayer;
using VisioForge.Core.Types;

public class ControllablePlayer
{
    private readonly MediaPlayerCore _player;
    private bool _isPaused;

    public ControllablePlayer(IVideoView videoView)
    {
        _player = new MediaPlayerCore(videoView);
    }

    public async Task PlayPauseAsync()
    {
        if (_isPaused)
        {
            await _player.ResumeAsync();
            _isPaused = false;
        }
        else
        {
            await _player.PauseAsync();
            _isPaused = true;
        }
    }

    public Task SeekAsync(TimeSpan position) =>
        _player.Position_Set_TimeAsync(position);

    public void SetVolume(int volume)
    {
        // volume: 0 (mute) … 100 (full) for the first audio output device.
        _player.Audio_OutputDevice_Volume_Set(0, volume);
    }

    public Task<TimeSpan> GetDurationAsync() => _player.Duration_TimeAsync();

    public Task<TimeSpan> GetPositionAsync() => _player.Position_Get_TimeAsync();
}
```

## Recipe — Capture the Current Frame

`Frame_GetCurrent()` returns the most recently rendered frame as a `System.Drawing.Bitmap`. Save it via the `Bitmap.Save` API or use `Frame_Save` for built-in disk output with `ImageFormat`. Call them while playback is running: after `Stop` they return `null` or `false` and report the reason through `OnError`.

```
using System.Drawing.Imaging;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

public Task<bool> SaveCurrentFrameAsync(MediaPlayerCore player, string outputPath)
{
    // Built-in helper: encodes the current frame to PNG (or any ImageFormat).
    return player.Frame_SaveAsync(outputPath, ImageFormat.Png);
}
```

## Recipe — Play a Network Stream

To consume RTSP, RTMP, HTTP, UDP, or TCP URLs through the FFmpeg back-end, switch `Source_Mode` to `MediaPlayerSourceMode.FFMPEG` and add the URL to the playlist like any other source.

```
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using VisioForge.Core.MediaPlayer;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.MediaPlayer;

public async Task PlayRtspAsync(MediaPlayerCore player, string url)
{
    player.Source_Mode = MediaPlayerSourceMode.FFMPEG;

    player.Playlist_Clear();
    player.Playlist_Add(url);

    await player.PlayAsync();
}
```

## Recipe — Playlist Navigation

The built-in playlist API tracks the current index for you. `Playlist_PlayNext` advances to the next item; `OnStop` fires on natural end-of-stream, where you can chain the next track.

```
using System;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using VisioForge.Core.MediaPlayer;
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.Events;

public class PlaylistPlayer
{
    private readonly MediaPlayerCore _player;

    public PlaylistPlayer(IVideoView videoView)
    {
        _player = new MediaPlayerCore(videoView);
        _player.OnStop += OnTrackFinished;
    }

    public void AddToPlaylist(string filePath) => _player.Playlist_Add(filePath);

    public Task PlayAsync() => _player.PlayAsync();

    public Task<bool> NextAsync() => _player.Playlist_PlayNextAsync();

    private async void OnTrackFinished(object sender, StopEventArgs e)
    {
        // Auto-advance to the next playlist entry on natural EOS.
        if (e.Successful)
        {
            await _player.Playlist_PlayNextAsync();
        }
    }
}
```

# Play a Video from Memory in C# WPF

[Media Player SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/media-player-sdk-net)

## The code behind the window

`MainWindow.xaml.cs`. The project has `ImplicitUsings` enabled, so `System`, `System.Threading.Tasks` and the other common namespaces are not listed.

```
using System.ComponentModel;
using System.IO;
using System.Windows;
using System.Windows.Controls.Primitives;
using System.Windows.Threading;
using Microsoft.Win32;
using VisioForge.Core;
using VisioForge.Core.MediaPlayer;
using VisioForge.Core.Types;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.MediaPlayer;

namespace MemoryPlaybackWpf;

public partial class MainWindow : Window
{
    private MediaPlayerCore _player;

    private Stream _source; // the player reads it while it plays: closed only after the stop

    private readonly DispatcherTimer _timer = new() { Interval = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(500) };

    private bool _timerMovesSlider; // true while the timer, not the user, moves the timeline

    public MainWindow()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private void Window_Loaded(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        _player = new MediaPlayerCore(VideoView1);
        _player.OnError += (_, args) => Dispatcher.InvokeAsync(() => edLog.AppendText(args.Message + Environment.NewLine));

        // Raised by StopAsync and at the end of the file; acted on only for the end of the file
        // (Stop is enabled), not for a late stop of the previous file (State is no longer Free)
        _player.OnStop += (_, _) => Dispatcher.InvokeAsync(() =>
        {
            if (btStop.IsEnabled && _player.State() == PlaybackState.Free) Stopped();
        });

        _timer.Tick += Timer_Tick;
    }

    private void btOpen_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        var dialog = new OpenFileDialog
        {
            Filter = "Video files|*.mp4;*.mkv;*.avi;*.mov;*.wmv;*.webm;*.ts|All files|*.*"
        };

        if (dialog.ShowDialog() == true) edFilename.Text = dialog.FileName;
    }

    private async void btPlay_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        ShowBusy();
        edLog.Clear();

        try
        {
            _source = rbByteArray.IsChecked == true
                ? new MemoryStream(await File.ReadAllBytesAsync(edFilename.Text)) // the whole file in memory
                : new FileStream(edFilename.Text, FileMode.Open, FileAccess.Read);
        }
        catch (Exception ex) when (ex is IOException or UnauthorizedAccessException or ArgumentException)
        {
            edLog.AppendText(ex.Message + Environment.NewLine);
            ShowPlaying(false);
            return;
        }

        // A seekable .NET stream, wrapped as the COM IStream the player reads; the LAV splitter
        // finds the video and audio in it
        _player.Source_MemoryStream = new MemoryStreamSource(new ManagedIStream(_source), _source.Length);
        _player.Source_Mode = MediaPlayerSourceMode.Memory_DS;

        if (!await _player.PlayAsync() || _player.State() == PlaybackState.Free)
        {
            Stopped(); // did not play (the reason is in the log), or has already ended
            return;
        }

        slTimeline.Maximum = (await _player.Duration_TimeAsync()).TotalSeconds;
        ShowPlaying(true);
        _timer.Start();
    }

    private async void btPause_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        btPause.IsEnabled = false;
        var paused = await _player.PauseAsync();
        if (!btStop.IsEnabled) return; // stopped meanwhile
        btResume.IsEnabled = paused;
        btPause.IsEnabled = !paused;
    }

    private async void btResume_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        btResume.IsEnabled = false;
        var resumed = await _player.ResumeAsync();
        if (!btStop.IsEnabled) return; // stopped meanwhile
        btPause.IsEnabled = resumed;
        btResume.IsEnabled = !resumed;
    }

    private async void btStop_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        _timer.Stop();
        ShowBusy();
        await _player.StopAsync();
        Stopped();
    }

    private void ShowBusy()
    {
        btPlay.IsEnabled = btPause.IsEnabled = btResume.IsEnabled = btStop.IsEnabled = false;
    }

    private void ShowPlaying(bool playing)
    {
        btPlay.IsEnabled = !playing;
        btPause.IsEnabled = btStop.IsEnabled = playing;
        btResume.IsEnabled = false;
    }

    private void Stopped()
    {
        _timer.Stop();
        ShowPlaying(false);

        _source?.Dispose(); // the player has let go of it
        _source = null;

        lbTime.Text = "00:00:00 / 00:00:00";
        _timerMovesSlider = true;
        slTimeline.Value = 0;
        _timerMovesSlider = false;
    }

    private async void Timer_Tick(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        var position = await _player.Position_Get_TimeAsync();
        if (!_timer.IsEnabled || slTimeline.IsMouseCaptureWithin) return; // stopped, or the user drags

        var duration = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(slTimeline.Maximum); // read once, after PlayAsync
        lbTime.Text = $"{position:hh\\:mm\\:ss} / {duration:hh\\:mm\\:ss}";

        _timerMovesSlider = true;
        slTimeline.Value = position.TotalSeconds;
        _timerMovesSlider = false;
    }

    // A click on the track seeks at once, a drag seeks once when it ends
    private async void slTimeline_ValueChanged(object sender, RoutedPropertyChangedEventArgs<double> e)
    {
        if (!_timerMovesSlider && !slTimeline.IsMouseCaptureWithin) await SeekAsync();
    }

    private async void slTimeline_DragCompleted(object sender, DragCompletedEventArgs e)
    {
        if (!e.Canceled && e.HorizontalChange != 0) await SeekAsync(); // not a press without a move
    }

    private async Task SeekAsync()
    {
        if (btStop.IsEnabled) await _player.Position_Set_TimeAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(slTimeline.Value));
    }

    private void Window_Closing(object sender, CancelEventArgs e)
    {
        _timer.Stop();
        _player.Dispose(); // stops playback; Stopped() then closes the stream, or the app's exit does
    }
}
```

## How it works

1. **The source** — with *Byte array* checked, `File.ReadAllBytesAsync` reads the whole file into memory and a `MemoryStream` wraps the array; otherwise a `FileStream` opened with `FileAccess.Read` reads the file as the player asks for it. A missing or locked file goes to the log, and the window stays stopped.
2. **Memory playback** — `ManagedIStream` (namespace `VisioForge.Core`) wraps the .NET stream as the COM `IStream` the DirectShow engine reads. `MemoryStreamSource` takes it together with the stream's length, and `Source_Mode = MediaPlayerSourceMode.Memory_DS` makes the player read from it. With the LAV package installed, the LAV splitter finds the video and audio tracks in the stream, so the two-argument constructor is enough.
3. **Play** — `PlayAsync` returns `false` when the stream cannot be played, and the reason arrives through `OnError`. `State()` returning `PlaybackState.Free` means it did not play, or a very short file has already ended. Otherwise `Duration_TimeAsync` is read once, for the timeline's scale.
4. **The stream's lifetime** — the player reads the stream for as long as it plays and seeks in it, so `Stopped()` is the one place that disposes it: after `StopAsync`, or when `OnStop` reports the end of the file. A `using` block around `PlayAsync` would close the stream while the video plays.
5. **Timeline** — a `DispatcherTimer` reads `Position_Get_TimeAsync` twice a second on the UI thread. The `_timerMovesSlider` flag tells the timer's own updates apart from the user's, so the timer never seeks. A click on the track seeks at once; a drag seeks once, in `Thumb.DragCompleted`. `Position_Set_TimeAsync` seeks inside the stream.
6. **Stop and close** — `OnStop` fires after `StopAsync` and at the end of the file, on another thread, so the handler goes back to the UI thread with `Dispatcher.InvokeAsync`, as `OnError` does. It acts only while Stop is enabled and `State()` is `PlaybackState.Free`. Closing the window calls `Dispose`, which stops playback and releases the player.

## Notes

- The stream must be readable and seekable, and its `Length` must be known: the player seeks in it to find the tracks and to follow the timeline. A network or decompression stream that cannot seek is copied into a `MemoryStream` first.
- A byte array holds the whole file in memory. For a large file, a `FileStream` reads only what the player needs.
- Without the LAV package the player cannot tell what the stream holds: use the constructor `MemoryStreamSource(IStream stream, bool? videoPresent, bool? audioPresent, long size)` and set both flags to what the stream really contains.
- `ManagedIStream` reads through any `Stream`, so a custom stream class — a decrypting stream, for example — plays the same way, as long as it is readable and seekable.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can I play a video from a byte array in C#?

Yes. Wrap the array in a `MemoryStream`, wrap that in `ManagedIStream`, and pass it to `MemoryStreamSource` with the array's length. Set `Source_Mode` to `MediaPlayerSourceMode.Memory_DS` and call `PlayAsync`. Keep the `MemoryStream` open until playback has stopped.

### Why does playback stop or fail right after it starts?

The stream is usually disposed too early, for example by a `using` block around `PlayAsync`, or the stream cannot seek. Keep the stream in a field and dispose it after `StopAsync` or at the end of the file.

### Can I play a stream downloaded from the network?

Copy it into a `MemoryStream` first. A network stream cannot seek and has no length, and the player needs both.

### Which formats play from memory?

What the LAV splitter and decoders read from a file: MP4, MKV, AVI, MOV, WMV, WebM, MPEG-TS and others. The stream holds the same bytes as the file.

### What we build

Let's play a video from memory in a C# WPF app, with the VisioForge Media Player SDK. Here's what we build. A WPF player that reads a .NET stream instead of a file name. Either a FileStream, or the whole file read into a byte array and wrapped in a MemoryStream. It has Play, Pause, Resume and Stop, and a timeline to seek. The same code plays a stream you got from anywhere else: a download, a database, or a file you decrypted in memory. This is the finished player. ### Prerequisites

You need Windows 10 or 11, and Visual Studio 2022 or 2026 with the .NET desktop development workload. The project is a WPF app on .NET 10. And a video file to play. The player here is MediaPlayerCore, the SDK's DirectShow engine, so this app runs on Windows.

### Create a WPF project

In Visual Studio, create a new project. Search for WPF, and pick WPF Application for C#. Name the project MemoryPlaybackWpf. Choose .NET 10 and click Create.

### Add the NuGet packages

Now add three NuGet packages. VisioForge.DotNet.Core holds MediaPlayerCore. Redist MediaPlayer holds the SDK's DirectShow filters, among them the source that reads the stream. And Redist LAV holds the LAV splitter and decoders, which find the video and audio in the stream and decode them. Or use the NuGet Package Manager: right-click the project, Manage NuGet Packages, and install VisioForge.DotNet.Core from the Browse tab. Then install the MediaPlayer and LAV redists for x64. The Installed tab lists all three. These are the x64 packages, so set PlatformTarget to x64 in the project file. A 32-bit app takes the x86 packages instead.

### Build the window in XAML

The window is written in XAML. First the window itself, with a grid and a VideoView, and the designer draws it right away. Map the VisioForge.Core.UI.WPF namespace to a prefix, here vf. The grid has two columns, the video and a 260-pixel settings column, and three rows: the video, the timeline and the buttons. The VideoView fills the first cell. The window also names its Loaded and Closing handlers. Under the video goes the timeline. A slider for the position, with the time on its right. IsMoveToPointEnabled makes a click on the track jump straight to that point. The slider names two handlers: ValueChanged, and DragCompleted of its thumb. Then the playback buttons. Play, Pause, Resume and Stop, each with a Click handler. Play is enabled from the start, because this engine needs no SDK initialization. The other three start disabled, until a file plays. Last, the settings column on the right. It holds the file name with a browse button, and two radio buttons that choose how the app reads the file: as a FileStream, or as a byte array in a MemoryStream. Stream is checked at first. Then a read-only text box for the error log. Every handler the XAML names goes into MainWindow.xaml.cs, and the next chapters write them.

### Create the player

MainWindow.xaml.cs starts with these usings: System.IO for the streams, WPF namespaces for the slider thumb and the timer, Microsoft.Win32 for the file dialog, and the VisioForge namespaces. The window keeps the player, the stream it plays, a timer for the timeline, and a flag. When the window loads, create MediaPlayerCore and pass it the VideoView, where the video is drawn. Errors arrive in the OnError event on another thread, so the handler goes back to the UI thread and adds them to the log. OnStop fires after StopAsync, and when the file reaches its end. The handler acts only while Stop is enabled and State is Free, which is the end of the file. Then Window\_Loaded wires up the timer's Tick handler. The browse button shows an OpenFileDialog filtered to video files, and puts the chosen path into the file name box.

### Play from memory

The Play handler first disables the buttons and clears the log. Then it opens the source. With Byte array checked, ReadAllBytesAsync reads the whole file into memory, and a MemoryStream wraps the array. Otherwise a FileStream reads the file as the player needs it. A file that is missing or locked goes to the log, and the window stays stopped. This is the part that plays from memory. ManagedIStream wraps the .NET stream as the COM IStream the DirectShow engine reads. MemoryStreamSource takes it with the stream's length, and Source\_Mode set to Memory\_DS makes the player read from it. The stream must be readable and seekable. The LAV splitter finds the video and audio tracks in it, so you do not tell the player what the stream holds. PlayAsync returns false when the stream cannot be played, and the reason arrives in OnError. State Free means it did not play, or a very short file has already ended, and the window goes back to stopped. Otherwise read the duration once, for the timeline's scale, switch the buttons to playing, and start the timer.

### Pause, resume and stop

Pause disables itself, awaits PauseAsync, and enables Resume when the player has paused. If playback stopped in the meantime, it leaves the buttons alone. Resume is the same, with ResumeAsync. Stop stops the timer, disables the buttons while it works, awaits StopAsync, and resets the window. Two small helpers set the buttons. ShowBusy disables all four. ShowPlaying enables either Play, or Pause and Stop. Stopped puts the window back, and it is the one place that closes the stream. The player reads the stream for as long as it plays, so dispose it only once the player has stopped, never right after PlayAsync. Then the time label and the timeline go back to zero.

### The timeline

The timer ticks twice a second on the UI thread. Each tick reads Position\_Get\_TimeAsync. While the user holds the slider, the tick leaves it alone. Otherwise it updates the time label and moves the slider, with the flag set, so that this move does not seek. A click on the track seeks at once, in ValueChanged. A drag seeks once, when the thumb is released, in DragCompleted. Both call Position\_Set\_TimeAsync while a file plays. Seeking works on a memory stream too, because the stream is seekable.

### Close the window

When the window closes, Dispose stops playback and releases the player. The stream is closed by Stopped, or with the app.

### Run it

Run the app from Visual Studio. Click the browse button and pick the video file. Stream is checked, so Play reads the file through a FileStream. The time label shows the position and the length. A click on the timeline seeks inside the stream. Pause holds the picture, Resume carries on from the same point, and Stop resets the window. Now check Byte array and click Play. The app reads the whole file into memory first, and the player plays it from the MemoryStream, with no file access while it plays. Stop, and close the window.

### Common mistakes

A few common mistakes. Disposing the stream while the player still reads it, for example with a using block around PlayAsync: close it only after the stop. A stream that cannot seek, such as a network stream: the player needs to seek and to know the length, so copy it into a MemoryStream first. Leaving out the LAV package: without it the player cannot tell what the stream holds. A byte array for a huge file, which takes that much memory, so prefer a FileStream there. And mixing the x86 and x64 packages.

## Play Video File Fragments and Segments in C# .NET Apps
**URL:** https://www.visioforge.com/help/docs/dotnet/mediaplayer/code-samples/play-fragment-file/
**Description:** Play precise time-based segments of video and audio files with VisioForge Media Player SDK .NET on Windows and cross-platform environments.
**Tags:** Media Player SDK, .NET, MediaPlayerCoreX, Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, Playback, MKV, C#
**API:** MediaPlayerCoreX, UniversalSourceSettings

# Playing Media File Fragments: Implementation Guide for .NET Developers

[Media Player SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/media-player-sdk-net)

When developing media applications, one frequently requested feature is the ability to play specific segments of a video or audio file. This functionality is crucial for creating video editors, highlight reels, educational platforms, or any application requiring precise media segment playback.

## Understanding Fragment Playback in .NET Applications

Fragment playback allows you to define specific time segments of a media file for playback, effectively creating clips without modifying the source file. This technique is particularly useful when you need to:

- Create preview segments from longer media files
- Focus on specific sections of instructional videos
- Create looping segments for demonstrations or presentations
- Build clip-based media players for sports highlights or video compilations
- Implement training applications that focus on specific video segments

The Media Player SDK .NET provides two primary engines for implementing fragment playback, each with its own approach and platform compatibility considerations.

## Windows-Only Implementation: MediaPlayerCore Engine

The MediaPlayerCore engine provides a straightforward implementation for Windows applications. This solution works across WPF, WinForms, and console applications but is limited to Windows operating systems.

### Setting Up Fragment Playback

To implement fragment playback with the MediaPlayerCore engine, you'll need to follow three key steps:

1. Activate the selection mode on your MediaPlayer instance
2. Define the starting position of your fragment (in milliseconds)
3. Define the ending position of your fragment (in milliseconds)

### Implementation Example

The following C# code demonstrates how to configure fragment playback to play only the segment between 2000ms and 5000ms of your source file:

```
// Step 1: Enable fragment selection mode
MediaPlayer1.Selection_Active = true;

// Step 2: Set the starting position to 2000 milliseconds (2 seconds)
MediaPlayer1.Selection_Start = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(2000);

// Step 3: Set the ending position to 5000 milliseconds (5 seconds)
MediaPlayer1.Selection_Stop = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(5000);

// When you call Play() or PlayAsync(), only the specified fragment will play
```

When your application calls the Play or PlayAsync method after setting these properties, the player will automatically jump to the selection start position and stop playback when it reaches the selection end position.

### Required Redistributables for Windows Implementation

For the MediaPlayerCore engine implementation to function correctly, you must include:

- Base redistributable package
- SDK redistributable package

These packages contain the necessary components for the Windows-based playback functionality. For detailed information on deploying these redistributables to end-user machines, refer to the [deployment documentation](../../deployment/).

## Cross-Platform Implementation: MediaPlayerCoreX Engine

For developers requiring fragment playback functionality across multiple platforms, the MediaPlayerCoreX engine provides a more versatile solution. This implementation works across Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, and Linux environments.

### Setting Up Cross-Platform Fragment Playback

The cross-platform implementation follows a similar conceptual approach but uses different property names. The key steps include:

1. Creating a MediaPlayerCoreX instance
2. Loading your media source
3. Defining the segment start and stop positions
4. Initiating playback

### Cross-Platform Implementation Example

The following example demonstrates how to implement fragment playback in a cross-platform .NET application:

```
// Step 1: Create a new instance of MediaPlayerCoreX with your video view
MediaPlayerCoreX MediaPlayer1 = new MediaPlayerCoreX(VideoView1);

// Step 2: Set the source media file
var fileSource = await UniversalSourceSettings.CreateAsync("video.mkv");
await MediaPlayer1.OpenAsync(fileSource);

// Step 3: Define the segment start time (2 seconds from beginning)
MediaPlayer1.Segment_Start = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(2000);

// Step 4: Define the segment end time (5 seconds from beginning)
MediaPlayer1.Segment_Stop = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(5000);

// Step 5: Start playback of the defined segment
await MediaPlayer1.PlayAsync();
```

This implementation uses the Segment\_Start and Segment\_Stop properties instead of the Selection properties used in the Windows-only implementation. Also note the asynchronous approach used in the cross-platform example, which improves UI responsiveness.

## Advanced Fragment Playback Techniques

### Dynamic Fragment Adjustment

In more complex applications, you might need to adjust fragment boundaries dynamically. Both engines support changing the segment boundaries during runtime:

```
// For Windows-only implementation
private void UpdateFragmentBoundaries(int startMs, int endMs)
{
    MediaPlayer1.Selection_Start = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(startMs);
    MediaPlayer1.Selection_Stop = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(endMs);

    // If playback is in progress, restart it to apply the new boundaries
    if (MediaPlayer1.State() == PlaybackState.Play)
    {
        MediaPlayer1.Position_Set_Time(MediaPlayer1.Selection_Start);
    }
}

// For cross-platform implementation
private async Task UpdateFragmentBoundariesAsync(int startMs, int endMs)
{
    MediaPlayer1.Segment_Start = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(startMs);
    MediaPlayer1.Segment_Stop = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(endMs);

    // If playback is in progress, restart from the new start position (State is a sync property on MediaPlayerCoreX)
    if (MediaPlayer1.State == PlaybackState.Play)
    {
        await MediaPlayer1.Position_SetAsync(MediaPlayer1.Segment_Start);
    }
}
```

### Multiple Fragment Playback

For applications that need to play multiple fragments sequentially, you can implement a fragment queue:

```
public class MediaFragment
{
    public TimeSpan StartTime { get; set; }
    public TimeSpan EndTime { get; set; }
}

private Queue<MediaFragment> fragmentQueue = new Queue<MediaFragment>();
private bool isProcessingQueue = false;

// Add fragments to the queue
public void EnqueueFragment(TimeSpan start, TimeSpan end)
{
    fragmentQueue.Enqueue(new MediaFragment { StartTime = start, EndTime = end });

    if (!isProcessingQueue && MediaPlayer1 != null)
    {
        PlayNextFragment();
    }
}

// Process the fragment queue
private async void PlayNextFragment()
{
    if (fragmentQueue.Count == 0)
    {
        isProcessingQueue = false;
        return;
    }

    isProcessingQueue = true;
    var fragment = fragmentQueue.Dequeue();

    // Set the fragment boundaries
    MediaPlayer1.Segment_Start = fragment.StartTime;
    MediaPlayer1.Segment_Stop = fragment.EndTime;

    // Subscribe to completion event for this fragment
    MediaPlayer1.OnStop += (s, e) => PlayNextFragment();

    // Start playback
    await MediaPlayer1.PlayAsync();
}
```

### Performance Considerations

For optimal performance when using fragment playback, consider the following tips:

1. For frequent seeking between fragments, use formats with good keyframe density
2. MP4 and MOV files generally perform better for fragment-heavy applications
3. Setting fragments at keyframe boundaries improves seeking performance
4. Consider preloading files before setting fragment boundaries
5. On mobile platforms, keep fragments reasonably sized to avoid memory pressure

## Conclusion

Implementing fragment playback in your .NET media applications provides substantial flexibility and enhanced user experience. Whether you're developing for Windows only or targeting multiple platforms, the Media Player SDK .NET offers robust solutions for precise media segment playback.

By leveraging the techniques demonstrated in this guide, you can create sophisticated media experiences that allow users to focus on exactly the content they need, without the overhead of editing or splitting source files.

For more code samples and implementations, visit our [GitHub repository](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples) where you'll find comprehensive examples of media player implementations, including fragment playback and other advanced media features.

**Description:** Implement playlist functionality in WinForms, WPF, and Console apps using VisioForge Media Player SDK .NET. Sequential and custom playback order.
**Tags:** Media Player SDK, .NET, MediaPlayerCore, Windows, Playback, MP4, C#
**API:** NewFilePlaybackEventArgs

# Complete Guide to Playlist API Implementation in .NET

[Media Player SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/media-player-sdk-net) [MediaPlayerCore](#)

## Introduction to Playlist Management

The Playlist API provides a powerful and flexible way to manage media content in your .NET applications. Whether you're developing a music player, video application, or any media-centric software, efficient playlist management is essential for delivering a seamless user experience.

This guide covers everything you need to know about implementing playlist functionality using the MediaPlayerCore component. You'll learn how to create playlists, navigate between tracks, handle playlist events, and optimize performance in various .NET environments.

## Key Features and Benefits

- **Simple Integration**: Easy-to-implement API that integrates seamlessly with existing .NET applications
- **Format Compatibility**: Support for a wide range of audio and video formats
- **Cross-Platform**: Works consistently across WinForms, WPF, and console applications
- **Performance Optimized**: Built for efficient memory usage and responsive playback
- **Event-Driven Architecture**: Rich event system for building reactive UI experiences

## Getting Started with Playlist API

Before diving into specific methods, ensure you have properly initialized the MediaPlayer component in your application. The following sections contain practical code examples that you can implement directly in your project.

### Creating Your First Playlist

Creating a playlist is the first step in managing multiple media files. The API provides straightforward methods to add files to your playlist collection:

```
// Initialize the media player (assuming you've added the component to your form)
// this.mediaPlayer1 = new MediaPlayer();

// Add individual files to the playlist
this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_Add(@"c:\media\intro.mp4");
this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_Add(@"c:\media\main_content.mp4");
this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_Add(@"c:\media\conclusion.mp4");

// Start playback from the first item
this.mediaPlayer1.Play();
```

This approach allows you to build playlists programmatically, which is ideal for applications where playlist content is determined at runtime.

## Core Playlist Operations

### Navigating Through Playlist Items

Once you've created a playlist, your users will need to navigate between items. The API provides intuitive methods for moving to the next or previous file:

```
// Play the next file in the playlist
this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_PlayNext();

// Play the previous file in the playlist
this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_PlayPrevious();
```

These methods automatically handle the transition between media files, including stopping the current playback and starting the new item.

### Managing Playlist Content

During application runtime, you may need to modify the playlist by removing specific items or clearing it entirely:

```
// Remove a specific file from the playlist
this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_Remove(@"c:\media\intro.mp4");

// Clear all items from the playlist
this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_Clear();
```

This dynamic content management allows your application to adapt to user preferences or changing requirements on the fly.

### Retrieving Playlist Information

Accessing information about the current state of the playlist is crucial for building an informative user interface:

```
// Get the current file's index (0-based)
int currentIndex = this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_GetPosition();

// Get the total number of files in the playlist
int totalFiles = this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_GetCount();

// Get a specific filename by its index
string fileName = this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_GetFilename(1); // Gets the second file

// Display current playback information
string statusMessage = $"Playing file {currentIndex + 1} of {totalFiles}: {fileName}";
```

These methods enable you to create dynamic interfaces that reflect the current state of media playback.

## Advanced Playlist Control

### Resetting and Repositioning

For more precise control over playlist navigation, you can reset the playlist or jump to a specific position:

```
// Reset the playlist to start from the first file
this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_Reset();

// Jump to a specific position in the playlist (0-based index)
this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_SetPosition(2); // Jump to the third item
```

These methods are particularly useful for implementing features like "restart playlist" or allowing users to select specific items from a playlist view.

### Custom Event Handling for Playlist Navigation

To create a responsive application, you'll want to implement custom event handling for playlist navigation. Since the MediaPlayerCore doesn't have a dedicated playlist item changed event, you can create your own tracking mechanism using the existing events:

```
private int _lastPlaylistIndex = -1;

// Track playlist position changes when playback starts
private void mediaPlayer1_OnStart(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    int currentIndex = this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_GetPosition();
    if (currentIndex != _lastPlaylistIndex)
    {
        _lastPlaylistIndex = currentIndex;

        // Handle playlist item change
        string currentFile = this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_GetFilename(currentIndex);
        UpdatePlaylistUI(currentIndex, currentFile);
    }
}

// Also track when a new file playback starts
private void mediaPlayer1_OnNewFilePlaybackStarted(object sender, NewFilePlaybackEventArgs e)
{
    int currentIndex = this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_GetPosition();
    _lastPlaylistIndex = currentIndex;

    // Handle playlist item change
    string currentFile = this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_GetFilename(currentIndex);
    UpdatePlaylistUI(currentIndex, currentFile);
}

// Handle playlist completion
private void mediaPlayer1_OnPlaylistFinished(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    // Handle playlist completion
    this.lblPlaybackStatus.Text = "Playlist finished";

    // Optionally reset or loop playlist
    // this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_Reset();
    // this.mediaPlayer1.Play();
}

private void UpdatePlaylistUI(int index, string filename)
{
    // Update UI elements with new information
    this.lblCurrentTrack.Text = $"Now playing: {Path.GetFileName(filename)}";
    this.lblTrackNumber.Text = $"Track {index + 1} of {this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_GetCount()}";

    // Update playlist selection in UI
    // ...
}
```

This approach allows you to detect and respond to playlist navigation events in your application by subscribing to the actual events provided by MediaPlayerCore:

```
// Subscribe to events
this.mediaPlayer1.OnStart += mediaPlayer1_OnStart;
this.mediaPlayer1.OnNewFilePlaybackStarted += mediaPlayer1_OnNewFilePlaybackStarted;
this.mediaPlayer1.OnPlaylistFinished += mediaPlayer1_OnPlaylistFinished;
```

### Async Playlist Operations

The MediaPlayerCore provides async versions of playlist navigation methods for improved responsiveness:

```
// Play the next file asynchronously
await this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_PlayNextAsync();

// Play the previous file asynchronously
await this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_PlayPreviousAsync();
```

Using these async methods is recommended for UI applications to prevent blocking the main thread during playback transitions.

## Implementation Patterns and Best Practices

### Implementing Repeat and Shuffle Modes

Most media players include repeat and shuffle functionality. Here's how to implement these common features:

```
private bool repeatEnabled = false;
private bool shuffleEnabled = false;
private Random random = new Random();

// Handle playlist navigation when a track finishes. OnStop fires for both normal end-of-file
// and explicit Stop() calls — use OnPlaylistFinished (below) to react only at the end of the
// whole playlist. StopEventArgs exposes Successful (bool) and Position (TimeSpan); there is no
// StopReason enum.
private void MediaPlayer1_OnStop(object sender, StopEventArgs e)
{
    if (!e.Successful)
    {
        return; // Error or aborted — don't auto-advance
    }

    if (repeatEnabled)
    {
        // Just replay the current item
        this.mediaPlayer1.Play();
    }
    else if (shuffleEnabled)
    {
        // Play a random item
        int totalFiles = this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_GetCount();
        int randomIndex = random.Next(0, totalFiles);
        this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_SetPosition(randomIndex);
        this.mediaPlayer1.Play();
    }
    else
    {
        // Standard behavior: play next if available
        if (this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_GetPosition() < this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_GetCount() - 1)
        {
            this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_PlayNext();
        }
        // Otherwise we've reached the end of the playlist — OnPlaylistFinished fires separately.
    }
}

// Subscribe to the stop event
this.mediaPlayer1.OnStop += MediaPlayer1_OnStop;
```

### Memory Management for Large Playlists

When dealing with large playlists, consider implementing lazy loading techniques:

```
// Store playlist information separately for large playlists
private List<string> masterPlaylist = new List<string>();

public void LoadLargePlaylist(string[] filePaths)
{
    // Clear existing playlist
    this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_Clear();
    masterPlaylist.Clear();

    // Store all paths
    masterPlaylist.AddRange(filePaths);

    // Load only the first batch of items (e.g., 100)
    int initialBatchSize = Math.Min(100, filePaths.Length);
    for (int i = 0; i < initialBatchSize; i++)
    {
        this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_Add(filePaths[i]);
    }

    // Start playback
    this.mediaPlayer1.Play();
}

// Implement dynamic loading as user approaches the end of loaded items
private void CheckAndLoadMoreItems()
{
    int currentPosition = this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_GetPosition();
    int loadedCount = this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_GetCount();

    // If we're near the end of loaded items but have more in master playlist
    if (currentPosition > loadedCount - 10 && loadedCount < masterPlaylist.Count)
    {
        // Load next batch
        int nextBatchSize = Math.Min(50, masterPlaylist.Count - loadedCount);
        for (int i = 0; i < nextBatchSize; i++)
        {
            this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_Add(masterPlaylist[loadedCount + i]);
        }
    }
}
```

## Cross-Platform Considerations

The Playlist API functions consistently across different .NET environments, but there are some platform-specific considerations:

### WPF Implementation Notes

When implementing in WPF applications, you'll typically use data binding with your playlist:

```
// Create an observable collection to bind to UI
private ObservableCollection<PlaylistItem> observablePlaylist = new ObservableCollection<PlaylistItem>();

// Sync the observable collection with the player's playlist
private void SyncObservablePlaylist()
{
    observablePlaylist.Clear();
    for (int i = 0; i < this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_GetCount(); i++)
    {
        string filename = this.mediaPlayer1.Playlist_GetFilename(i);
        observablePlaylist.Add(new PlaylistItem
        {
            Index = i,
            FileName = System.IO.Path.GetFileName(filename),
            FullPath = filename
        });
    }
}
```

## Conclusion

The Playlist API provides a robust foundation for building feature-rich media applications in .NET. By using the methods and patterns outlined in this guide, you can create intuitive playlist management systems that enhance the user experience of your application.

For more advanced scenarios, explore the additional capabilities of the MediaPlayerCore component, including custom event handling, media metadata extraction, and format-specific optimizations.

## Reverse Video Playback and Frame Stepping in C# .NET
**URL:** https://www.visioforge.com/help/docs/dotnet/mediaplayer/code-samples/reverse-video-playback/
**Description:** Play video backwards in C# with a negative playback rate and step frame by frame in reverse, using MediaPlayerCoreX or a Media Blocks pipeline.
**Tags:** Media Player SDK, Media Blocks SDK, .NET, MediaPlayerCoreX, MediaBlocksPipeline, Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, Playback, MP4, C#
**API:** MediaPlayerCoreX, MediaBlocksPipeline, UniversalSourceBlock, UniversalSourceSettings, MediaPlayerCore

# Reverse Video Playback in C# and .NET

Reverse playback in Media Player SDK .NET and Media Blocks SDK .NET is a negative playback rate. `Rate_SetAsync(-1.0)` plays the file backwards from the current position to its start at normal speed; `-2.0` plays it backwards twice as fast, `-0.5` at half speed. The same call works on `MediaPlayerCoreX` and on a `MediaBlocksPipeline`. The UI snippets below use WPF.

Reverse playback needs a seekable source: a media file, not a live stream such as a camera or RTSP.

## YouTube tutorial

[Source code on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Media%20Player%20SDK%20X/_VideoTutorials/reverse-playback-csharp-wpf)

The film in the video is [Big Buck Bunny](https://peach.blender.org/) (c) Blender Foundation, under [CC BY 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/).

The video creates the project on .NET 10, which needs Visual Studio 2026; in Visual Studio 2022, choose .NET 8 or .NET 9.

## Reverse Playback with MediaPlayerCoreX

### Open, Play, Then Reverse

```
using System.Diagnostics;
using VisioForge.Core;
using VisioForge.Core.MediaPlayerX;

// A field of the window
private MediaPlayerCoreX player;

// In the window's Loaded handler
await VisioForgeX.InitSDKAsync(); // once per application

player = new MediaPlayerCoreX(VideoView1);
player.OnError += (_, e) => Debug.WriteLine(e.Message);

await player.OpenAsync(@"C:\Videos\sample.mp4");
await player.PlayAsync();
```

Switch to reverse while the file is playing, for example from a button:

```
private async void btReverse_Click(object sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
{
    // Plays backwards from the current position to the start of the file
    await player.Rate_SetAsync(-1.0);
}
```

`Rate_SetAsync` returns `false` and raises `OnError` when the rate cannot be applied. Three rules come from the SDK:

- **Reverse is set once playback has started.** While the file is not playing (after `OpenAsync` and before `PlayAsync`, or paused at the end by `PauseOnStop`), a negative rate is refused; only a positive rate is stored for the next start.
- **The rate seek needs a position.** Right after `PlayAsync` the pipeline may not report one yet, so call it once playback is running, not on the line after `PlayAsync`.
- **Each file starts at 1.0.** After `StopAsync`, or the end of the file without `PauseOnStop`, every rate is refused until the next `OpenAsync`; set the rate again after it.

### Play the Whole File Backwards from the End

Reverse plays from the current position. To play the whole file backwards, turn the reverse rate on and then seek to the end. A seek made while the rate is negative plays from that position back to the start. Seek only when the rate was applied; otherwise the seek goes forward to the end and playback ends at once:

```
if (await player.Rate_SetAsync(-1.0))
{
    await player.Position_SetAsync(await player.DurationAsync());
}
```

### Reverse Speed and Back to Forward

```
// Twice as fast, backwards
await player.Rate_SetAsync(-2.0);

// Half speed, backwards (slow motion)
await player.Rate_SetAsync(-0.5);

// Back to normal forward playback from the current position
await player.Rate_SetAsync(1.0);

// Which direction is playing now
bool isReverse = await player.Rate_GetAsync() < 0;
```

A rate of `0` is rejected; use `PauseAsync` to stop the picture.

### Position and the Start of the File

`MediaPlayerCoreX` raises no position event. Read the position on a timer, as for forward playback:

```
// A field of the window
private readonly DispatcherTimer _timer = new() { Interval = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(500) };

// In the window constructor or its Loaded handler
_timer.Tick += async (_, _) =>
{
    var position = await player.Position_GetAsync();
    var duration = await player.DurationAsync();
    lbTime.Text = $"{position:hh\\:mm\\:ss} / {duration:hh\\:mm\\:ss}";
};
```

Call `_timer.Start()` after `PlayAsync`. When reverse playback reaches the start of the file, playback ends the same way it does at the end of a forward run, and `OnStop` is raised:

```
player.OnStop += (_, _) => Dispatcher.InvokeAsync(() =>
{
    _timer.Stop();
    btPlay.IsEnabled = true;
});
```

With `PauseOnStop = true` the player pauses on the first frame instead of stopping, and raises `OnPause` instead of `OnStop`. Call `ResumeAsync` to play the file again; `PlayAsync` would close the file instead.

### Step Frame by Frame in Reverse

Two methods move by exactly one frame. Both pause playback first and work with files only:

| Method | Forward playback | Reverse playback |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NextFrame()` | one frame forward | one frame **back**, the reverse rate is kept |
| `PrevFrame()` | one frame **back**, the rate is set to 1.0 | one frame forward, the reverse rate is kept |

```
// One frame back while the file plays forward
player.PrevFrame();

// Keep stepping backwards: set the reverse rate once, then step
await player.Rate_SetAsync(-1.0);
player.NextFrame();
player.NextFrame();

// Stepping leaves playback paused; resume it to play on
await player.ResumeAsync();
```

`NextFrame` needs a video renderer (a `VideoView`). `PrevFrame` seeks to the previous frame and waits for the seek on the calling thread, up to a second, so it is slower, and its precision depends on the codec and the distance between keyframes. From a button handler, call it as `await Task.Run(player.PrevFrame);` to keep the window responsive.

## Reverse Playback with Media Blocks

A `MediaBlocksPipeline` takes the same rate calls. Build a player pipeline, start it, and set a negative rate while it runs:

```
graph LR
    UniversalSourceBlock -- video --> VideoRendererBlock
    UniversalSourceBlock -. audio .-> AudioRendererBlock
```

```
using System.Diagnostics;
using VisioForge.Core;
using VisioForge.Core.MediaBlocks;
using VisioForge.Core.MediaBlocks.AudioRendering;
using VisioForge.Core.MediaBlocks.Sources;
using VisioForge.Core.MediaBlocks.VideoRendering;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.X.Sources;

// A field of the window
private MediaBlocksPipeline pipeline;

// In the window's Loaded handler
await VisioForgeX.InitSDKAsync(); // once per application

pipeline = new MediaBlocksPipeline();
pipeline.OnError += (_, e) => Debug.WriteLine(e.Message);
pipeline.OnStop += (_, _) => Debug.WriteLine("Reached the start of the file");

var sourceSettings = await UniversalSourceSettings.CreateAsync(@"C:\Videos\sample.mp4");
var fileSource = new UniversalSourceBlock(sourceSettings);

var videoRenderer = new VideoRendererBlock(pipeline, VideoView1);
pipeline.Connect(fileSource.VideoOutput, videoRenderer.Input);

// A file without audio has no AudioOutput
if (fileSource.AudioOutput != null)
{
    var audioRenderer = new AudioRendererBlock();
    pipeline.Connect(fileSource.AudioOutput, audioRenderer.Input);
}

await pipeline.StartAsync();
```

Then, once it plays (for example from a button, not on the line after `StartAsync`):

```
// Backwards from the current position
await pipeline.Rate_SetAsync(-1.0);
```

To play the whole file backwards instead, seek to the end once the reverse rate is on:

```
if (await pipeline.Rate_SetAsync(-1.0))
{
    await pipeline.Position_SetAsync(await pipeline.DurationAsync());
}
```

Step and go forward again:

```
// One frame back during reverse playback (pauses first)
pipeline.NextFrame();

// Forward again: the step left the pipeline paused, so resume it
await pipeline.Rate_SetAsync(1.0);
await pipeline.ResumeAsync();
```

As with `MediaPlayerCoreX`, the negative rate is set after `StartAsync` and the seek to the end runs only once it was applied, `OnStop` is raised at the start of the file, and `NextFrame` needs the `VideoRendererBlock`. Unlike the player, a positive rate set after a stop is applied at the next `StartAsync`. The pipeline has no `PrevFrame`; it belongs to `MediaPlayerCoreX`.

When the window closes, release the engine and then the SDK:

```
// MediaPlayerCoreX: Dispose stops playback first
player.Dispose();

// MediaBlocksPipeline
await pipeline.StopAsync();
await pipeline.DisposeAsync();

// Once per application, after the last engine is released
VisioForgeX.DestroySDK();
```

## Windows: Reverse Frames with MediaPlayerCore

The Windows `MediaPlayerCore` engine (DirectShow) steps backwards through a cache of decoded frames instead of a negative rate. While reverse playback is enabled, the frames that play are kept in the cache; the feature requires the Professional edition.

```
using VisioForge.Core.MediaPlayer;

// MediaPlayer1 is a MediaPlayerCore; number of decoded frames kept for stepping back
MediaPlayer1.ReversePlayback_CacheSize = 100;
MediaPlayer1.ReversePlayback_Enabled = true;
```

Once some frames have played, step through the cache. Each call pauses playback first:

```
MediaPlayer1.ReversePlayback_PreviousFrame();
MediaPlayer1.ReversePlayback_NextFrame();

// Jump to a cached frame; 0 is the oldest one
MediaPlayer1.ReversePlayback_GoToFrame(50);

// Back to normal playback: frees the cache and resumes if paused
MediaPlayer1.ReversePlayback_Enabled = false;
```

A larger cache lets you go further back and uses more memory, which grows with the video resolution.

## Video Transcript

### What we build

Let's play a video backwards in a C# WPF app, with the VisioForge Media Player SDK. Here's what we build. In this SDK, reverse playback is a negative playback rate. The player plays backwards from the current point, or the whole file from its end. A speed slider changes how fast it plays, in either direction. And a button steps back one frame at a time. This is the finished player, playing backwards at normal speed. The film is Big Buck Bunny, by the Blender Foundation, under a Creative Commons Attribution license.

### Prerequisites

You need Windows 10 or 11, and Visual Studio 2026 with the .NET desktop development workload. The project is a WPF app on .NET 10; in Visual Studio 2022, choose .NET 8 or .NET 9. And a video file, because reverse playback needs a source you can seek in: a file, not a live stream. The player is MediaPlayerCoreX, which also runs on macOS, Linux, Android and iOS.

### Create a WPF project

In Visual Studio, create a new project. Search for WPF, and pick WPF Application for C#. Name the project ReversePlaybackWpf. Choose .NET 10 and click Create. Visual Studio opens MainWindow.xaml, with the designer above and the XAML below.

### Add the NuGet packages

Now add three NuGet packages. The Media Player SDK itself. CrossPlatform Core, the GStreamer runtime the player is built on. And CrossPlatform Libav, with the FFmpeg codecs that decode most video files. Or use the NuGet Package Manager: right-click the project, Manage NuGet Packages, and install VisioForge.DotNet.MediaPlayer from the Browse tab. Then install the Core and Libav packages for Windows x64. The Installed tab lists all three. These are the x64 packages, so set PlatformTarget to x64 in the project file.

### Build the window in XAML

The window is written in XAML. First the window itself, with a grid and a VideoView, and the designer draws it right away. Map the VisioForge.Core.UI.WPF namespace to a prefix, here vf. The grid has two columns, the video and a 260-pixel settings column, and four rows: the video, the time, the playback buttons and the reverse buttons. The VideoView fills the first cell. The window also names its Loaded and Closing handlers. Under the video go the time and the direction. Two text blocks. The position and the length on the left, with hundredths of a second, so a single frame step shows. The direction and the speed on the right. Then the playback buttons. Play, Pause, Resume and Stop, each with a Click handler. They all start disabled: Play until the SDK has loaded, the others until a file plays. The second row holds the reverse buttons. Reverse plays backwards from where the film is. Forward plays on forwards. From the end plays the whole file backwards. And Frame back steps one frame back. Last, the settings column on the right. It holds the file name with a browse button, a speed slider from 0.5 to 2 in steps of 0.25, and a read-only text box for the error log. Every handler the XAML names goes into MainWindow.xaml.cs, and the next chapters write them.

### Initialize the SDK

MainWindow.xaml.cs starts with these usings: WPF namespaces for the window and the timer, Microsoft.Win32 for the file dialog, and the VisioForge namespaces. The window keeps the player and a timer that ticks four times a second. When the window loads, await VisioForgeX.InitSDKAsync once. Then create MediaPlayerCoreX and pass it the VideoView, where the video is drawn. Errors arrive in the OnError event on another thread, so the handler goes back to the UI thread and adds them to the log. OnStop fires after StopAsync, and when playback runs out of the file: at its end going forwards, and at its start going backwards. The handler acts only while Stop is enabled and State is Free. Then Window\_Loaded wires up the timer and enables Play. The browse button shows an OpenFileDialog filtered to video files, and puts the chosen path into the file name box.

### Open and play

The Play handler disables the buttons and clears the log. OpenAsync opens the file, and PlayAsync plays it forwards at normal speed. Reverse comes later, from its own button: a negative rate is accepted only once the file is playing. State Free means the file did not open or play, and the window goes back to stopped. Otherwise the buttons switch to playing, and the timer starts.

### Play backwards

This is the whole of reverse playback. Rate\_SetAsync with a negative rate plays the file backwards, from the current position to the start. Minus one is normal speed, minus two twice as fast. Forward sets the same speed, positive, and the film plays on forwards from the same point. When the speed slider moves during playback, Rate\_GetAsync tells which way the film plays. A negative rate means backwards, so the new speed is set negative too, and the direction stays the same. To play the whole file backwards, turn the reverse rate on first, then seek to the end with Position\_SetAsync and the duration. A seek made while the rate is negative plays from that point back to the start. Seek only when the rate was applied: otherwise the seek goes forwards to the end, and playback ends at once.

### Step frame by frame

Two methods move by one frame, and both leave the picture paused. NextFrame steps along the playback direction, so while the film plays backwards, it steps one frame back. PrevFrame steps against the direction, so going forwards, it is the one that steps back. PrevFrame seeks and waits for the seek, so it runs on a worker thread with Task.Run. It also resets a forward rate to one, so the handler sets the chosen speed again.

### Pause, resume and stop

Pause and Resume are one call each, and Resume carries on in the same direction. Stop stops the timer, disables the buttons while it works, awaits StopAsync, and resets the window. Small helpers set the buttons: ShowBusy disables them all, and ShowPlaying enables either Play, or every playback and reverse button. Stopped puts the window back: the buttons, the time and the direction.

### Show the position and the direction

The player raises no position event, so the timer reads it. Each tick reads Position\_GetAsync, the duration and the rate. If playback stopped in the meantime, it leaves the labels alone. Otherwise it shows the position with hundredths of a second, and the direction and the speed from the sign and the size of the rate. Going backwards, the position counts down.

### Close the window

When the window closes, Dispose stops playback and releases the player, and DestroySDK releases the SDK. While the SDK still loads, or a file opens or stops, the window does not close yet.

### Run it

Run the app from Visual Studio. Once the SDK has loaded, Play is enabled. Click the browse button and pick the video file. Click Play. The film plays forwards at normal speed, and the label on the right says so. Drag the speed to two. Now it plays forwards twice as fast; here it is sped up further, to get into the film. Click Reverse. The film plays backwards from where it was, at twice the speed, and the time counts down. Drag the speed back to one. The direction stays: backwards, at normal speed. Forward plays on forwards from the same point. Frame back steps one frame back on each click, and the picture stays paused. Watch the hundredths. Resume plays on. From the end jumps to the end of the file and plays it backwards, towards the start. Frame back works while the film plays backwards, too, and Resume carries on backwards. Stop resets the window. Then close it.

### Common mistakes

A few common mistakes. Setting a negative rate before the file plays: the player refuses it, so set it once playback has started. Seeking to the end before the reverse rate is on: the file then ends at once. Trying reverse on a live stream, such as a camera: it needs a file you can seek in. Calling PrevFrame on the UI thread, which freezes the window while it seeks. And leaving out the Libav package, so many formats do not decode.

### Next steps

There are also guides for a full video player with a timeline and volume, for the same reverse playback in a Media Blocks pipeline, for playing only a fragment of a file, and for deploying the redists with your app. The full source is on GitHub, and the docs are at visioforge.com/help. Thanks for watching.

## Display First Frame of Video in C# .NET Applications
**URL:** https://www.visioforge.com/help/docs/dotnet/mediaplayer/code-samples/show-first-frame/
**Description:** Show the first video frame in WinForms, WPF, and Console apps with C# examples using VisioForge Media Player SDK .NET for thumbnail previews.
**Tags:** Media Player SDK, .NET, VideoCaptureCore, Windows, Capture, Playback, Streaming, C#

# Displaying the First Frame of Video Files in .NET Applications

[Media Player SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/media-player-sdk-net) [VideoCaptureCore](#)

## Overview

When developing media applications, it's often necessary to preview video content without playing the entire file. This technique is particularly useful for creating thumbnail galleries, video selection screens, or providing users with a visual preview before committing to watching a video.

## Implementation Guide

The Media Player SDK .NET provides a simple yet powerful way to display the first frame of any video file. This is achieved through the `Play_PauseAtFirstFrame` property, which when set to `true`, instructs the player to pause immediately after loading the first frame.

### How It Works

When the `Play_PauseAtFirstFrame` property is enabled:

1. The player loads the video file
2. Renders the first frame to the video display surface
3. Automatically pauses playback
4. Maintains the first frame on screen until further user action

If this property is not enabled (set to `false`), the player will proceed with normal playback after loading.

## Code Implementation

### Basic Example

```
// create player and configure the file name
// ...

// set the property to true
MediaPlayer1.Play_PauseAtFirstFrame = true;

// play the file
await MediaPlayer1.PlayAsync();
```

Resume playback from the first frame:

```
// resume playback
await MediaPlayer1.ResumeAsync();
```

## Practical Applications

This feature is particularly useful for:

- Providing preview capabilities in video editing applications
- Generating video poster frames for streaming applications
- Implementing "hover to preview" functionality in media browsers

## Required Components

To implement this functionality in your application, you'll need:

- Base redist package
- SDK redist package

For more information on distributing these components with your application, see: [How can the required redists be installed or deployed to the user's PC?](../../deployment/)

## Additional Resources

Find more code samples and implementation examples in our [GitHub repository](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples).

## Technical Considerations

When implementing this feature, keep in mind:

- First frame display is nearly instantaneous for most video formats
- Resource usage is minimal as the player doesn't buffer beyond the first frame
- Works with all supported video formats including MP4, MOV, AVI, and more
- In `MediaPlayerCore`, the property applies to one start and is then reset to `false`; it is not applied with `ConsoleUsage`, whose `Play()` waits for the end of the file, nor to a live source that reports it cannot show a frame while paused, which plays instead

## Deploy .NET Video Player - NuGet and Runtime Setup
**URL:** https://www.visioforge.com/help/docs/dotnet/mediaplayer/deployment/
**Description:** Configure NuGet packages and runtime dependencies for VisioForge Media Player SDK .NET apps on Windows and cross-platform environments.
**Tags:** Media Player SDK, .NET, DirectShow, MediaPlayerCoreX, Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, Playback, Streaming, Decoding, IP Camera, MP4, WebM, OGG, FLAC, Vorbis, NuGet

# Media Player SDK .NET Deployment Guide

[Media Player SDK .NET](https://www.visioforge.com/media-player-sdk-net)

This comprehensive guide covers all deployment scenarios for the Media Player SDK .NET, ensuring your applications work correctly across different environments. Whether you're developing cross-platform applications or Windows-specific solutions, this guide provides the necessary steps for successful deployment.

## Engine Types Overview

The Media Player SDK .NET offers two primary engine types, each designed for specific deployment scenarios:

### MediaPlayerCoreX Engine (Cross-Platform)

MediaPlayerCoreX is our cross-platform solution that works across multiple operating systems. For detailed deployment instructions specific to this engine, refer to the main [Cross-Platform Deployment Guide](../../deployment-x/).

### MediaPlayerCore Engine (Windows-Only)

The MediaPlayerCore engine is optimized specifically for Windows environments. When deploying applications that use this engine on computers without the SDK pre-installed, you must include the necessary SDK components with your application.

> **Important**: For AnyCPU applications, you should deploy both x86 and x64 redistributables to ensure compatibility across different system architectures.

## Deployment Options

There are three primary methods for deploying the Media Player SDK .NET components:

1. Using NuGet packages (recommended for most scenarios)
2. Using automatic silent installers (requires administrative privileges)
3. Manual installation (for complete control over the deployment process)

## NuGet Package Deployment

NuGet packages provide the simplest deployment method, automatically handling the inclusion of necessary files in your application folder during the build process.

### Required NuGet Packages

#### Core Packages (Always Required)

- **SDK Base Package**:
- [x86 Version](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.Base.x86/)
- [x64 Version](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.Base.x64/)
- [ARM64 Version](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.Base.arm64/) (.NET 5 or later)
- **Media Player SDK Package**:
- [x86 Version](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.MediaPlayer.x86/)
- [x64 Version](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.MediaPlayer.x64/)
- ARM64: not available yet

#### Feature-Specific Packages (Add as Needed)

##### Media Format Support

- **FFMPEG Package** (for file playback using FFMPEG source mode):
- [x86 Version](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.FFMPEG.x86/)
- [x64 Version](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.FFMPEG.x64/)
- **MP4 Output Package**:
- [x86 Version](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.MP4.x86/)
- [x64 Version](https://www.nuget.org/packages/VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.MP4.x64/)

> **Windows ARM64:** LAV Filters exist for x86 and x64 only. There is no upstream ARM64 build, so the SDK has no ARM64 LAV package. `LAV` is the default `Source_Mode` of `MediaPlayerCore`, so a `MediaPlayerCore` app running as an ARM64 process fails to play. AnyCPU apps usually run as ARM64 there too. On Windows ARM64, set `Source_Mode` to `MediaPlayerSourceMode.File_VLC` and add the VLC ARM64 package (playback works, but VisioForge filters that have no ARM64 build yet, such as YUV2RGB, still raise `OnError`), use `MediaPlayerCoreX` or Media Blocks SDK .NET, or build the app for x64 (`PlatformTarget` set to `x64`; it runs under emulation).

## Manual Installation

For advanced deployment scenarios requiring precise control over component installation, follow these steps:

### Step 1: Runtime Dependencies

- **With Administrative Privileges**: Install the VC++ 2022 (v143) runtime (x86/x64) and OpenMP runtime DLLs using redistributable executables or MSM modules.
- **Without Administrative Privileges**: Copy the VC++ 2022 (v143) runtime (x86/x64) and OpenMP runtime DLLs directly to your application folder.

### Step 2: Core Components

- Copy the VisioForge\_MFP/VisioForge\_MFPX (or x64 versions) DLLs from the Redist\Filters directory to your application folder.

### Step 3: .NET Assemblies

- Either copy the .NET assemblies to your application folder or install them to the Global Assembly Cache (GAC).

### Step 4: DirectShow Filters

- Copy and COM-register SDK DirectShow filters using [regsvr32.exe](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/regsvr32) or another suitable method.

### Step 5: Environment Configuration

- Add the folder containing the filters to the system PATH environment variable if your application executable is located in a different directory.

## Media Player SDK .NET FAQ — Streams, Seeking, Speed, WPF
**URL:** https://www.visioforge.com/help/docs/dotnet/mediaplayer/faq/
**Description:** Answers to common Media Player SDK .NET questions — network URLs, frames after seeking, speed and frame stepping, synchronized start, WPF and karaoke.
**Tags:** Media Player SDK, .NET, DirectShow, MediaPlayerCoreX, Windows, Playback, RTSP, WPF, Troubleshooting
**API:** MediaPlayerCore, MediaPlayerCoreX, CDGSourceSettings, MediaInfoReader, MediaInfoReaderX

# Media Player SDK .NET FAQ

Answers to the questions developers ask most often about Media Player SDK .NET, for both engines: `MediaPlayerCore` (Windows, DirectShow) and `MediaPlayerCoreX` (cross-platform). Deployment errors are collected in [Troubleshooting](../../general/troubleshooting/).

## Network sources

### "Unable to load source file or stream" — a network stream does not open

`MediaPlayerCore` reports this message, or `Unable to set URL to network VLC source filter` with the `HTTP_RTSP_VLC` source mode, when the source engine could not open the URL. Check, in this order:

1. The URL is the address of the stream itself (for example `rtsp://host:554/path` or `http://host/stream.m3u8`), not of a web page or just the IP address of the camera.
2. The same URL opens in VLC on the same computer. If it does not, the problem is the URL, the network or a firewall, not the player.
3. Credentials are included: `rtsp://login:password@host:port/path`.
4. The port is reachable from the computer that runs the application, not only from the development machine.

For IP cameras that need more than a URL, such as ONVIF discovery or a low-latency connection, see [Video Capture SDK FAQ](../../videocapture/faq/#ip-cameras).

## Seeking, speed and frames

### Frame\_GetCurrent returns the previous frame right after a seek

`Position_Set_Time` returns when the seek is requested, before the new frame has been decoded and rendered, so an immediate `Frame_GetCurrent()` still sees the old one. Take the frame from the `OnVideoFrameBitmap` event after the seek instead: set a flag when you seek, and keep a copy of `e.Frame` (`new Bitmap(e.Frame)`) the first time the handler runs after that; the event's own bitmap belongs to the SDK. To read frames from a file without playing it, see [Get a frame from a video file](../code-samples/get-frame-from-video-file/).

### How do I play faster or slower, step by frame or play backwards?

With `MediaPlayerCore`:

- `SetSpeedAsync(2.0)` plays at double speed; values below 1.0 slow it down.
- `NextFrame()` and `PreviousFrame()` pause playback and step one frame.
- Continuous backward playback uses the reverse playback mode — see [Reverse video playback](../code-samples/reverse-video-playback/).

With `MediaPlayerCoreX`, use `Rate_SetAsync(rate)` and `NextFrame()`.

Stepping backwards is expensive with formats that use key frames (H.264, HEVC and most others): the decoder has to go back to the previous key frame and decode forward again. Seeking with `Position_Set_Time` to an earlier position is the general way to go back.

### How do I start playback at an exact moment, or several players at once?

Preload the file and start it later. `PlayAsync(true)` builds and prepares the playback graph without starting it; `PlayDelayed()` then starts playback with almost no delay:

```
await player1.PlayAsync(true);
await player2.PlayAsync(true);

// at the moment you need
player1.PlayDelayed();
player2.PlayDelayed();
```

This is the way to synchronize video with an external clock or audio track on Windows. Media Player SDK .NET supports WinForms, WPF, WinUI 3, MAUI, Avalonia and Uno applications; UWP apps are not supported.

## WPF

### Can I put WPF controls over the video, or capture it with a VisualBrush?

Yes. The WPF `VideoView` is a WPF element, not a hosted WinForms window, so it takes part in WPF layout, transforms and z-order when it renders in a composable mode. Use the D3D11 composable renderer for GPU rendering, or the software mode. Only the native window renderers draw over everything — see [WPF controls over video](../../general/code-samples/wpf-controls-over-video/).

## Files and formats

### How do I play karaoke CDG files (MP3+G or ZIP) with pitch shifting?

`MediaPlayerCoreX` opens them with `CDGSourceSettings`, for a CDG and audio file pair or a ZIP archive that contains both:

```
var settings = new CDGSourceSettings("song.zip");
settings.EnablePitchShifting = true;
settings.PitchSemitones = -2;
await player.OpenAsync(settings);
await player.PlayAsync();
```

`Rate_SetAsync` changes the tempo of karaoke files too. The [Karaoke Demo](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Media%20Player%20SDK%20X/WinForms/Karaoke%20Demo) shows a complete karaoke player.

## Hardware decoding

### Which hardware decoder should the FFMPEG source engine use?

With `Source_Mode` set to `MediaPlayerSourceMode.FFMPEG`, set `Source_FFMPEG_HWDecoder` before `PlayAsync`. For IP cameras in Video Capture SDK .NET, the same choice is `FFMPEG_HWDecoder` in `IPCameraSourceSettings` with the `Auto_FFMPEG` engine. `DXVA2Native` is not available there.

```
player.Source_Mode = MediaPlayerSourceMode.FFMPEG;
player.Source_FFMPEG_HWDecoder = FFMPEGHWDecoder.Direct3D11;
```

| Value | Use it when |
| --- | --- |
| `Auto` (default) | You want the behaviour of earlier versions: software decoding. |
| `Software` | The video must be decoded on the CPU, for example to work around a driver problem. |
| `NvidiaCUDA` | The computer has an NVIDIA GPU. |
| `IntelQuickSync` | The computer has Intel graphics. |
| `Direct3D11` | Any GPU. A good first choice when you do not know the GPU vendor. |
| `DXVA2CopyBack` | Any GPU, including older drivers without Direct3D 11 video decoding. |
| `DXVA2Native` | The lowest CPU use, with EVR or madVR and without video effects or the sample grabber. |

`NvidiaCUDA`, `IntelQuickSync`, `Direct3D11` and `DXVA2CopyBack` copy the decoded frames back to system memory, so every renderer, video effect and the sample grabber work with them.

Every value except `Auto` is strict. When the computer has no such GPU, the GPU cannot decode the video (codec, profile, bit depth or frame size), or `DXVA2Native` has no renderer that accepts its surfaces, playback does not start and `OnError` names the decoder and the reason. The SDK never falls back to software decoding silently: handle `OnError` and choose another decoder, or `Auto`.

---END OF PAGE---
