## Frequently Asked Questions

### How do I cut and merge videos programmatically in C#?

Create a VideoEditCoreX instance, add source files to the timeline with start and end timestamps for trimming, arrange clips in the desired order, set the output format, and call Start(). The SDK handles frame-accurate cutting, re-encoding, and audio synchronization automatically.

### What output formats does the Video Edit SDK support?

The SDK supports MP4 (H.264/H.265), WebM (VP8/VP9), AVI, WMV, MKV, MPEG-1/2/4, and GIF output. Audio can be exported as MP3, AAC, OGG Vorbis, OPUS (VideoEditCoreX), FLAC, and WAV. You can also configure custom encoding parameters for bitrate, resolution, and frame rate.

### Can I add effects and transitions between video clips?

Yes. The SDK includes 50+ built-in video effects such as blur, sharpen, and color correction, plus chroma key and picture-in-picture on VideoEditCore. You can add smooth transitions between clips, overlay text and images with customizable positioning, and apply real-time audio effects.

### Can I render edited videos in batch?

Yes. Build each timeline in code (clips, trims, titles, transitions) and render the jobs one after another or in parallel, for example to produce templated videos from a list of inputs. Each job has its own output format, resolution, frame rate and encoding settings. For FFmpeg-based transcoding on Windows, see Video Edit SDK FFmpeg .NET.

### Is hardware-accelerated encoding available for video editing?

Yes. The SDK supports GPU-accelerated encoding via NVIDIA NVENC, Intel Quick Sync Video, and AMD AMF. Hardware encoding dramatically speeds up video export operations, especially for high-resolution content like 4K video.

### What platforms are supported for video editing?

The SDK supports WinForms, WPF, MAUI, Uno Platform, and Avalonia on Windows. Cross-platform editing works on macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android. Both .NET Framework 4.6.1+ and .NET 6/8/9+ are supported.

### Can I edit or render video in Unity?

Yes. Video Edit SDK .NET ships a ready-to-import .unitypackage. The VideoEditCoreX engine builds a timeline of clips with effects and transitions, previews it live into a Unity Texture2D, and renders the result to MP4 — all from inside your Unity build, on Windows, Android, macOS, and iOS.

### Can I render a timeline to MP4 from a Unity app?

Yes. After composing the timeline, set an MP4 output and start the VideoEditCoreX engine to render the finished movie to disk with hardware-accelerated H.264 / HEVC encoding (NVENC and Quick Sync on Windows, MediaCodec on Android, VideoToolbox on macOS / iOS).

### Can I build an Android or iOS video editor app in C#?

Yes. Create a .NET MAUI app, add the VisioForge.DotNet.VideoEdit package and the platform redistributables, and use VideoEditCoreX as on the desktop: append clips with Input\_AddAudioVideoFile, preview them in VideoView and render with MP4Output. The SimpleEdit sample on GitHub joins clips from the gallery into one MP4 on Android and iOS.

### How long does it take to integrate a video editing SDK?

The engine side is small. Add the VisioForge.DotNet.VideoEdit NuGet package and the redistributable package for each target platform, then create VideoEditCoreX, add clips, set Output\_Format and call Start. The SimpleEdit sample for .NET MAUI joins clips from the gallery into an MP4 in about 250 lines of C#, UI handlers included, and the Video Join Demo X samples do the same in WinForms and WPF. The 30-day trial is fully functional, so the whole integration can be built and tested before you buy.

### How does the video editing pipeline work?

Clips are placed on a timeline with the Input\_Add methods. When Start is called, VideoEditCoreX, built on GStreamer Editing Services, decodes each clip, applies transitions, effects and overlays, encodes the result and writes it in the output format you set. With no output format, the same timeline plays as a preview in the video view.

### Can I use Video Edit SDK .NET in a web browser?

No. The SDK runs inside .NET applications on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS, not in a browser. A web product can still use it on the server, for example in a background service that renders an uploaded set of clips to MP4 and returns the file.

# Media Blocks SDK .NET — Build Modular Media Pipelines in C#

Build video pipelines from blocks in C# — camera, codec, effect, output — recording to MP4, MKV or AVI and streaming over HLS, RTMP or RTSP.

[Download 30-Day Free Trial](https://files.visioforge.com/trials/visioforge_sdks_installer_dotnet_setup.exe)[View Pricing](https://www.visioforge.com/media-blocks-sdk-net#pricing)[Code Samples on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples)

From €500/year · Lifetime from €1,800 [Bundles from €700/year](https://www.visioforge.com/media-blocks-sdk-net#bundles)

Create powerful multimedia applications easily and flexibly with Media Blocks SDK .NET — a modular toolkit that lets you build complex video workflows like a visual constructor (camera → codec → output). It supports recording to MP4, MKV, and AVI, as well as streaming via HLS, RTMP, and RTSP, offering a rich set of effects including color correction, deinterlacing, watermarks, screen capture, and audio processing. With built-in computer vision, QR-code recognition, face tracking, and full support for Blackmagic and ONVIF devices, it brings professional-grade features to any project. The SDK works seamlessly with Unity, WinForms, WPF, MAUI, Uno Platform, Xamarin, and Avalonia, making it easy to integrate advanced media capabilities into desktop, mobile, and game-engine apps.

Want a ready-made component instead of a pipeline you assemble yourself? [Video Capture SDK .NET](/video-capture-sdk-net) · [Media Player SDK .NET](/media-player-sdk-net) · [Video Edit SDK .NET](/video-edit-sdk-net)

## Key Benefits

### Modular Architecture

200+ processing blocks that connect like building blocks to create custom media pipelines

### Cross-Platform

Works on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS with all major .NET UI frameworks

### Hardware Acceleration

GPU-accelerated encoding/decoding with NVIDIA, Intel, and AMD support for maximum performance

Media Blocks SDK .NET is the pipeline layer of the VisioForge .NET stack: instead of configuring one ready-made component, you assemble an application from individual blocks — a source, any number of processing blocks, and one or more sinks — and connect them with MediaBlocksPipeline.Connect. The 200+ blocks cover file and webcam sources, RTSP and ONVIF IP cameras with PTZ, Blackmagic DeckLink, Basler and FLIR industrial cameras, colour correction, deinterlacing, chroma key, overlays and audio processing, AI inference, recording to MP4, MKV, MOV, WebM, MPEG-TS and MXF, and streaming over HLS, RTMP, RTSP, SRT and NDI. A single pipeline can record, stream and preview at the same time by splitting the flow through a TeeBlock. The SDK installs from the VisioForge.DotNet.MediaBlocks NuGet package and runs on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS with WinForms, WPF, MAUI, Uno Platform, Avalonia and Unity.

## Built on GStreamer

Media Blocks SDK .NET is a commercial .NET SDK built on GStreamer. Its blocks wrap GStreamer elements in typed C# classes, so you connect sources, encoders and sinks instead of writing string pipelines, and CustomMediaBlock adds any GStreamer element the SDK does not cover. On Windows, macOS, Android and iOS the GStreamer libraries come in the NuGet packages, and on Android the app also references a Java bindings project; on Linux the SDK uses the system GStreamer.

[GStreamer for .NET: how the SDK compares with the bindings →](/solutions/gstreamer-dotnet)

## Pipeline Examples

### SIMPLE PLAYER

C#

View Code

The simple player pipeline uses the UniversalSourceBlock to read and decode the source file, the VideoRendererBlock to display video, and the AudioRendererBlock to play audio.

```csharp
// Create MediaBlocks pipeline
_pipeline = new MediaBlocksPipeline();

// Add file source
var fileSourceSettings = await UniversalSourceSettings.CreateAsync("video.mp4");
var videoStreamAvailable = fileSourceSettings.GetInfo().VideoStreams.Count > 0;
var audioStreamAvailable = fileSourceSettings.GetInfo().AudioStreams.Count > 0;

var fileSource = new UniversalSourceBlock(fileSourceSettings);

// Add video renderer
if (videoStreamAvailable)
{
    var videoRenderer = new VideoRendererBlock(_pipeline, VideoView1);
    _pipeline.Connect(fileSource, videoRenderer);
}

// Add audio output
if (audioStreamAvailable)
{
    var audioOutputDevice = (await DeviceEnumerator.Shared.AudioOutputsAsync())[0];
    var audioOutput = new AudioRendererBlock(
        new AudioRendererSettings(audioOutputDevice));
    _pipeline.Connect(fileSource, audioOutput);
}

// Start playback
await _pipeline.StartAsync();
```

### ADVANCED PLAYER

C#

View Code

The advanced player pipeline includes the UniversalSourceBlock for decoding files or streams, video and audio renderers, and effects processing blocks.

```csharp
// Create MediaBlocks pipeline
_pipeline = new MediaBlocksPipeline();

// Add file source
var fileSourceSettings = await UniversalSourceSettings.CreateAsync(edFilename.Text);
var videoStreamAvailable = fileSourceSettings.GetInfo().VideoStreams.Count > 0;
var audioStreamAvailable = fileSourceSettings.GetInfo().AudioStreams.Count > 0;

var fileSource = new UniversalSourceBlock(fileSourceSettings);

// Add video renderer, text overlay and image overlay
if (videoStreamAvailable)
{
    var videoRenderer = new VideoRendererBlock(_pipeline, VideoView1);
    var textOverlay = new TextOverlayBlock(new TextOverlaySettings("Hello world!"));
    var imageOverlay = new ImageOverlayBlock(new ImageOverlaySettings("logo.png"));

    _pipeline.Connect(fileSource, textOverlay);
    _pipeline.Connect(textOverlay, imageOverlay);
    _pipeline.Connect(imageOverlay, videoRenderer);
}

// Add audio output and equalizer
if (audioStreamAvailable)
{
    var audioOutputDevice = (await DeviceEnumerator.Shared.AudioOutputsAsync())[0];
    var audioOutput = new AudioRendererBlock(new AudioRendererSettings(audioOutputDevice));

    var equalizer = new EqualizerParametricBlock();
    // set some equalizer settings

    _pipeline.Connect(fileSource, equalizer);
    _pipeline.Connect(equalizer, audioOutput);
}

// Start playback
await _pipeline.StartAsync();
```

### CAMERA PREVIEW

C#

View Code

The camera/microphone simple preview pipeline contains device source blocks and video/audio renderer blocks. Default devices will be used.

```csharp
// Create MediaBlocksPipeline object
_pipeline = new MediaBlocksPipeline();

// Add default video and audio sources
var videoSources = (await DeviceEnumerator.Shared.VideoSourcesAsync()).ToList();
var videoSource = new SystemVideoSourceBlock(
    new VideoCaptureDeviceSourceSettings(videoSources[0]));

var audioSources = (await DeviceEnumerator.Shared.AudioSourcesAsync()).ToList();
var audioSource = new SystemAudioSourceBlock(audioSources[0].CreateSourceSettings());

// Add video renderer
var videoRenderer = new VideoRendererBlock(_pipeline, videoView: VideoView1);

// Add audio renderer
var audioRenderers = (await DeviceEnumerator.Shared.AudioOutputsAsync()).ToList();
var audioRenderer = new AudioRendererBlock(new AudioRendererSettings(audioRenderers[0]));

// Connect everything
_pipeline.Connect(videoSource, videoRenderer);
_pipeline.Connect(audioSource, audioRenderer);

// Start preview
await _pipeline.StartAsync();
```

### RTSP PREVIEW

C#

View Code

The RTSP preview pipeline, which includes the RTSP source block (with decoders inside), video and audio renderers.

```csharp
// Create Media Blocks pipeline
_pipeline = new MediaBlocksPipeline();

// Create video renderer
var videoRenderer = new VideoRendererBlock(_pipeline, VideoView1);

// Add RTSP camera source
var rtsp = await RTSPSourceSettings.CreateAsync(new Uri(edURL.Text),
    edLogin.Text, edPassword.Text, audioEnabled: cbAudioStream.Checked);
var rtspSource = new RTSPSourceBlock(rtsp);

_pipeline.Connect(rtspSource, videoRenderer);

// Add audio output (if required)
if (cbAudioStream.Checked && rtsp.IsAudioAvailable())
{
    var audioOutputDevice = (await DeviceEnumerator.Shared.AudioOutputsAsync())[0];
    var audioOutput = new AudioRendererBlock(new AudioRendererSettings(audioOutputDevice));
    _pipeline.Connect(rtspSource, audioOutput);
}

// Start IP camera preview
await _pipeline.StartAsync();
```

### CAPTURE WITH PREVIEW

C#

View Code

The capture pipeline has two tee blocks that are used to split video and audio streams, allowing video/audio preview along with video capture.

```csharp
// Create the pipeline
_pipeline = new MediaBlocksPipeline();

// Add video and audio sources
var videoSources = (await DeviceEnumerator.Shared.VideoSourcesAsync()).ToList();
var videoSource = new SystemVideoSourceBlock(new VideoCaptureDeviceSourceSettings(videoSources[0]));

var audioSources = (await DeviceEnumerator.Shared.AudioSourcesAsync()).ToList();
var audioSource = new SystemAudioSourceBlock(audioSources[0].CreateSourceSettings());

// Add video renderer and specify VideoView control
var videoRenderer = new VideoRendererBlock(_pipeline, videoView: VideoView1);

// Add audio renderer
var audioRenderers = (await DeviceEnumerator.Shared.AudioOutputsAsync()).ToList();
var audioRenderer = new AudioRendererBlock(new AudioRendererSettings(audioRenderers[0]));

// Configure MP4 output
var output = new MP4OutputBlock(Path.Combine(
    Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.MyVideos), "output.mp4"));

// Add video and audio tees
var videoTee = new TeeBlock(2, MediaBlockPadMediaType.Video);
var audioTee = new TeeBlock(2, MediaBlockPadMediaType.Audio);

// Connect everything
_pipeline.Connect(videoSource, videoTee);
_pipeline.Connect(audioSource, audioTee);

_pipeline.Connect(videoTee, videoRenderer);
_pipeline.Connect(audioTee, audioRenderer);

_pipeline.Connect(videoTee, output);
_pipeline.Connect(audioTee, output);

// Start MP4 recording
await _pipeline.StartAsync();
```

## AI Video Analytics & Speech

Add AI inference, privacy redaction, open-vocabulary detection, vision-language understanding, semantic search, and speech recognition directly to Media Blocks SDK .NET pipelines.

Each AI feature in Media Blocks SDK .NET is a pipeline block from the VisioForge.DotNet.Core.AI or VisioForge.DotNet.Core.AI.Whisper package. It connects between sources, renderers, encoders and streaming outputs like any other block. YOLOObjectDetectorBlock runs YOLOX, YOLOv8 or RT-DETR models, and ObjectAnalyticsBlock adds ByteTrack IDs, line crossings and zone counters. OcrBlock and LicensePlateRecognizerBlock read text and plates, FaceRecognitionBlock matches faces against an enrolled gallery, and PIIRedactionBlock blurs faces, plates and text. The ONNX Runtime blocks run on the CPU or on CUDA, DirectML and CoreML when the matching runtime is installed. SpeechToTextBlock transcribes audio locally with Whisper and Silero VAD and writes SRT or VTT subtitles. For example, an RTSP camera pipeline can count people crossing a line while it records to MP4. Model files are supplied or downloaded by the application, so teams keep control over model choice and licensing.

Browse the AI blocks

### [OCR and ANPR](/solutions/license-plate-recognition-dotnet)

Recognize text and license plates in live video or files with ONNX blocks — PaddleOCR models for text, FastALPR models for plates — and structured detection events.

### Object Detection and Analytics

Run YOLOX, YOLOv8, or RT-DETR models, then add ByteTrack IDs, line crossings, polygon zones, counters, and overlays.

### Face Recognition

Detect faces, enroll identities, match against a FaceGallery, and draw recognized people into the video stream.

### Background Removal

Use ONNX matting models for background blur, solid color replacement, image replacement, or transparent RGBA output.

### Custom ONNX Inference

Attach your own ONNX model to video frames and receive raw tensor outputs for application-specific post-processing.

### Offline Whisper Captions

Transcribe audio locally with Whisper, segment speech with Silero VAD, render live subtitles, or write SRT/VTT files.

### PII Redaction

Automatically blur, pixelate, or solid-fill faces, license plates, and on-screen text, with optional regex filtering for emails and phone numbers.

### Open-Vocabulary Detection & Vision-Language Understanding

Detect objects from a free-text prompt with OWLv2 or Grounding DINO instead of a fixed class list, or use a Florence-2 vision-language block for frame captioning, OCR, and phrase grounding — swap prompts and confidence thresholds at runtime.

### Semantic Video Search

Build a CLIP-based embedding index while processing video, then search it with natural-language queries to find matching frames.

The same block instances also plug directly into VideoCaptureCoreX and MediaPlayerCoreX via Video\_Processing\_AddBlock/Audio\_Processing\_AddBlock — no manual MediaBlocksPipeline required. See the AI features on the Video Capture SDK .NET and Media Player SDK .NET pages.

[View AI blocks documentation](https://www.visioforge.com/help/docs/dotnet/general/ai/)

## Live Video Compositor

Build OBS-like live video production software with the Live Video Compositor — a real-time, multi-input, multi-output video composition engine built on top of Media Blocks SDK .NET. Dynamically add and remove cameras, screen captures, media files, RTSP/IP camera feeds, and NDI sources as layered inputs, mix them with GPU-accelerated rendering, and simultaneously output to recording files and live streaming platforms. Designed for multi-camera switching, picture-in-picture layouts, live overlays, and broadcast-quality audio mixing — all fully controllable from C# code at runtime.

The Live Video Compositor is a multi-input, multi-output composition engine built on the same pipeline model. You create it with a canvas size and frame rate — LiveVideoCompositorSettings(1920, 1080, new VideoFrameRate(25)) — then add each source as an input with its own destination rectangle and Z-order: a camera filling the background, a screen capture as a picture-in-picture overlay, a media file, an RTSP camera or an NDI feed. Inputs and outputs are added and removed with Input\_AddAsync and Output\_AddAsync while the composition is running, and each input runs in its own isolated pipeline, so one failing source does not stop the others. Layers are mixed with GPU-accelerated OpenGL rendering with a CPU fallback, and the result can go to several destinations at once — an MP4 or WebM recording, a YouTube or Facebook live stream, a DeckLink card and an on-screen preview.

### Dynamic Inputs & Outputs

Add or remove video and audio sources and output destinations at any time — even while the compositor is running. Each input operates in its own isolated pipeline, so one failing source never disrupts the entire composition.

### GPU-Accelerated Mixing

Composite multiple video layers in real time using cross-platform GPU-accelerated rendering (OpenGL) or CPU fallback. Position each source with pixel-precise rectangles, control Z-order stacking, and choose from letterbox, stretch, or fill resize policies.

### Record + Stream + Preview

Output to multiple destinations simultaneously — record to MP4 or WebM, stream live to YouTube and Facebook, send video to Decklink hardware, and display an on-screen preview — all from a single compositor instance running in real time.

### Live Overlays & Effects

Apply text overlays, image watermarks, and post-composition video effects dynamically — no pipeline rebuild required. Real-time audio VU metering provides professional-grade level monitoring during live production.

### Live Video Compositor Setup in C#

C#

View Code

```csharp
// Create the Live Video Compositor (GPU-accelerated)
var settings = new LiveVideoCompositorSettings(1920, 1080, new VideoFrameRate(25));
var compositor = new LiveVideoCompositor(settings);

// Add the first camera as a full-screen background layer
var camera = (await DeviceEnumerator.Shared.VideoSourcesAsync())[0];
var cameraSettings = new VideoCaptureDeviceSourceSettings(camera); // picks an HD format when available
var cameraInfo = new VideoFrameInfoX(cameraSettings.Format.Width,
    cameraSettings.Format.Height, cameraSettings.Format.FrameRate);
var cameraInput = new LVCVideoInput(
    "Camera", compositor,
    new SystemVideoSourceBlock(cameraSettings), cameraInfo,
    new Rect(0, 0, 1920, 1080), autostart: true);
await compositor.Input_AddAsync(cameraInput);

// Start compositing — sources and outputs can be added/removed at any time
await compositor.StartAsync();

// Dynamically add screen capture (Windows) as picture-in-picture overlay
var screenSettings = new ScreenCaptureDX9SourceSettings
{
    Rectangle = new Rect(0, 0, 1920, 1080),
    FrameRate = new VideoFrameRate(25)
};
var screenInfo = new VideoFrameInfoX(1920, 1080, screenSettings.FrameRate);
var screenInput = new LVCVideoInput(
    "Screen", compositor,
    new ScreenSourceBlock(screenSettings), screenInfo,
    new Rect(1400, 50, 500, 300), autostart: true);
screenInput.ZOrder = 1;
await compositor.Input_AddAsync(screenInput);

// Dynamically add MP4 recording output while compositing is running
// (the camera is video-only, so the AAC track carries the compositor's audio mix)
var mp4Output = new LVCVideoAudioOutput(
    "Recording", compositor,
    new MP4OutputBlock(new MP4SinkSettings("recording.mp4"),
        new OpenH264EncoderSettings(), new AVENCAACEncoderSettings()),
    autostart: true);
await compositor.Output_AddAsync(mp4Output, start: true);

// Dynamically remove the screen overlay
await compositor.Input_RemoveAsync(screenInput.ID);

// Dynamically remove the recording output
await compositor.Output_RemoveAsync(mp4Output.ID);
```

The Live Video Compositor works with all input sources and output formats supported by Media Blocks SDK .NET, including cameras, screen capture, media files, RTSP/IP cameras, NDI, Decklink, and all recording and streaming outputs.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is Media Blocks SDK and how does it differ from other VisioForge SDKs?

Media Blocks SDK uses a modular pipeline architecture where you connect individual processing blocks (sources, encoders, effects, sinks) like building blocks. Unlike the Video Capture or Media Player SDKs that provide ready-made workflows, Media Blocks gives you full control over every stage of the media pipeline, making it ideal for custom or complex scenarios.

### How do I build a media pipeline in C#?

Create a MediaBlocksPipeline instance, add source blocks (file, camera, RTSP, screen capture), connect processing blocks (encoders, effects, overlays), and attach output blocks (file sink, renderer, network stream). Call StartAsync() to run. The SDK handles threading, synchronization, and hardware acceleration automatically.

### Is Media Blocks SDK .NET based on GStreamer?

Yes. Media Blocks SDK .NET is a commercial .NET SDK built on GStreamer. You work with typed blocks rather than the raw GStreamer API, and CustomMediaBlock adds any GStreamer element or bin description to a pipeline. The GStreamer libraries ship in the VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Core.\* NuGet packages on Windows, macOS, Android and iOS. On Android the app also references a Java bindings project from the VisioForge samples repository. On Linux the SDK uses the distribution's GStreamer, version 1.22 or later (Ubuntu 24.04 ships 1.24), installed with the distribution's package manager, plus the VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Core.Linux.x64 or VisioForge.CrossPlatform.Core.Linux.arm64 package.

### Does Media Blocks SDK work on macOS, Linux, and mobile platforms?

Yes. Media Blocks SDK supports Windows, macOS 12+, Ubuntu 22.04/24.04, Android 9+, and iOS 16.4+. It works with WinForms, WPF, MAUI, Uno Platform, Avalonia, and Xamarin. The same pipeline code runs across all platforms with platform-specific rendering and hardware acceleration.

### Can I stream video over RTMP, RTSP, or HLS?

Yes. The SDK includes dedicated streaming output blocks for RTMP (YouTube Live, Facebook Live), RTSP server, HLS, SRT, NDI, and Shoutcast. You can combine streaming with local recording and preview by using Tee blocks to split the pipeline into multiple outputs.

### Is GPU-accelerated encoding and decoding supported?

Yes. Media Blocks SDK supports hardware-accelerated encoding via NVIDIA NVENC, Intel Quick Sync, and AMD AMF, as well as hardware decoding. On mobile platforms, iOS and Android hardware codecs are used automatically. This enables real-time 4K processing with minimal CPU usage.

### Can I use industrial cameras (GigE Vision, USB3 Vision) and Blackmagic Decklink?

Yes. The SDK includes source blocks for GenICam-compatible industrial cameras (Basler, Allied Vision, FLIR/Teledyne) via GigE Vision and USB3 Vision. Blackmagic Decklink devices are supported with dedicated source and sink blocks for professional video capture and output.

### What is the Live Video Compositor and how does it differ from building pipelines manually?

The Live Video Compositor is a high-level real-time video composition engine built on top of Media Blocks SDK. While you can assemble custom mixing pipelines manually with individual blocks, the compositor provides a complete architecture for OBS-like applications out of the box — including bridge-based input isolation, GPU-accelerated compositing, dynamic source and output management at runtime, Z-order layer control, live text and image overlays, post-composition effects, and audio VU metering. It is ideal for building multi-camera switching systems, live streaming software, or broadcast production tools in C# and .NET.

### Can I use Media Blocks SDK in Unity?

Yes. Media Blocks SDK .NET ships a single, cross-platform .unitypackage for Unity 6 that targets Windows, Android, macOS, and iOS from one import. You get the complete SDK — capture, sources, decoders and encoders, effects, mixing, recording, and streaming — and render any pipeline into a Unity RawImage. Two sample scenes (a media-file player and a live RTSP / IP-camera viewer) are included as starting points. See the Unity documentation for setup and per-platform build guides.

### How is this different from Unity's built-in Video Player?

Unity's Video Player is fine for bundled clips, but it has no RTSP / IP-camera input, a limited codec set, and no capture or streaming. Media Blocks SDK adds live RTSP and IP-camera playback, a much wider range of formats and codecs (H.264, H.265, AV1, VP8/VP9, ProRes, MJPEG and more), device capture, recording, and outbound streaming — all through one consistent pipeline that behaves the same across Windows, Android, macOS, and iOS.

### Can I record or stream video from a Unity app?

Yes. From inside a Unity build you can record to MP4, MKV, or WebM and broadcast over RTMP, SRT, HLS, or a built-in RTSP server, using hardware-accelerated H.264 / H.265 encoders on mobile. Combine sources, overlays, and a video mixer to compose exactly what you record or stream — on desktop and mobile.

### Can I build AI video analytics pipelines in C#?

Yes. Media Blocks SDK .NET includes VisioForge.DotNet.Core.AI blocks for OCR, ANPR, object detection, object analytics, face recognition, background removal, and custom ONNX inference. You connect these blocks inside the same MediaBlocksPipeline as cameras, RTSP streams, renderers, encoders, file outputs, and streaming outputs.

### Does Whisper speech-to-text run offline?

Yes. The VisioForge.DotNet.Core.AI.Whisper package runs Whisper locally through the GGML/whisper.cpp backend and can use optional Silero VAD for speech segmentation. It can generate live subtitles, recognized speech events, and side-car SRT or VTT subtitle files without sending audio to a cloud service.

### Can I use custom ONNX models?

Yes. OnnxInferenceBlock lets you run a custom ONNX Runtime model over video frames and receive raw tensor outputs for your own decoder or post-processing code. For common detector families, YOLOObjectDetectorBlock already handles YOLOX, YOLOv8, and RT-DETR preprocessing, decoding, coordinate mapping, and overlays.

### Can I use these AI blocks with VideoCaptureCoreX or MediaPlayerCoreX instead of a manual pipeline?

Yes. Every AI block also implements the processing-block interfaces used by VideoCaptureCoreX and MediaPlayerCoreX, so you register the same block instances with Video\_Processing\_AddBlock or Audio\_Processing\_AddBlock before StartAsync (capture) or OpenAsync/PlayAsync (playback) — no manual MediaBlocksPipeline required.

---END OF PAGE---

## Transcode Video with FFmpeg in C#

Convert a file to MP4 from a console app: typed FFMPEGEXEOutput settings, a GPU encoder chosen automatically, progress and error events.

### Convert AVI to MP4 (H.264 + AAC) with FFmpeg

C#

View Code

```csharp
// NuGet packages:
//   VisioForge.DotNet.VideoEdit
//   VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VideoEdit.x64
//   VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.FFMPEG.x64   (FFmpeg.exe)

using System;
using VisioForge.Core.VideoEdit;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoEdit;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.Output;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.FFMPEGEXE;

// .NET 6+ console app (top-level statements), no preview window
await using var core = new VideoEditCore();
core.ConsoleUsage = true;
core.Mode = VideoEditMode.Convert;

// Source file: its video and audio streams
var input = @"C:\Video\input.avi";
if (!await core.Input_AddVideoFileAsync(input))
{
    Console.WriteLine("Cannot open " + input);
    return 1;
}

// The second argument keeps the audio in sync with the video of the same file
if (!await core.Input_AddAudioFileAsync(input, input))
{
    Console.WriteLine("Could not add the audio track of " + input);
}

// MP4 with H.264 + AAC. The profile picks the first available GPU encoder
// (Intel Quick Sync, AMD AMF, NVIDIA NVENC), else Media Foundation H.264.
var ffmpeg = new FFMPEGEXEOutput(DefaultsProfile.MP4_H264_AAC, networkStreaming: false);

// Optional: choose the encoder yourself, e.g. HEVC on an NVIDIA GPU
// ffmpeg.Video = new HEVCNVENCSettings();

core.Output_Format = ffmpeg;
core.Output_Filename = @"C:\Video\output.mp4";

var errors = 0;
core.OnProgress += (s, e) => Console.WriteLine("Progress: " + e.Progress + "%");
core.OnError += (s, e) => { errors++; Console.WriteLine("Error: " + e.Message); };

// With ConsoleUsage = true, StartAsync returns when the conversion has finished
if (!await core.StartAsync() || errors > 0)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Failed");
    return 1;
}

Console.WriteLine("Done: " + core.Output_Filename);
return 0;
```

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is Video Edit SDK FFmpeg .NET?

Video Edit SDK FFmpeg .NET is an FFmpeg-powered video editing and converting SDK for .NET developers. It enables video timeline editing, format conversion, effects processing, and encoding in C# and VB.NET applications. Built on the Windows VideoEditCore engine that encodes via FFmpeg.exe (FFMPEGEXEOutput), it supports 1000+ media formats and runs on Windows.

### How do I use FFmpeg in C# without building command lines?

Create a VideoEditCore instance, add the source file with Input\_AddVideoFileAsync and Input\_AddAudioFileAsync, and set Output\_Format to an FFMPEGEXEOutput object. Its typed properties choose the container (OutputMuxer), the video encoder (for example H264NVENCSettings or HEVCQSVSettings) and the audio encoder, and the SDK builds the FFmpeg.exe arguments for you. Subscribe to OnProgress and OnError, then call StartAsync; in a console app (ConsoleUsage = true) it returns when the conversion has finished. Raw FFmpeg flags can still be added through Custom\_AdditionalVideoArgs and Custom\_AdditionalAudioArgs.

### What formats and codecs are supported?

The SDK supports virtually any format available in FFmpeg, including MP4, AVI, MKV, WebM, MPEG, MOV, and FLV containers. Video codecs include H.264, H.265/HEVC, VP8, VP9, AV1, ProRes, and MPEG-1/2/4. Audio codecs include AAC, MP3, OGG Vorbis, FLAC, Speex, Opus, WAV, and WMA. Image formats like PNG, JPEG, BMP, and animated GIF are also supported for overlays.

### Does it support cross-platform development?

No. This FFmpeg-engine SDK is built on the Windows VideoEditCore engine (a DirectShow pipeline that encodes via FFmpeg.exe) and runs on Windows only (10 and 11, Server 2016+). If you need macOS or Linux support, use the cross-platform Video Edit SDK .NET, which is powered by the VideoEditCoreX (GStreamer) engine.

### What .NET frameworks are supported?

The SDK supports .NET Framework 4.7.2 and later, .NET Core 3.1, and .NET 5 through .NET 10. It works with WinForms, WPF, console applications, web backends, and Windows services. The SDK is distributed via NuGet for easy integration into any .NET project.

### Does it support GPU-accelerated encoding?

Yes. The SDK leverages FFmpeg's hardware acceleration support for encoding with NVIDIA NVENC, Intel Quick Sync Video, and AMD VCE/AMF. GPU-accelerated encoding significantly reduces processing time for H.264 and H.265/HEVC output, especially for HD and 4K content.

### Can I apply filters and effects during editing?

Yes. The SDK provides extensive video effects including image and text overlays, brightness/contrast/saturation/hue adjustments, deinterlacing, denoising, chroma-key (green screen), rotation, resize, crop, pan/zoom, and motion detection. Audio effects include equalization, normalization, and volume boosting. FFmpeg's full filter graph capabilities are available for advanced processing.

### How does it differ from Video Edit SDK .NET?

Both products share the Windows VideoEditCore engine, a DirectShow pipeline with a timeline. Video Edit SDK FFmpeg .NET is the Windows-only edition that encodes through FFmpeg.exe (FFMPEGEXEOutput); choose it when the job is transcoding and format coverage on Windows: 1000+ formats, AV1, VP9. Video Edit SDK .NET adds native DirectShow and Media Foundation encoders and the cross-platform VideoEditCoreX (GStreamer) engine for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS; choose it for editing apps and for any cross-platform target.

### What are the differences between the trial and commercial versions?

The trial version provides full functionality for 30 days and may display a watermark or an unregistered notice, depending on the engine and output. Paid licenses include royalty-free distribution rights and email support. Annual licenses include 12 months of updates; Lifetime·Team licenses include minor and major updates for the product lifetime. Standard, Professional, and Premium feature tiers are available.

# Virtual Camera SDK — A Virtual Webcam and Microphone for Your Windows App

Virtual Camera SDK is a Windows SDK that adds one virtual webcam and one virtual microphone to the system. Video and audio reach the devices in one of two ways. ## How a Virtual Camera Works

A virtual camera is a software device that other applications open exactly as they open a USB webcam. With Virtual Camera SDK, your application feeds that device in one of two ways: a DirectShow graph that ends in the Virtual Camera Sink filter, or .NET code that pushes frames through VirtualVideoWriter. Either way, the frames travel through shared memory to the Virtual Camera Source filter, which is registered on the system as a video capture device. When Zoom, OBS Studio or a browser opens that device, it receives your frames.

What that means in practice:

-   Anything your application produces can become the camera picture: a video file, a capture device or your own filter in a DirectShow graph, or BGRA, BGR24 and YUY2 frames that your .NET code renders.
-   The virtual microphone works the same way: an audio sink in your graph, or PCM samples pushed through VirtualAudioWriter, become an audio capture device for other applications.
-   The camera offers YUY2 at fixed sizes from 320×180 to 4096×2160, landscape and portrait, at 1–60 fps. The frames you send are scaled to the size the receiving application picks.
-   When nothing is streaming, the camera shows an image you choose, or starts an application you specify, instead of a black frame.
-   The camera is visible to applications that list DirectShow devices. The Windows Camera app, the camera list in Windows Settings and UWP apps use Media Foundation only and do not show it.

One installation provides one virtual camera and one virtual microphone. Several applications can open the camera at the same time and receive the same picture.

## What You Get with Virtual Camera SDK

Virtual Camera SDK is for developers who need a webcam and a microphone that their own software controls: a conferencing product, a test rig, a computer-vision pipeline, a kiosk. It is not an end-user webcam application; the picture comes from the code you write.

### A Webcam Other Applications Recognize:

The Virtual Camera Source filter is registered as a video capture device, so Zoom, OBS Studio and browser applications such as Google Meet in Chrome or Edge list it next to physical cameras.

### Up to 4096×2160 at 1–60 fps:

The camera offers YUY2 at fixed sizes from 320×180 through 1920×1080, 3840×2160 and 4096×2160, plus the matching portrait sizes, at any frame rate from 1 to 60 fps.

### Automatic Scaling:

The frames you send are scaled to the size the receiving application selects, so your graph does not have to follow every application's choice.

### Virtual Microphone:

A separate pair of filters, the Virtual Audio Card, turns the audio of your graph, or PCM samples pushed from .NET, into a microphone that other applications can select.

### Several Applications at Once:

More than one application can open the virtual camera at the same time; each receives the same picture.

### Custom Device Names:

Rename the camera and the microphone so that users see your product name in their device lists.

### Any DirectShow Source, or No Graph:

The sink accepts video from whatever your graph builds: file sources, capture devices, VisioForge SDKs or your own filters. Without a graph, the VisioForge.DotNet.VirtualCamera package pushes frames from your code; it targets .NET Framework 4.7.2, .NET 8 and .NET 10.

### No-Signal Image or Application:

When no video arrives, the camera shows a background image you choose, or starts an application you specify, instead of a black frame.

### Royalty-Free Distribution:

Ship the filters with your application to any number of end users without per-user fees. A source code license is available.

### Samples in C#, C++ and Delphi:

Working sample projects for .NET, native C++ and Delphi are on GitHub, among them a WPF demo of the .NET Push API, and email support answers integration questions.

## Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between trial and licensed versions?

The trial is fully functional for 30 days, and its video carries a TRIAL watermark. Setting a license key removes the watermark. Paid licenses include email support; Annual includes 12 months of updates and Lifetime·Team includes minor and major updates for the product lifetime.

Can I use the SDK in commercial applications?

Yes, with a commercial license you can distribute your applications royalty-free. The SDK license covers unlimited deployments of your application to end users.

Which programming languages are supported?

Samples are provided for C#, VB.NET, C++ and Delphi. Any other language that can use DirectShow COM components can use the filters too. .NET applications can also skip DirectShow and use the Push API package, VisioForge.DotNet.VirtualCamera, on .NET Framework 4.7.2, .NET 8 or .NET 10.

Does it work with Windows 11?

Yes, on Windows 10 and Windows 11, in 32-bit and 64-bit applications. The camera is a DirectShow device: Zoom, OBS Studio and Chromium-based browsers see it, while the Windows Camera app, the Settings camera list and UWP apps, which use Media Foundation only, do not.

Can multiple applications use the virtual camera simultaneously?

Yes. Several applications can open the virtual camera at the same time, and each receives the same picture. One installation provides one virtual camera and one virtual microphone.

Can I play a video file as a webcam?

Yes. Build a DirectShow graph that opens the file with a source filter and ends in the Virtual Camera Sink; Zoom, OBS Studio or a browser then show the file as the camera picture, and the Virtual Audio Card sink can carry its sound to the virtual microphone. The SDK documentation has this file-to-camera example in C# and C++. A .NET application that decodes or renders frames itself can push them through VirtualVideoWriter instead.

What is the Windows virtual camera?

Windows 11 has its own API for virtual cameras, MFCreateVirtualCamera in Media Foundation. A camera created with it is also seen by the Windows Camera app and UWP apps, but it is video only, and you write its media source yourself in C++. Virtual Camera SDK is a DirectShow virtual camera: it runs on Windows 10 and Windows 11, adds a virtual microphone, and is fed from a DirectShow graph or from .NET code, while the Camera app, the Settings camera list and UWP apps do not list it.

Is Virtual Camera SDK a virtual webcam app for my PC?

No. It is an SDK for developers: the camera shows whatever your own application sends to it. To appear on a call with an overlay or a different background, a free application such as OBS Studio with its virtual camera is the better fit. Virtual Camera SDK is for software that gives its users a camera of its own, under your product name and distributed royalty-free.

Does it work on Windows on ARM?

Yes. The filters are built for x86, x64 and ARM64, and the ARM64 camera and audio filters ship in the VisioForge.DotNet.Core.Redist.VirtualCamera.arm64 NuGet package. The SDK installer itself is an x64 package and does not run on 32-bit Windows or on Windows 10 on ARM, so on those machines your own installer registers the filters with regsvr32.

# Video Encryption SDK — Protect Video Files with AES-256 Encryption

Video Encryption SDK is a video encryption library for Windows: DirectShow filters that encode video to MP4 (H.264/AAC) and encrypt it with AES-128 or AES-256, keyed by a password or binary data. A matching decryptor filter plays the protected files, in x86 and x64 apps, with optional GPU encoding.

[Download 30-Day Free Trial](https://files.visioforge.com/trials/visioforge_video_encryption_sdk_setup.exe)[View Pricing](https://www.visioforge.com/video-encryption-sdk#pricing)[Samples on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/directshow-samples)[Video Encryptor Sample](https://files.visioforge.com/trials/visioforge_video_encryptor_setup.exe)

From €500/year · Lifetime from €1,800

The Video Encryption SDK allows users to encode video in MP4 H264/AAC format and apply encryption using either a password or binary data. Within this SDK, DirectShow filters are provided for seamless integration into any DirectShow application. These filters come with implemented interfaces for simple configuration of filter parameters, simplifying the process of securing your video content.

## What is video encryption?

Video encryption turns a video file into data that only the holder of the key can play. Video Encryption SDK does this inside your own Windows application: it writes H.264 video and AAC audio into an MP4 file and encrypts the streams with AES-256, or with AES-128 where compatibility requires it. The key is a password, a key file or binary data. A protected file plays in an application that has the SDK's decryptor filter and the same key, with seeking as in any MP4. This makes the SDK a building block for products that ship protected video, such as course videos or internal training, rather than a tool for encrypting one file by hand; for that, the Video Encryptor sample app below uses the same engine.

## Implementation Details

SDK can use string, files, and binary data as encrypting keys. SDK uses an open AES-256 crypto algorithm to encrypt video and audio streams. You can seek encrypted video files like any other video file. AAC codec will be used for an audio stream, and H264 codec will be used for a video stream. Also, you can re-mux any source H264/AAC file or stream without reencoding.

Video Encryption SDK is already integrated into Video Capture SDK .Net, Video Edit SDK .Net, and Media Player SDK .Net but requires an independent license.

AES-256 may require licensing in some countries. SDK can also use AES-128 for compatibility. Please get in touch with us if you want to use alternative encryption algorithms.

Video Encryption SDK can be used in any DirectShow code as two filters: muxer (encryptor) and demuxer (decryptor). Seeking is supported for demuxer.

You can use SDK as a core of your DRM video files system.

## Filter Usage in DirectShow Graph

The SDK provides two DirectShow filters that can be integrated into any DirectShow application for encryption and decryption of video content.

## C# example: encrypt a video and play it back

In the .NET SDKs, encryption is a property of the MP4 output. This example renders an encrypted MP4 with Video Edit SDK .NET, which takes the same MP4Output as Video Capture SDK .NET, and plays it with Media Player SDK .NET using the same key.

### C#

C#

Collapse

Copy

```csharp
using VisioForge.Core.Types.MediaPlayer;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.Output;
using VisioForge.Core.Types.VideoEdit;

// Encrypt: VideoEditCore here; VideoCaptureCore takes the same MP4Output
var mp4Output = new MP4Output
{
    Encryption = true,
    Encryption_Format = EncryptionFormat.MP4_H264_SW_AAC,
    Encryption_Mode = EncryptionMode.V9_AES256,
    Encryption_KeyType = EncryptionKeyType.String,
    Encryption_Key = "lesson-key"
};

await videoEdit.Input_AddVideoFileAsync("lesson-01-source.mp4");
await videoEdit.Input_AddAudioFileAsync("lesson-01-source.mp4");

videoEdit.Mode = VideoEditMode.Convert;
videoEdit.Output_Filename = "lesson-01.mp4";
videoEdit.Output_Format = mp4Output;
await videoEdit.StartAsync();

// Play: MediaPlayerCore with the same key
mediaPlayer.Source_Mode = MediaPlayerSourceMode.Encrypted_File_DS;
mediaPlayer.Encryption_KeyType = EncryptionKeyType.String;
mediaPlayer.Encryption_Key = "lesson-key";
mediaPlayer.Playlist_Clear();
mediaPlayer.Playlist_Add("lesson-01.mp4");
await mediaPlayer.PlayAsync();
```

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the Video Encryption SDK?

Video Encryption SDK is a Windows SDK of DirectShow filters that encode video to MP4 with H.264 video and AAC audio and encrypt both streams with AES-256. The key can be a password string, a file or binary data. The muxer filter encrypts, the demuxer filter decrypts, and seeking works in an encrypted file as in any other MP4. Existing H.264/AAC files and streams can be re-muxed into an encrypted MP4 without re-encoding. Additionally, GPU encoders from the DirectShow Encoding Filters pack can speed up encoding. For example, an e-learning product can ship course videos that play only in an application holding the key. Samples cover C#, C++ and Delphi. Video Capture SDK .NET, Video Edit SDK .NET and Media Player SDK .NET are already integrated with the SDK and need a separate license for it.

### What encryption algorithms are supported?

The SDK supports AES-256 (256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard) as the primary encryption algorithm and AES-128 for broader compatibility. Encryption keys can be provided as text strings, file paths, or binary data. The SDK encrypts both video (H.264) and audio (AAC) streams independently within an MP4 container.

### Can I seek within encrypted video files?

Yes. The SDK's decryptor (demuxer) filter fully supports seeking, so users can navigate to any position in an encrypted video file just like a regular MP4 file. This enables standard media player controls including fast-forward, rewind, and jumping to specific timestamps.

### Which programming languages are supported?

The SDK provides APIs for C# (.NET), VB.NET, C++, and Delphi. For .NET developers, the VisioForge.DirectShowAPI NuGet package provides convenient interface wrappers. The SDK is also integrated into Video Capture SDK .Net, Video Edit SDK .Net, and Media Player SDK .Net (separate license required).

### Can I encrypt live streams or only files?

The SDK can encrypt both pre-recorded files and live streams. The muxer filter works within a DirectShow filter graph, so it can encrypt output from any source — including live camera feeds, screen captures, and network streams. You can also re-mux existing H.264/AAC content without re-encoding for faster processing.

### Is the encryption compatible with standard media players?

Encrypted files require the SDK's decryptor filter to play back. Standard media players cannot open encrypted files without the decryptor component installed. This is by design — it ensures only authorized applications with the correct decryption key can access the protected content, making it suitable as a foundation for DRM systems.

### What are the differences between the trial and commercial versions?

The trial version is fully functional for 30 days and may display a watermark or an unregistered notice. Paid licenses include royalty-free distribution rights and email support. Annual licenses include 12 months of updates; Lifetime·Team licenses include minor and major updates for the product lifetime.

### Are there export restrictions on AES-256 encryption?

AES-256 encryption may require export licensing or compliance with regulations in some countries. The SDK also supports AES-128 as an alternative for regions with stricter encryption export controls. Contact VisioForge if you need guidance on encryption regulations or require alternative encryption algorithms for your target markets.

### How do I encrypt a video file in C#?

In Video Capture SDK .NET or Video Edit SDK .NET, create an MP4Output with Encryption set to true, choose EncryptionMode.V9\_AES256 or V8\_AES128, pass the key in Encryption\_Key with its type in Encryption\_KeyType, and start the capture or the render: the file is written as an encrypted MP4. In a DirectShow graph of your own, the Encrypt Muxer filter does the same and takes the key through its IVFCryptoConfig interface. The C# example on this page shows both encryption and playback.

### How do I play or decrypt an encrypted video?

In Media Player SDK .NET, set Source\_Mode to MediaPlayerSourceMode.Encrypted\_File\_DS and set Encryption\_Key and Encryption\_KeyType to the key the file was encrypted with. In a DirectShow graph, the Decrypt Demuxer filter takes the key through IVFCryptoConfig and passes the H.264 and AAC streams on to the decoders. The key must be the same one used for encryption.

### Can I protect course videos for online classes?

Yes, when the lessons are watched in your own Windows application. Encrypt each lesson to MP4 with a key, distribute the files, and play them in an app built on Media Player SDK .NET or on the decryptor filter, which supplies the key. The SDK does not include a web player, a streaming server or key management: how keys reach the students' app is decided by your application.

### Can encrypted videos play in a browser or on a phone?

No. The files play only through the SDK's decryptor filter, a DirectShow filter that runs in Windows applications. Browsers, Android and iOS cannot open them.

# Video Fingerprinting SDK .NET / C++ — Detect Duplicate & Pirated Video Content

Identify copies of a video despite re-encoding, resizing or a new file format — even when only a fragment is embedded inside another video.

[Download 30-Day Free Trial](https://www.visioforge.com/video-fingerprinting-sdk#download)[View Pricing](https://www.visioforge.com/video-fingerprinting-sdk#pricing)[Samples on GitHub](https://github.com/visioforge/.Net-SDK-s-samples/tree/master/Video%20Fingerprinting%20SDK)

From €900/year · Lifetime from €2,400

Our state-of-the-art video fingerprinting technology incorporates the latest advances in scene analysis, object tracking, and motion estimation to analyze the content of any video to identify its unique characteristics, such as colors, scene structure, and the motion of objects. This allows a copy of the video to be identified despite changes in resolution, bitrate, method of encoding, or file format. The video can even be detected when it is included inside another video or when just a fragment of the video is reproduced. Our SDK lets you integrate this video identification functionality into your applications and services. ## Key Benefits

### Compact Fingerprints

~1KB per video second for unique identification

### Robust Detection

Identifies videos despite resolution, format, or quality changes

### Ultra-Fast Processing

300ms per second processing, 1-2ms matching

## What is a video fingerprint?

A video fingerprint is a compact digital descriptor of a video's content: its colors, scene structure and the motion of objects. Video Fingerprinting SDK extracts one from a video file, a recorded TV broadcast or a live stream, and the result takes about 1 KB per second of video. Fingerprints can then be stored, copied and compared without the original files. A match survives changes in resolution, bitrate, encoding and file format, and a short fragment can be found inside a longer video. Indexing one second of video takes about 300 milliseconds, and comparing two 10-second fingerprints takes 1–2 milliseconds. For example, a TV clipping service can find every airing of a client's ad in a day of recorded broadcasts. The SDK is available for .NET on Windows, macOS and Linux and for C++ on Windows and Linux, and the .NET version includes a MongoDB helper for fingerprint storage.

### Video Duplicates Finder

Use the Video Duplicates Finder as a sample application to find similar video files.

### Media Monitoring Tool

Use the Media Monitoring Tool as a sample application to find one video fragment (TV commercial, for example) in another (full broadcast recording).

.Net SDK version has a helper for MongoDB usage as fingerprint storage.

## Use Cases

Some of the ways you can put our Video Fingerprinting SDK to use:

### Video Hosting Services

An online video hosting service like YouTube could use video fingerprints to avoid copyright infringement. A database of video fingerprints of the copyrighted material would be developed and compared to the video fingerprint materials submitted by users to prevent the illegal submission of pirated videos.

### Video Archive Service

A video archive service could use video fingerprints to save space and block duplicate uploads. A video fingerprint would be extracted from each video in the archive.

### Video Organizer Software

Video Organizer software could use video fingerprints to identify copies of the same movie or video clip and group them despite differences in format, resolution, or bitrate.

### Set-top Box Interactive Ads

Set-top box software could use video fingerprints to develop interactive advertisements by identifying when specific TV ads are shown and displaying a clickable URL.

### Video Search Engine

A search engine for videos could be developed using our Video Fingerprinting SDK – a unique, revolutionary service implementing a video-by-video search functionality.

### TV Clipping Service

A TV Clipping Service could use video fingerprinting technology to automate TV broadcast monitoring and TV ad verification to detect when a client's ad is aired.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What operating systems are supported?

• C++ SDK supports Windows and Linux, or any other POSIX-compatible operating system (available by request)

• .Net SDK supports Windows 10 and later, macOS 12 or later, and Linux

### What is the size of a video fingerprint file?

Each second of a video stream analyzed requires about 1kb for its video fingerprint. Duplicate detection generally only requires 3-5 seconds of each video to be indexed. Indexing of full videos is required in order to identify a video that has been included inside another.

### How much time is required for computations?

Indexing one second of video takes about 300 milliseconds – the actual processing of the file accounts for nearly half of that time (150 milliseconds), while video decompression accounts for the rest. Matching a pair of 10-second-long fingerprints takes 1-2 milliseconds. These times were established by testing with an Intel i3 processor and FFMPEG filters for video compression.

### Is video reading or decoding software included?

• C++: No. You will need some other library (FFmpeg, for example, demo available) to implement video reading in your application

• .NET: Yes. Decoding is built in, through GStreamer

### What code samples are available?

The following code samples are included with your purchase:

#### C++:

-   • FFmpeg-based console application that indexes videos and builds fingerprints (Windows, Linux)
-   • A console application that compares two fingerprints to detect duplicates (Windows, Linux)
-   • A console application that searches for entries of one fingerprint inside another (Windows, Linux)
-   • Source code of a full Media Monitoring Tool application (Windows, Linux)

#### .NET:

-   • Media Monitoring Tool and Media Monitoring Tool Live source code (cross-platform)
-   • Video Duplicates Finder source code (cross-platform)
-   • Console samples (cross-platform)
-   • MAUI samples (cross-platform)

### What other documentation is available?

#### C++:

-   • VFCompare API – a video fingerprinting algorithm implementation that is optimized for the detection of duplicate videos
-   • VFSearch API – a video fingerprinting algorithm implementation that is optimized for searching video in video

#### .NET:

-   • Full API is described in a help file

### How can I try-out and evaluate the technology?

We suggest you download and experiment with the trial versions of our Media Monitoring Tool application and the Video Duplicates Finder application and familiarize yourself with the API and code samples.

• The .Net version of SDK is available as an independent installer with sample applications and sample source code inside.

• MMT/VDF tools' source code is included (tools require .Net 4.5 for SOAP export. SDK can be used in .Net 4.0 and later).

• The C++ version of SDK is available as an independent installer.

## Media Monitoring Tool (Live) Sample

Our demo app is a fully functional media monitoring tool that can be used for ad tracking and broadcast media monitoring. It enables the detection of ad samples in a broadcast dump.

### How it works

Our Media Monitoring Tool can detect when a reference sample video is played in a recorded TV broadcast. The TV broadcast stream is registered as an array of 5-minute-long video files, and then they are compared to the specified sample reference video. The application will automatically detect all inclusions of the selected video in the recorded files.

### Benefits

#### Accurate results

The program's content-based video search technology ensures accuracy and speed. The algorithm quickly and accurately identifies all instances of the reference video in the recorded broadcast video stream without any human intervention.

#### Reduced costs

Because you no longer have to pay people to sit and stare at a TV screen and manually record the details of when the commercial is aired, your operation costs are dramatically reduced.

#### Easy use

The program's easy-to-learn intuitive interface allows custom searches to be defined and performed in seconds. The user selects the folder that contains the broadcast dump and specifies the video reference samples.

## Delphi example: record a webcam or an IP camera to MP4

Both procedures follow the TVFVideoCapture guide in the documentation: choose the source, set the output file and format, pick the mode, then call Start. The ActiveX control has the same properties.

### Delphi

Delphi

Collapse

Copy

```delphi
procedure TForm1.StartCapture;
begin
  // Devices by display name, as listed by Video_CaptureDevices_GetItem
  VideoCapture1.Video_CaptureDevice := cbVideoDevices.Text;
  VideoCapture1.Audio_CaptureDevice := cbAudioDevices.Text;
  VideoCapture1.Audio_RecordAudio := True;
  VideoCapture1.Audio_PlayAudio := False; // no speaker monitoring while recording

  VideoCapture1.Output_Filename := 'C:\Videos\capture.mp4';
  VideoCapture1.Output_Format := Format_MP4;

  VideoCapture1.Mode := Mode_Video_Capture;
  VideoCapture1.Start;
end;

procedure TForm1.CaptureIPCamera;
begin
  // RTSP over TCP through the FFmpeg engine; IP_Auto_VLC uses the bundled VLC source
  VideoCapture1.IP_Camera_URL := 'rtsp://user:password@192.168.1.100:554/stream';
  VideoCapture1.IP_Camera_Type := IP_RTSP_TCP;

  // Record the camera's own audio, not a local microphone (as in the IP Capture demo)
  VideoCapture1.IP_Camera_Audio_Capture := True;
  VideoCapture1.Audio_RecordAudio := True;
  VideoCapture1.Audio_PlayAudio := False;

  VideoCapture1.Output_Filename := 'C:\Videos\camera.mp4';
  VideoCapture1.Output_Format := Format_MP4;

  VideoCapture1.Mode := Mode_IP_Capture;
  VideoCapture1.Start;
end;
```

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What does the All-in-One Media Framework include?

The framework bundles three core libraries: Video Capture for recording from webcams, IP cameras, and screens; Video Edit for cutting, joining, and processing video files; and Media Player for playing video, audio, DVDs, and network streams. All cores include video and audio effects, frame grabbing, and on-screen display.

### Which Delphi versions are supported?

The framework supports RAD Studio and Delphi versions from Delphi 6 through the latest RAD Studio release. It provides native VCL components for seamless integration into Delphi projects. Both 32-bit and 64-bit compilation targets are supported.

### Can I use the framework with ActiveX and VB6?

Yes. The framework provides ActiveX controls that work with Visual Basic 6, C++ Builder, and any COM-compatible development environment. The ActiveX components offer the same full feature set as the Delphi VCL components.

### What video capture sources are supported?

The framework supports USB webcams, DV/HDV camcorders, TV tuners, IP cameras (RTSP, HTTP, MMS), and screen capture. Several sources can be combined into one picture-in-picture video. DV/HDV camcorders and TV tuners are supported on Windows only.

### Does the framework include a media player component?

Yes. The Media Player core plays all popular video and audio formats, DVDs, Blu-ray discs, and network streams. It includes features like frame-by-frame navigation, playback speed control, audio visualization, subtitle rendering, and custom video overlays.

### Is there an ActiveX control for video capture?

Yes. TVFVideoCapture ships both as a Delphi VCL component and as an ActiveX control, so Visual Basic 6, Visual Studio, C++ Builder and other COM hosts get the same capture features: webcams and capture cards, IP cameras, screen recording, and output to MP4, AVI, WMV and other formats. The ActiveX trial is a separate download.

### How do I connect an IP camera in Delphi?

Set IP\_Camera\_URL to the camera's RTSP or HTTP address and choose the engine with IP\_Camera\_Type, for example IP\_RTSP\_TCP for RTSP over TCP through FFmpeg or IP\_Auto\_VLC for the bundled VLC source. Then start in Mode\_IP\_Preview to watch or Mode\_IP\_Capture to record.

### Can I use FFmpeg from Delphi?

Yes, through the components rather than by calling FFmpeg libraries yourself. TVFVideoCapture reads IP camera streams with its FFmpeg engine and can write files through FFmpeg-based output formats (Format\_FFMPEGX), and TVFMediaPlayer has an FFmpeg source for files and streams.

### Can I build 64-bit Delphi applications?

Yes, from Delphi XE2 on. Add the 64-bit library path for the Win64 target and install the design-time package that matches your IDE; the 64-bit packages guide in the documentation walks through both. Visual Basic 6 applications stay 32-bit.

### Is there a free trial available?

Yes. Download the fully functional 30-day trial to evaluate all features. Depending on the engine and output, the trial may display a watermark or an unregistered notice. Both Delphi VCL and ActiveX versions are available for testing.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the DirectShow Encoding Filters Pack?

The DirectShow Encoding Filters Pack is a comprehensive collection of DirectShow filters for encoding and decoding video and audio in various formats. It includes H.264, H.265/HEVC, VP8, VP9, MJPEG video encoders, AAC, MP3, Vorbis audio encoders, plus an MP4 muxer and RTSP source/streamer — all designed for seamless integration into DirectShow applications.

### What encoding formats and codecs are supported?

Video encoders include H.264 (with Intel QuickSync support), H.265/HEVC, NVIDIA CUDA H.264, VP8, VP9, MJPEG, and FFmpeg-based MPEG-1/2/4 and Flash Video encoders. Audio encoders include AAC, MP3 (LAME), and Ogg Vorbis. The MP4 muxer supports H.264/HEVC video with AAC audio, and GPU-accelerated encoding is available via the MP4 MF Muxer.

### Does it support GPU-accelerated encoding?

Yes. The pack includes GPU-accelerated encoding via NVIDIA CUDA for H.264, Intel QuickSync for H.264/HEVC, and AMD hardware encoding. The MP4 MF Muxer provides additional GPU-accelerated H.264/HEVC encoding. Hardware encoding can reduce encoding time by 5–10x compared to software encoding, especially for HD and 4K content.

### Can I use it for live streaming (RTSP/RTMP)?

Yes. The pack includes an RTSP source filter for receiving streams and an RTSP streamer for broadcasting. Combined with the H.264 encoder and AAC encoder, you can build complete live streaming pipelines within DirectShow. The filters support both local network streaming and internet broadcasting scenarios.

### Which programming languages are supported?

The SDK provides APIs for .NET (C#/VB.NET), C++, and Delphi. Demo applications with source code are available in multiple programming languages. The VisioForge.DirectShowAPI NuGet package simplifies .NET integration with strongly-typed interfaces.

### Can I use it with GraphEdit or GraphStudioNext?

Yes. All filters register as standard DirectShow filters and appear in GraphEdit and GraphStudioNext filter lists. You can visually build and test encoding pipelines by connecting source filters, processing filters, encoders, and muxers in the graph editor — no code required. This is useful for prototyping and debugging filter graphs before implementing them programmatically.

### What are the differences between the trial and commercial versions?

The trial version is fully functional for 30 days and may display a watermark or an unregistered notice. Paid licenses include royalty-free distribution rights and email support. Annual licenses include 12 months of updates; Lifetime·Team licenses include minor and major updates for the product lifetime.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the FFmpeg Source DirectShow Filter?

The FFmpeg Source DirectShow Filter is a professional media decoder built on the FFmpeg library that integrates into any DirectShow application. It acts as a source filter in a DirectShow filter graph, enabling playback of 200+ video and audio formats — including MP4, MKV, WebM, AVI, HEVC, VP9, and ProRes — without installing additional codec packs.

### What media formats and codecs are supported?

The filter supports all formats provided by FFmpeg, including containers like MP4, AVI, MKV, WebM, MPEG-TS, MOV, FLV, and OGG. Video codecs include H.264, H.265/HEVC, VP8, VP9, MPEG-1/2/4, ProRes, and DNxHD. Audio codecs include AAC, MP3, FLAC, Vorbis, Opus, Speex, AC3, and DTS. Custom FFmpeg filters are also supported for advanced processing.

### Does it support hardware-accelerated GPU decoding?

Yes. The filter supports NVIDIA NVDEC, Intel Quick Sync Video, and AMD VCE hardware-accelerated decoding. GPU decoding is enabled by default and reduces CPU usage by 70–90%, enabling efficient 4K and 8K video playback. The filter automatically falls back to software decoding when hardware acceleration is unavailable.

### Can I play network streams and IP cameras?

Yes. The filter supports HTTP, HTTPS, RTSP, RTMP, HLS, UDP/RTP, and SRT streaming protocols. You can play live streams from IP cameras, media servers, and streaming services by passing the stream URL to the filter's IFileSourceFilter::Load method. Configurable connection timeouts, buffering strategies, and RTSP transport options (TCP/UDP) are available.

### Which programming languages are supported?

The filter provides APIs for C# (.NET Framework 4.0+ and .NET 5+), VB.NET, C++, and Delphi. For .NET developers, the VisioForge.DirectShowAPI NuGet package provides strongly-typed interfaces and COM interop wrappers. C++ developers can use the native DirectShow interfaces directly. Demo applications with full source code are included for all supported languages.

### Which Windows versions are compatible?

The filter runs on Windows 7, Windows 8/8.1, Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server 2016 and later. Both 32-bit (x86) and 64-bit (x64) architectures are supported. The filter integrates with any DirectShow-based application and is compatible with GraphEdit and GraphStudioNext for visual testing.

### How does it compare to the VLC Source DirectShow Filter?

Both filters serve as universal media decoders for DirectShow applications. The FFmpeg Source Filter is built on FFmpeg and offers 200+ format support, frame-accurate seeking, custom FFmpeg filter pipelines, and professional formats like ProRes and DNxHD. The VLC Source Filter is built on libVLC and provides a different decoding engine. Choose based on your format requirements, performance needs, and whether you need advanced FFmpeg filter capabilities.

### Using VLC Source Filter with GraphEdit

GraphEdit is Microsoft's DirectShow graph visualization and debugging tool that provides DirectShow graph editing capabilities. The VLC Source DirectShow Filter integrates seamlessly with GraphEdit for rapid prototyping and testing.

#### Setting Up VLC Source in GraphEdit

1.  1.

    **Launch GraphEdit:** Start GraphEdit with administrator privileges for full filter registration access

2.  2.

    **Insert VLC Source Filter:**

    -   • Right-click in the graph area
    -   • Select "Insert Filters..."
    -   • Navigate to "DirectShow Filters" category
    -   • Locate "VLC Source" filter
    -   • Click "Insert Filter"

3.  3.

    **Configure Media Source:**

    -   • Right-click the VLC Source filter
    -   • Select "Properties"
    -   • In the file dialog, specify your media file path or network URL
    -   • The filter accepts local files (C:\\media\\video.mp4) and network streams (http://example.com/stream.m3u8)

4.  4.

    **Add Renderers:**

    -   • For video: Insert "Enhanced Video Renderer (EVR)" or "Video Mixing Renderer 9 (VMR-9)"
    -   • For audio: Insert "Default DirectSound Device" or "Audio Renderer (WaveOut)"

5.  5.

    **Connect Pins:**

    -   • Drag from VLC Source video output pin to video renderer input pin
    -   • Drag from VLC Source audio output pin to audio renderer input pin
    -   • GraphEdit will automatically negotiate media types

### Using VLC Source Filter with GraphStudio

GraphStudio provides an alternative DirectShow graph editing environment with advanced debugging features and comprehensive filter analysis tools.

#### GraphStudio Integration Steps

1.  1.

    **Filter Registration Verification:**

    -   • Open GraphStudio
    -   • Navigate to "View" → "Filters" tab
    -   • Verify "VLC Source" appears in the registered filters list
    -   • Note the filter's CLSID: `{77493EB7-6D00-41C5-9535-7C593824E892}`

2.  2.

    **Creating Filter Graph:**

    -   • Use "Insert Filter" button or drag from filters panel
    -   • Locate VLC Source under DirectShow filters category
    -   • Drag VLC Source to graph workspace

3.  3.

    **Media Configuration:**

    -   • Right-click VLC Source → "Load File..."
    -   • Browse to media file or enter network URL
    -   • GraphStudio displays real-time connection status

4.  4.

    **Automatic Graph Building:**

    -   • Use GraphStudio's "Render" feature
    -   • Right-click VLC Source output pins → "Render Pin"
    -   • GraphStudio automatically inserts appropriate decoders and renderers

VLC Source Filter configured in GraphStudio with connected video and audio renderers

**Pro Tip:** GraphStudio provides superior debugging capabilities with real-time media type inspection, pin property analysis, and filter performance monitoring, making it ideal for professional DirectShow development.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the VLC Source DirectShow Filter?

The VLC Source DirectShow Filter is a software component that integrates VLC media player's decoding engine into the Windows DirectShow multimedia framework. It acts as a source filter in a DirectShow filter graph, enabling any DirectShow-compatible application to play over 100 video and audio formats — including MKV, WebM, HEVC, VP9, AV1, and network streams — without installing additional codec packs.

### What media formats and codecs are supported?

The filter supports all formats available in libVLC, including containers like MP4, AVI, MKV, WebM, MPEG-TS, MOV, FLV, and OGG. Video codecs include H.264, H.265/HEVC, VP8, VP9, AV1, MPEG-1/2/4, DivX, and Theora. Audio codecs include AAC, MP3, FLAC, Vorbis, Opus, AC3, DTS, and WMA. Network protocols such as RTSP, HTTP/HTTPS, HLS, DASH, RTMP, UDP, and SRT are also supported.

### Can I use it to play network streams and IP cameras?

Yes. The filter supports RTSP, RTP, HTTP, HTTPS, HLS, DASH, RTMP, UDP multicast/unicast, MMS, and SRT protocols. You can play live streams from IP cameras, media servers, and streaming services by passing the stream URL to the filter's IFileSourceFilter::Load method, just as you would a local file path.

### Which programming languages and environments are supported?

The filter provides native COM interfaces accessible from C++, C# (.NET Framework 4.0+ and .NET 5+), VB.NET, and Delphi. For .NET developers, interface definitions are available via the VisioForge.DirectShowAPI NuGet package. C++ developers can use the ivlcsrc.h header file from our GitHub repository. It works with Visual Studio 2010–2022 and C++ Builder XE2+.

### Does the filter support hardware-accelerated GPU decoding?

Yes. The filter supports DXVA2 (Windows native), NVIDIA NVDEC, Intel Quick Sync Video, AMD VCE hardware acceleration. GPU decoding can reduce CPU usage by 70–90%, enabling efficient 4K and 8K video playback and allowing multiple simultaneous decoded streams with minimal system load.

### Which Windows versions are compatible?

The filter runs on Windows 7 SP1, Windows 8/8.1, Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server 2016 and later. Both 32-bit (x86) and 64-bit (x64) architectures are supported, including mixed-mode applications and COM-compatible environments.

### What are the differences between the trial and commercial versions?

The trial version is fully functional with no API restrictions for 30 days and may display a watermark or an unregistered notice. Paid licenses include royalty-free distribution rights and email support. Annual licenses include 12 months of updates; Lifetime·Team licenses include minor and major updates for the product lifetime.

### How do I switch audio tracks and subtitles at runtime?

Use the IVlcSrc COM interface to manage audio and subtitle tracks. Call GetAudioTracksCount and GetAudioTrackInfo to enumerate available audio streams, then SetAudioTrack to switch. Similarly, use GetSubtitlesCount, GetSubtitleInfo, and SetSubtitle to control subtitles. Pass -1 to SetSubtitle to disable subtitles entirely.
